article_title: Lectura Proactiva/ Intervenciones tempranas de la lectura
citation: Lectura Proactiva (Intervenciones tempranas de la lectura) — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program summary, no author line printed. https://www.evidenceforesight.org/
title: Deliver Lectura Proactiva with extensive professional development and coaching, since the same level of PD is essential to expect positive outcomes
description: The article states that in its successful evaluations the intervention was delivered by bilingual certified teachers who “received extensive professional development and coaching from the developers,” specifically 18 hours of professional development plus frequent staff development sessions and coaching. It concludes that “The same level of PD is essential to expect positive outcomes,” making implementation fidelity through training a condition of effectiveness.
requirements: Bilingual certified teachers as interventionists
18 hours of professional development plus frequent staff development sessions and coaching from the developers
constraints: Positive outcomes should not be expected without the same level of professional development
target_learners: Spanish-speaking early readers in elementary grades
target_learning_goals: Accelerating the transition to reading in English
examples: In the research schools, intervention teachers received 18 hours of professional development, in addition to frequent staff development sessions and coaching.
key_sources: Lectura Proactiva (Intervenciones tempranas de la lectura) — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program summary, no author line printed. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/lectura-proactiva-intervenciones-tempranas-de-la-lectura/

article_title: Use of Evidence to Drive Decision-Making in Government
citation: Julieta Lugo-Gil, Dana Jean-Baptiste, Livia Frasso Jaramillo. (2019). Use of Evidence to Drive Decision-Making in Government. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Leadership support and staff buy-in are needed for evidence use in government decision-making
description: This principle holds that government agencies seeking to use evidence in program and policy decisions need leaders who actively promote evidence use and staff who accept and support that practice. Interview respondents identified "having leadership that supports and promotes the use of evidence and buy-in from the organization's staff" as a factor facilitating evidence use. It complements related facilitators such as collaborative relationships and trust in the evidence researchers produce.
requirements: Leadership that supports and promotes the use of evidence
Buy-in from the organization's staff
target_learners: Government leaders and staff in agencies making program or policy decisions
target_learning_goals: Using research evidence to inform decisions
examples: Phase 2 interview respondents named leadership support and organizational buy-in among factors facilitating evidence use in government.
key_sources: Julieta Lugo-Gil, Dana Jean-Baptiste, Livia Frasso Jaramillo. (2019). Use of Evidence to Drive Decision-Making in Government. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/use-of-evidence-to-drive-decision-making-in-government

article_title: Effects of Scenario-Based Assessment on Students' Writing Processes
citation: Hongwen Guo, Mo Zhang, Paul Deane, Randy E. Bennett. (2020). Effects of Scenario-Based Assessment on Students’ Writing Processes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 12, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/
title: Place lead-in tasks before the essay in a single-scenario design to reduce working-memory load during writing
description: The article’s theoretically motivated scenario-based design presents a topical scenario with source materials, then lead-in tasks (reading, summarizing, critiquing, analyzing arguments) before the essay. The authors conclude that “the original single-scenario & essay-last form with the theoretically motivated assessment design may have reduced students’ working memory load while they planned and reviewed their essays,” yielding more efficient and fluent text production and freeing attention for monitoring and revising text. The design simulates a condensed writing project in the order a skilled practitioner might follow.
requirements: A single coherent scenario shared by lead-in tasks and the essay; lead-in tasks that engage students with the sources and activate needed skills
constraints: The benefit was observed for the single-scenario design; a mixed-scenario essay-last design lowered scores, possibly via added working-memory load and reduced motivation; the authors note results may not generalize to broader populations or different conditions
target_learners: Middle-school (eighth-grade) students writing argumentative essays from sources
target_learning_goals: Argumentative writing from sources
Efficient and fluent text production
Self-monitoring and revision of text
examples: Students randomly assigned within classrooms to four test forms; the essay-last single-scenario group produced essays of similar quality in less time with fewer words than essay-first students
key_sources: Hongwen Guo, Mo Zhang, Paul Deane, Randy E. Bennett. (2020). Effects of Scenario-Based Assessment on Students’ Writing Processes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 12, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/443

article_title: Illuminating the Mechanisms of Character Development
citation: Key Questions: How might learning environments "build character" in children and youth?. (2017). Journal of Character Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Theorize character-education mechanisms by leveraging theory and empirical work from other disciplines
description: Because program evaluations and extant character-development studies make identifying promising practices difficult, the article recommends a more thorough use of theoretical and empirical work from other disciplines. It suggests "a more thorough leveraging of both theoretical work and empirical studies in other disciplines (e.g., neuroscience, cognitive science, social psychology, developmental psychology, sociology, philosophy) to theorize about potential mechanisms whereby school practices develop character."
requirements: Access to theoretical and empirical literatures from neuroscience, cognitive science, social psychology, developmental psychology, sociology, and philosophy
target_learners: children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: character development
examples: The author applies this approach by using the Foundations for Young Adult Success framework to propose ten developmental experiences as mechanisms
key_sources: Key Questions: How might learning environments "build character" in children and youth?. (2017). Journal of Character Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: The instructional legacy of COVID-19: Teacher adaptation in response to the pandemic
citation: Connolly, H., Abowd, N., & Chase, C. C. (2022). The instructional legacy of COVID-19: Teacher adaptation in response to the pandemic. Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences – ICLS 2022. https://www.isls.org
title: Treat periods of forced instructional change as opportunities to foster teacher adaptation and transfer of new practices
description: Because the pandemic transition to distance learning led most surveyed teachers to plan transfer of what they learned to in-person teaching, and 30% to plan transformative practices, the article supports treating disruptive change as a lever for professional growth rather than only a disruption to manage. The authors state that "One positive outcome of the pandemic is that it promoted teacher adaptation."
requirements: Teachers must experience a substantial change in teaching conditions that requires adaptation, and their learning during that period should be surfaced and supported
constraints: Evidence comes from a single Spring 2020 survey of 71 K-8 teachers reporting planned, not observed, future practice
target_learners: K-8 teachers
target_learning_goals: Developing adaptive teaching practices that persist beyond the disruptive episode
examples: The study surveyed 71 K-8 teachers during the sudden 2020 shift to distance learning and found most planned to transfer their learning to future in-person teaching
key_sources: Connolly, H., Abowd, N., & Chase, C. C. (2022). The instructional legacy of COVID-19: Teacher adaptation in response to the pandemic. Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences – ICLS 2022. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-instructional-legacy-of-covid-19-teacher-adaptation-in-response-to-the-pandemic/

article_title: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Design multiple modes of learner-instructor communication available outside class time and on demand
description: The brief's fourth principle is facilitating frequent communication between instructor and learner, because adult learners have a particularly strong need for connection with and encouragement from their teachers given the barriers and weaker skills they face. Technology can provide reflective activities (blogs, emails, videos), regular feedback (emails, discussion threads, videos), office-hour chats, and anytime communication so learners can reach instructors when they need support between life commitments.
requirements: Communication tools must allow learners to contact instructors when they need to, not just during class meetings
Multiple communication modes should be built in
target_learners: adult basic learners
adult English language learners
target_learning_goals: learner confidence
persistence and progress in learning
examples: myPLACE instructors contact students via personal emails, discussion boards, LMS messages, and global announcements; CyberESL students have weekly one-on-one Skype coaching sessions for individualized instruction and practice
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Support and Scaffolding. (2016). Digital Promise, Accelerating Change. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0b18a16a-2f1d-400b-9fed-df5675ba40cf

article_title: Computational Thinking for an Inclusive World: A Resource for Educators to Learn and Lead, Quick Start and Discussion Guide
citation: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead, Quick start and discussion guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/140
title: District and school leaders must build shared leadership and professional learning capacity to scale computational thinking integration
description: The guide argues that integrating computational thinking into every classroom cannot be left to individual educators; leaders at district and school levels must prioritize the initiative and build teacher capacity. It notes that strong CT examples often exist in isolated pockets but are rarely consistent across classrooms or schools, which yields fewer and less robust opportunities for students experiencing marginalization. The guide states that "In order to scale and sustain computational thinking integration within districts and schools, educators must promote shared leadership between districts and schools and designing professional learning experiences for pre- and in-service teachers."
requirements: Shared leadership between districts and schools and professional learning experiences for pre- and in-service teachers
constraints: Pockets of strong CT integration within districts often leave students experiencing marginalization with fewer and less robust computing learning opportunities
target_learners: K-12 students district-wide, especially those experiencing marginalization
target_learning_goals: Equitable, sustained access to computational thinking learning opportunities
examples: The guide poses reflection prompts asking educators how to engage teacher, school and district leaders to build capacity for computational thinking
key_sources: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead, Quick start and discussion guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/140

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Leverage DLP process data on user behavior to address analytic questions and measure intermediate outcomes
description: The report urges researchers to use the robust log data DLPs generate, such as which tasks students begin, time spent, and detailed progress. Such data can reveal attrition or compliance indirectly and "may serve as a measure of important intermediate outcomes, or mediators, that are often very difficult to collect in conventional research settings." Researchers unfamiliar with log data should work with platform teams and review codebooks and data dictionaries.
requirements: Working with the platform team to understand how users interact with the system to generate the desired log data; reviewing codebooks and data dictionaries from prior studies
constraints: Researchers are not always provided direct information on attrition or compliance; platforms vary in ability to create or add instruments for more distal outcomes
target_learners: Education researchers, particularly those trained in conventional classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Measuring engagement, progress, and mediating processes during learning
examples: Time stamps of activities such as reading a prompt or attempting to solve a problem allow identifying students who stopped participating or skipped certain materials
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: Market Signals for Research-Based Innovations
citation: Sierra Noakes. (2019). Market Signals for Research-Based Innovations. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/
title: Incorporate learning sciences research findings into edtech design and development to serve the full spectrum of learners
description: The report argues that because advances in learning sciences show how people learn and that people learn differently, developers who incorporate learning sciences research findings can create powerful learning experiences for the full spectrum of learners. It states research-driven edtech can meet this potential by "attending to the most difficult content to teach and learn; creating opportunities for differentiation; and providing guidance to support seamless implementation."
requirements: Developers must actually use learning sciences research findings in product design and development
constraints: Without established standards or clear signals, the report says it is challenging to demand that developers attend to authentic learner needs through research incorporation
target_learners: edtech product developers
the full spectrum of learners, including marginalized learner populations
target_learning_goals: equitable, high-quality learning opportunities and experiences for every learner
examples: Digital Promise's 2017 work with two districts piloting edtech for English Learners found few products are designed for marginalized learner populations
key_sources: Sierra Noakes. (2019). Market Signals for Research-Based Innovations. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/7c36b6fa-e221-437f-92d5-f4d3a89c0a1f

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Use inclusive language and design in LER onboarding
description: This principle holds that LER onboarding should welcome users regardless of age, technological familiarity, or pathway shape. The report states that "LERs should reduce assumptions about linear career pathways so as not to invalidate the lived experiences of learners and workers," and recommends offering opportunities to elevate skills developed through community, cultural, and caregiving contexts. It also suggests querying learners' goals up front so prompts can be tailored to individual journeys.
requirements: Onboarding prompts must allow users to showcase a wide variety of skills and experiences, including contexts outside formal institutions
constraints: Onboarding prompts limited to transcripts and employment history may inadvertently exclude important aspects of skills and background
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded adult learners and workers, including multilingual learners and those experiencing poverty
target_learning_goals: successful onboarding and adoption of learning and employment record technology
examples: Workshop participants asked to change "work" experience to just "experience" and requested adding military credentials and cultural identity as skills
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Make the LER value proposition clear to learners and employers
description: This principle directs LER vendors to articulate, in plain language, why a learner should create an interoperable learner record and how employers and education institutions derive value from the data. The report found that "Many participants expressed confusion between LERs and LinkedIn, Indeed, and services like TopResume because the purpose of the LER was not immediately clear." It recommends embedding LER education in onboarding, using video, static visuals, plain-language text, and inline tips throughout the process.
requirements: Product descriptions must clearly differentiate LERs from social networking and resume-building tools
The value proposition for employers and education institutions must be articulated so learners understand how their data may be used
constraints: Value revealed only after completion is limited: outcomes like matched positions "were not apparent at the beginning of the journey"
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded adult learners and workers onboarding to LER technology
target_learning_goals: understanding the purpose and value of LERs and the tradeoffs of contributing personal data
examples: Participants suggested adding a "why" section in build prompts to explain things to people
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Communicate and create resources to ensure data integration accuracy
description: This principle requires that information auto-populated from third parties be correct and thorough, that users can edit it, and that vendors communicate where data comes from. The report states that "data integrations that populate incorrect or incomplete information without a mechanism for learners to correct the errors breeds frustration," and proposes a way to report inaccuracies and request edits without jeopardizing verification integrity, plus troubleshooting information and FAQs for broken or delayed integrations.
requirements: A mechanism for learners to report inaccuracies and request edits
Transparent communication about where the tool pulls information from
constraints: The value of a single, reliable, cumulative learning record depends on the accuracy of third-party data pulls
target_learners: adult learners and workers onboarding to LERs with integrated postsecondary transcripts
target_learning_goals: trusting and accurately representing skills and credentials in a learning and employment record
examples: A participant whose newly earned associate's degree was missing and bachelor's degree shown as completed could not edit the record
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Offer technology and content support during LER onboarding
description: This principle calls for live support options, examples and encouragement during profile creation, and explicit explanation of why different data types are required and when alternatives exist. The report observes that "Not all learners onboarding to LERs will have extensive digital or career navigation skills," and that some participants got stuck at login or were leery about which data were required versus optional, especially those with past extractive or exploitive experiences with technology.
requirements: Live support options for login and onboarding assistance
Explicit statements of how each step ensures safety and security and why sharing personal information is advantageous
constraints: Participants varied widely in digital literacy; chatbots may not suffice for those who do not know which questions to ask
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded adult learners and workers with limited digital literacy
target_learning_goals: completing LER account creation and onboarding independently
examples: Participants reported difficulty verifying email and phone and forgetting user IDs; one said a person to talk to would have helped where a chatbot would not
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records
citation: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194
title: Conduct ongoing user testing for continuous improvement of LERs
description: This principle directs vendors to iteratively solicit feedback from employers and end users, including people unaffiliated with institutions or on nonlinear journeys, to share timely updates on platform changes, and to provide an accessible in-platform space for suggestions. The report states that "Collecting user feedback is necessary for attaining buy-in and developing trust across demographics, especially for HSE communities," and that iterative testing signals the technology is of value and values its users, fostering intuitive onboarding and retention.
requirements: Iterative feedback collection from both employers and end users
An accessible space on the platform for users to share suggestions at any time
constraints: Targeted feedback on accessibility of language, design, and technology support is needed because HSE learners are disproportionately impacted by limited access to digital resources and skills training
target_learners: historically and systematically excluded learners and workers, including those with nonlinear journeys
target_learning_goals: sustained adoption and use of LER technology
examples: Participants reported limited skill and industry options, which vendors could use to build a more robust and accurate data library
key_sources: Hodge, M., Shah, Z., Patterson, M., Luke Luna, C. (2023, September). Onboarding and Education Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/194

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Give adult learners control over pace and support self-directed goal setting, planning, and monitoring
description: Self-directed learning theory posits that adults "can and should be active participants in their own learning." The report recommends pace control — replaying video, more practice, choosing order, anytime access — plus goal setting, planning, and progress monitoring, since students who do these "are more likely to persist in learning and ultimately achieve positive outcomes."
requirements: Offer self-assessments such as pre-tests "so students understand what they know and what they need to learn," plus tools for planning and goal setting.
constraints: Low-skilled learners "often struggle with these tasks because they lack confidence in their learning" and need help and guidance to develop goal-setting, planning, and persisting skills.
target_learners: low-skilled adult learners
adult literacy and language learners using mobile programs
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills
persistence and program completion
examples: Cell-Ed lets students choose when to call in for short lessons and when to text-practice, and "has found that students are completing lessons at a faster pace than they would in a traditional classroom"; myPlace Online guides learners through creating their own learning plans, with directors reporting increased retention and completion.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Computational Thinking for an Inclusive World: A Resource for Educators to Learn and Lead
citation: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/138
title: Educational leaders must prioritize CT integration and build teacher capacity; it cannot be left to individual educators
description: The report frames system-level leadership as a precondition for inclusive CT integration: "Integrating computational thinking into every classroom is not something that can be left to individual educators." It calls for educational leaders at district and school levels to prioritize the initiative and build capacity for teachers, elaborated as three leadership strategies: promoting shared leadership among districts, schools and teachers; developing sustained, individualized professional learning opportunities; and integrating CT into pre-service teacher education. The report also notes that CT mostly exists as optional content with no formal assessment, making it hard for educators to prioritize against tested subjects.
requirements: District, school, and teacher leaders must prioritize the initiative and develop systems of professional learning for integrating CT and addressing inclusivity challenges
constraints: The report notes computational thinking mostly exists as optional content with no formal assessment, so tested subjects receive priority
target_learners: K-12 students served by district and school computing initiatives
target_learning_goals: scaled and sustained inclusive computational thinking integration across classrooms
examples: The report describes developing sustained, individualized professional learning opportunities and integrating CT into pre-service teacher education as capacity strategies
key_sources: Mills, K., Coenraad, M., Ruiz, P., Burke, Q., & Weisgrau J. (2021, December). Computational thinking for an inclusive world: A resource for educators to learn and lead. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/138

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Learning theories should drive the design and evaluation of emerging learning technologies
description: The report argues that theories about how people learn should drive the design of emerging technologies, their implementation, and the metrics used to evaluate efficacy. It cites traditions including Dewey's experiential learning, Piaget's constructivism, Vygotsky's social constructivism, Bandura's social cognitive theory, and Papert's constructionism, which 'mutually reinforce that learning is actively constructed based on experiences and in connection with other humans.' Technology adopting these lenses should promote learner agency, open-ended problems, and human connection.
requirements: Developers consult a multidisciplinary team including learning scientists with technological, pedagogical, and content-area expertise
target_learners: all learners using emerging technology tools
target_learning_goals: subject-area learning grounded in research-based instructional models
examples: The report points to concrete-to-representational-to-abstract sequencing in math and science-of-reading frameworks in literacy as research-based models developers can apply
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Measure edtech efficacy with learning outcomes data, not satisfaction or engagement alone
description: The report recommends that efficacy of learning tools be measured by learning outcomes data, prioritizing research-validated assessments for their demonstrated validity and reliability, supplemented by formative or platform performance data. It warns that 'using satisfaction and usability data in isolation can give misleading perspectives on learner benefit,' and that behavioral measures like logins and time on platform are only proxies. Other data sources should be used in conjunction with validated assessments for a comprehensive understanding.
requirements: Measures must be directly tied to theory and evidence about learning
constraints: Research-validated assessments can be difficult to access or slow to return results
target_learners: learners using emerging technology tools in classrooms and at home
target_learning_goals: demonstrated understanding, application, or transfer of skills or knowledge
examples: The report describes ESSA Tiers of Evidence as a guide for developers choosing study designs matching their research questions and resources
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: A Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Pattenhouse, M.*, Noakes, S.*, Mills, K., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025, November). Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/275
title: Learner-centered design: promote agency, foster metacognition, and enable accessibility
description: The framework's Learner-Centered principle holds that emerging technology tools "can realize learner variability, helping all students reach their full potential, when they promote agency, foster metacognition and when developers enable accessibility." Practices include personalizing for learners, making learning relevant, grounding in purpose, enabling productive struggle, providing reflection opportunities, assistive technologies, multimodality, and translanguaging, each with safety spotlights on privacy, explainability, and fairness.
requirements: Tools must promote agency, foster metacognition, and enable accessibility to realize learner variability
constraints: Safety spotlights note privacy, explainability, and fairness must be addressed within each practice
target_learners: All learners, including multilingual learners and learners with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Learner agency, metacognition, and equitable access to learning
examples: Strategies include allowing users to opt out of adaptive AI features and aligning content with learners' funds of knowledge
key_sources: Pattenhouse, M.*, Noakes, S.*, Mills, K., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025, November). Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/275

article_title: Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges
citation: Nan L. Maxwell and Ann E. Person, editors. (2016). Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Successful comprehensive reform requires executive leadership complemented by strong faculty involvement, guided by an explicit and shared vision for student success
description: Across the volume's chapters, the editors report that "a few components emerge as critical for the success of comprehensive reform efforts, in particular, executive leadership complemented by strong faculty involvement, guided by an explicit and shared vision for success." This principle directs reform designers to pair top-level leadership with faculty engagement around a common vision.
requirements: An explicit and shared vision for student success must guide the reform
target_learners: community college students
target_learning_goals: improved student success outcomes
examples: The editors synthesized this component from the original analyses presented across the volume's chapters
key_sources: Nan L. Maxwell and Ann E. Person, editors. (2016). Comprehensive Reform for 21st Century Success: New Directions for Community Colleges. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/comprehensive-reform-for-21st-century-success-new-directions-for-community-colleges

article_title: The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools
citation: Zohal Shah, Marilys Galindo, Chioma Aso-Hernandez, Christina Luke Luna, Keun-woo Lee, Josh Weisgrau, Teresa Solorzano, Britney Jacobs. (2024). The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Learning and Employment Record (LER) technologies and digital wallets
description: LER technologies digitally store, share, and collect records of a person's learning and employment, documenting learning wherever it occurs — education, workplace, credentialing, or military training. Their infrastructure is based on interoperability, giving learners transparent, secure records and the ability to curate profiles and control what is shared with employers and institutions. Examples include North Dakota's digital wallets for high school students, which allow sharing "digitally verifiable transcripts, diplomas, and other credentials with any employer or institution," and Canada's MyCreds credential wallet.
requirements: Interoperability standards and governance approaches
Long-term access to learning records at no additional cost after learners leave issuing institutions
constraints: Risk of compromising user data privacy without adequate protection; verifiable technical skills may take priority over durable skills in matching
target_learners: K-12 students, postsecondary learners, and workers
target_learning_goals: Documenting, verifying, and transmitting skills and qualifications across education and employment contexts
examples: North Dakota was the first state to launch digital wallets for high school students; MyCreds launched in Canada for secure credential storage and transfer.
key_sources: Zohal Shah, Marilys Galindo, Chioma Aso-Hernandez, Christina Luke Luna, Keun-woo Lee, Josh Weisgrau, Teresa Solorzano, Britney Jacobs. (2024). The Promise of Micro-credentials and Learning and Employment Record Technologies for Youth and K-12 Schools. article_title: Leveraging Community Cultural Wealth to Support K-8 CT Education in Kentucky Appalachia

description: The article advocates culturally responsive CS/CT education in which local assets and computing education are mutually reinforcing. It states the panel "will share how CS/CT education and Appalachian community cultural wealth mutually reinforce one another," and that the project's team continuously attends to strengthening local vision, goals, priorities and processes rather than importing an external program.

article_title: Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career
citation: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244
title: Learning and Employment Record (LER) technologies as learner-curated lifelong skill portfolios
description: The report describes Learning and Employment Record technologies, sometimes called wallets, as records that 'enable learners to track and document their skills development across different contexts, from school to the workplace'. They are digital portfolios curated by learners, serving as repositories of competencies that transfer across disciplines, careers, and life experiences. The report recommends K-12 learners practice stewarding their own learning data and tailoring what they share with different audiences.

learner practice composing and tailoring a portfolio of achievements
constraints: Realizing the vision requires new models and systems of assessment co-designed inclusively across workforce, postsecondary, learners, educators, and researchers
target_learners: K-12 learners
postsecondary students
job seekers
target_learning_goals: documenting and showcasing transferable skills
learner agency over learning data
examples: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation's T3 Innovation Network, launched in 2018, works on data interoperability so credentials and LER technologies can make job-market information shareable

description: Through the district's Learn.Plan.Succeed. (LPS) initiative, students track their completion of college and career exploration and preparation milestones via an Individualized Learning Plan (ILP). The report states the district has established software, curricula, and advising frameworks to monitor and support LPS, making it a promising system for organizing college and career advising across students over time. LPS requires students to select one of six postsecondary pathways by grade 12 and provide evidence of their plan to graduate.

college and career exploration

article_title: Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Establish a learning culture that frames mistakes as improvement and uses data for inquiry rather than penalizing teachers
description: Because teachers will likely make mistakes while adjusting their practices as they learn CRSE, the brief urges leaders to examine how accountability structures affect teachers' willingness to adopt it. It notes that policies penalizing low standardized-test performance may encourage teaching to the test, leaving little room for experimentation. Leaders should frame learning from mistakes as a step toward improvement, clarify that data gathering supports inquiry rather than assessment or penalty, and create internal structures where experienced CRSE teachers coach colleagues.
requirements: Leaders must clarify that data such as test scores or climate survey results are gathered to support inquiry and learning rather than to assess or penalize teachers and students
constraints: Accountability policies that penalize low test performance may undermine teachers' willingness to experiment with CRSE practices
target_learners: K-12 mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: Sustained adoption of culturally responsive and sustaining instructional practices
examples: The brief suggests giving teachers more experienced with CRSE designated additional planning time to coach less experienced colleagues
key_sources: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673516

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Learning goals and success criteria open the formative assessment process and represent disciplinary practices including language
description: The brief positions learning goals and success criteria as "the first part of the formative assessment process." Learning goals articulate what students are expected to know and do beyond what they can already do autonomously, and success criteria "outline how students will demonstrate that they have met the learning goal and indicate an observable action." Teachers of English learners include the language required to engage in disciplinary content in these goals, and use success criteria as look-fors and listen-fors to interpret evidence during lessons.
requirements: Teachers ground goals and criteria in knowledge of disciplinary learning progressions, language patterns of analytic practices, student assets, and students' current language and content learning
target_learners: English learners across grade levels
target_learning_goals: Content, analytic-practice, and language-focused learning goals
examples: An early elementary science lesson on plants includes the success criterion of using linking words like 'because' and 'then' to explain how plant parts work together

article_title: Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception
citation: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org/
title: Learner variability as a universal characteristic embracing both struggling and thriving learners
description: The paper defines learner variability as a term describing all students, not only those with identified learning differences. It states that learner variability "embraces both students who struggle and those who thrive" because of natural variability in each person. Variability includes poverty, English learners, trauma, stereotype threat, working memory and attention challenges, and advanced learners who are bored by one-size-fits-all instruction.
requirements: Recognition that all students differ, grounded in learning sciences research showing these differences matter for learning
constraints: The paper notes the term is sometimes tightly defined to mean only struggling students, but rejects that narrower usage
target_learners: all K-12 learners, including students who struggle and those who thrive
target_learning_goals: understanding and addressing individual differences to support confident learning in school and beyond
examples: The paper illustrates variability with the student who already excels beyond the curriculum pace and is bored, and the learner with working memory or decoding challenges who retreats into silence
key_sources: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b7b14506-0b46-4279-9f9e-675c694b06a6

article_title: Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity
citation: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185
title: Seven co-designed Learning Transition Design Principles for LER technologies
description: The report's central artifact is a set of seven design principles stating that LER technology should: connect people to supports; connect people to opportunities; include indicators of skills and learning; be inclusive of people's identity, movement, and language; empower people with skills-based practices; adopt a comprehensive approach to digital credentialing; and integrate with a variety of tools. "Together, 31 learners and workers from HSE communities co-designed seven learning transition design principles to guide the further development of LERs and associated LER technologies." The principles complement existing Inclusive Design and Interoperable Design Principles by focusing on the value and usefulness of LERs during transitions, and serve both as design guidance and as evaluation criteria for existing designs.
requirements: Design and development with (not for) HSE learners and workers, so context expertise informs the technology
constraints: The principles focus on value and usefulness during learning transitions and do not replace principles addressing ease of use, access, and data/tech design
target_learners: HSE adult learners and workers, including those experiencing poverty and multilingual learners
target_learning_goals: sharing and accessing skills data to pursue education, career, and life opportunities during transitions
examples: Principle 1 states LER technologies should, with user consent, match people to supporters, mentors and counselors, and career networking services
key_sources: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., and Shah, Z., (2023, July). Learning Transition Design Principles for Learning and Employment Records: Co-designing for Equity. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/185

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should foster shared understanding of what formative assessment is and is not
description: The brief recommends that leaders develop deep knowledge of formative assessment — "what it looks like in the classroom, how it differs from current instructional practice, how to distinguish it from 'just good teaching,' and how to address persistent misinterpretations." Because implementation "is not a simple matter of adhering to a prescribed set of activities" but requires internalizing new principles, leaders who succeeded immersed themselves in learning, developed an anchor definition, and addressed misconceptions as they arose.
requirements: Leaders need deep knowledge of formative assessment and its grounding principles before fostering others' understanding
constraints: Teachers must internalize new principles and examine personal beliefs, so extensive leadership support is needed
target_learners: school leaders and leadership teams
target_learning_goals: building shared staff understanding of formative assessment practice
examples: Observed leaders developed a definition of formative assessment that served as an anchor for teachers and developed routines to visit classrooms and notice emerging practices
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should communicate a compelling vision highlighting changes in the student role
description: The brief states that a "compelling vision of formative assessment — what it is, what it looks like in practice, and why it is important — provides stakeholders with motivation and clarity." Leaders may frame the vision around metacognition, disciplinary knowledge and learner identity, or motivation and self-efficacy, all of which "contribute to supporting equity goals." When the vision becomes community-wide, "coherence and momentum around this work increase."
requirements: Vision must align with existing site goals and initiatives and be prioritized among competing expectations
constraints: Diverse viewpoints and misconceptions about learning exist across communities that the vision must address
target_learners: teachers, students, parents, and district stakeholders
target_learning_goals: mobilizing commitment to formative assessment implementation
examples: Observed leaders clarified what teachers would see more of and less of as students developed metacognition and agency, and met with superiors to validate formative assessment as a core improvement strategy
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should model an adult learning culture that mirrors formative assessment norms
description: The brief argues that formative assessment requires a classroom culture where students "take risks, show what they don't know, give and receive feedback, and learn from peers," and that teachers need the same supportive culture. Leaders must therefore "model an adult learning culture that moves away from a tight focus on accountability to building norms that give permission and encourage teachers to identify what they don't yet know," communicating that everyone is a learner.
requirements: Leaders must be transparent about their own learning and engage in inquiry together with teachers and students
constraints: Many schools' existing policies and norms reflect a compliance mindset that differs from the needed culture
target_learners: school leaders, teachers
target_learning_goals: building norms of risk-taking, feedback exchange, and evidence use among adults
examples: Observed leaders were transparent about their own learning related to formative assessment and provided feedback in ways that engender trust, respect, and empathy
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should apply change-management knowledge and align policies to sustain scaling
description: The brief states that leaders nurturing conditions for scaling should "learn and apply change management models to predict, notice, and respond to stages of individual and systems-level change," citing Coburn's Four Dimensions of Scale as an example. Because formative assessment is typically adopted by small groups of teachers adding others over years, teachers will be at very different stages. Leaders should also review and align building-level policies — "particularly grading and reporting policies, or required assessment practices" — that support or hinder the work.
requirements: Leaders need a range of models and strategies for guiding change and tolerance for messiness
constraints: At any given time, groups of teachers will be at very different stages of understanding; conflicting policies such as teacher evaluation forms can inhibit change
target_learners: school and district leaders managing multi-year implementation
target_learning_goals: sustaining and scaling formative assessment across a site
examples: During the How I Know Project, observed leaders aligned building-level policies to reduce conflicting expectations and supported revision of systems-level practices that inhibited change
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Sound Basic Education for All: An Action Plan for North Carolina
citation: WestEd, Learning Policy Institute, & Friday Institute for Educational Innovation at North Carolina State University. (2019). Sound Basic Education for All: An Action Plan for North Carolina. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The Leandro sound basic education framework: four constitutional components every North Carolina student is entitled to
description: The framework, affirmed unanimously by the Supreme Court of North Carolina in Leandro v. State (1997), defines a "sound basic education" as one providing at least four components: sufficient ability to read, write, and speak English and knowledge of fundamental mathematics and physical science; fundamental knowledge of geography, history, and basic economic and political systems for informed choices; and sufficient academic and vocational skills to engage in postsecondary education or training and to compete on an equal basis in further education or employment. The action plan uses this definition as the standard against which it assesses state compliance and organizes its recommendations across educators, leaders, funding, early childhood, and assessment and accountability.
requirements: State action must enable every student, including those at risk, an equal opportunity to obtain a sound basic education as defined in Leandro
constraints: The report notes the definition must enable students to function in a complex and rapidly changing society, so the bar for proficiency has been raised as standards were updated
target_learners: All North Carolina K-12 public school students, including at-risk students and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Foundational literacy and mathematics
Informed civic and economic decision-making
Readiness for postsecondary education, vocational training, and gainful employment
examples: Judge Lee's 2018 order charged the independent consultant with recommending actions to provide a competent, certified, well-trained teacher in every classroom, a well-trained competent principal in every school, and the resources necessary for an equal opportunity to a sound basic education
key_sources: WestEd, Learning Policy Institute, & Friday Institute for Educational Innovation at North Carolina State University. (2019). Sound Basic Education for All: An Action Plan for North Carolina. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606141

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection
citation: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.info
title: Leading indicators of distress versus lagging indicators of failure
description: The report distinguishes two kinds of school-quality signals. Indicators of distress are "characteristics that occur early in a school's decline suggesting a school that is struggling to achieve or maintain high levels of quality," while indicators of failure are "output data points that occur later in a school's decline to measure how a school performed." Distress indicators are harder to measure but easier to influence; failure indicators are easier to measure but require more substantive interventions.
requirements: Authorizer data collection systems capable of capturing early, harder-to-measure signals
constraints: Indicators of distress tend to be more difficult to measure than lagging indicators
target_learners: Charter school authorizers
target_learning_goals: Monitoring school quality and identifying struggling schools prior to failure
examples: The toolkit recommends focusing on research-based indicators of distress rather than just indicators of failure such as standardized test scores
key_sources: Aimee Evan, Hannah Sullivan, and Laura Groth (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616212

article_title: Acceptance of AI-Assisted English Language Learning Tools in Higher Education: Psychological Correlates Across Disciplinary and Proficiency Groups
citation: Wu J, Wang Y, He Y, Yin X, Chen F and Wan B (2026) Acceptance of AI-assisted English language learning tools in higher education: psychological correlates across disciplinary and proficiency groups. Front. Psychol. 17:1806457. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1806457
title: A learner-centered extension of TAM framing psychological resources, affective correlates, and contextual grouping variables alongside baseline acceptance constructs
description: The study retains the Technology Acceptance Model's baseline constructs — perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, and satisfaction — and adds learner-centered correlates rather than replacing TAM. As the article states, "the present study retains PU, PEOU, BI, and satisfaction as baseline acceptance-related constructs, while examining learning motivation, self-eﬃcacy, anxiety, and risk perception as theoretically informed or exploratory correlates." Motivation (self-determination theory) addresses the value dimension, self-efficacy (social cognitive theory) the capability dimension, while anxiety and risk perception are treated as affective and evaluative correlates whose direction remains an empirical question. Disciplinary affiliation and English proficiency serve as contextual grouping variables for mean-level and subgroup-specific analyses.
requirements: Cross-sectional survey measurement of the four acceptance constructs and the psychological correlates; the framework organizes regression-based association analyses rather than causal or mediation models.
constraints: The article states the framework "does not imply causal ordering, mediation, temporal sequencing, or process-based eﬀects" given the cross-sectional design.
target_learners: Non-English-major undergraduates in higher education English courses
target_learning_goals: Acceptance and sustained use of AI-assisted English language learning tools
examples: The framework was applied to survey data from 210 Chinese undergraduates, with full-sample adjusted regressions, mean-level group comparisons by discipline and CET-4 proficiency, and exploratory subgroup-specific regressions.
key_sources: Wu J, Wang Y, He Y, Yin X, Chen F and Wan B (2026) Acceptance of AI-assisted English language learning tools in higher education: psychological correlates across disciplinary and proficiency groups. Front. Psychol. 17:1806457. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1806457

article_title: AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High
citation: Misan Paul Etchie, Olutosin Taiwo. (2026). AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High School and Beyond. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07544
title: Learning-context personalization engine: mastery, spacing, and help-seeking signals guide when and how AI assistance is delivered
description: The article's learning-context modeling approach maintains student-level learning state to tailor support and sequencing. The engine 'aggregates signals such as mastery by concept, attempt history, time-on-task, spacing intervals, and help-seeking behavior', and on that basis determines when to recommend review, when to escalate to teacher attention, and what scaffolding type fits the student's current context. This operationalizes feedback, self-regulated help-seeking, and spaced-practice mechanism families from the learning sciences inside the LMS.
requirements: Item-level assessment so performance can be interpreted at the level of specific concepts and skills
Logging of attempts, revisions, hint usage, and AI interaction metadata
target_learners: Middle school students
target_learning_goals: Skill mastery and retention
Self-regulated learning and effective help-seeking
examples: Spaced review recommendations and reminders based on mastery history and time since last practice; escalation to teacher attention on sustained struggle
key_sources: Misan Paul Etchie, Olutosin Taiwo. (2026). AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High School and Beyond. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07544

article_title: A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching
citation: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632
title: Worked lesson-design capability task with a 0–9 scoring rubric for performance-based AI-TPACK measurement
description: A performance-based assessment instrument operationalising the capability construct: teachers design a short AI-integrated lesson segment and justify the role of AI. The exemplar prompt asks the teacher to "Design a 40-minute Grade 10 biology lesson segment on enzyme activity in which a generative AI tool is used to produce differentiated formative feedback on learners’ predictions about reaction rates." Responses are scored 0–3 per criterion on pedagogical alignment, justification quality, and verification and ethical safeguards (total 0–9, Table 2). The article recommends double-scoring a random 20% of responses with inter-rater agreement of at least κ = .70 before single-scoring.
requirements: Double-scoring of a random 20% of responses with inter-rater agreement of at least κ = .70 (or intraclass correlation of .75 for continuous rubric totals) as the acceptability threshold
Parallel exemplars for prompt-evaluation and content-validity tasks seeded with discipline-typical errors
constraints: Completion requires approximately 30–40 min in piloting
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers in teacher-education programmes
target_learning_goals: AI-integrated lesson design, output verification, and ethical safeguarding competence
examples: The article provides the Grade 10 biology enzyme-activity prompt and the three-criterion rubric in Table 2 as a worked exemplar of the first of four indicator types
key_sources: Mnguni L (2026) A Capability–Decision Model of teacher readiness for AI integration in teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1897632. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1897632

article_title: WIP: Bridging the Gap Between Instructional Design and Pedagogical Use: A Framework for Mathematics Educators
citation: Estefany Castillo Ventura, Javier Ulises Solis Lastra, Anarosa Alves Franco Brandão. (2026). WIP: Bridging the Gap Between Instructional Design and Pedagogical Use: A Framework for Mathematics Educators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20934
title: A five-level scale of learning-theory operationalization (L0 mention to L4 operational implementation)
description: To analyze the role of theory in studies of digital educational technologies, the article defines a scale distinguishing ways learning theories influence research, "ranging from simple conceptual mention to their implementation as functional components of educational technologies." The levels are L0 Mention (general reference without influence), L1 Justification, L2 Analytical use, L3 Design principles, and L4 Operational implementation as functional components of the system.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable by the role learning theories play in them, from mention to functional implementation
constraints: The article states the classification of the level of operationalization involves a degree of interpretation
target_learners: high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: analyzing how learning theories are used in digital educational technology research
examples: Applied in Table 2 to classify identified theories: APOS at L2, Kolb at L3, cognitive constructivism at L0–L1, sociocultural constructivism at L1 and L3, self-regulated learning at L3, among others.
key_sources: Estefany Castillo Ventura, Javier Ulises Solis Lastra, Anarosa Alves Franco Brandão. (2026). WIP: Bridging the Gap Between Instructional Design and Pedagogical Use: A Framework for Mathematics Educators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20934

article_title: The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth — a differentiated framework and testable propositions
citation: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070
title: Match the AI role to the cognitive-processing level: efficiency tool, scaffold, or dialog partner
description: The framework prescribes level-appropriate AI roles: at surface level AI reduces extraneous load as an efficiency tool; at intermediate level AI should function as a scaffold providing worked examples, guided prompts, and structured feedback, contingent on metacognitive scaffolds; at deep level "AI should function only as a dialog partner: a Socratic interlocutor that poses questions, offers counterarguments, and prompts the learner to justify, refine, and reflect on their reasoning, but does not perform the cognitive work itself". The principle follows from the claim that offloading germane processing impairs learning while offloading extraneous processing can benefit it.
requirements: At the intermediate level, effectiveness is contingent on metacognitive scaffolds—prompts that require learners to explain, elaborate on, or self-explain AI-generated content.
constraints: The article notes preliminary studies are consistent with Socratic dialog supporting deeper engagement but do not establish that a Socratic design is necessary or sufficient across domains.
target_learners: students at all educational levels using generative AI, with roles calibrated to developmental stage and prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: preserving germane cognitive processing and critical-thinking development during AI-integrated tasks
examples: The article cites Lee and Wu's (2025) 15-week randomized controlled trial in which a scaffolded ChatGPT system enhanced cognitive engagement compared with standard ChatGPT, but only when structured prompts guided learners through knowledge integration phases.
key_sources: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070

article_title: Profiling cognitive offloading in LLM-mediated synthesis writing: Volume vs. content
citation: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434
title: A Salomon-based dynamic interactionist framework for learner-LLM distributed cognitive systems
description: The article adapts Salomon's dynamic interactionist view of distributed cognition to learner-LLM systems, treating them as comprising "three elements of a distributed cognitive system: (1) individual cognition, (2) the activity that affords distribution, and (3) the distribution of the cognitive process between a learner and a tool". Individual cognition is represented by prior knowledge; the affording activity is comprehension, structured by Kintsch and van Dijk's micro- and macro-levels; and distribution is captured by the learner's role (active/passive) at each comprehension level, reflecting Salomon's distinction between shared activity and division of labour.
requirements: The activity affording distribution must be specified; the article treats comprehension as this activity because it underpins many tasks and requires selection, organisation, and generation of information
constraints: Existing theories were not designed for tools with the range and flexibility of offloading that LLMs enable, motivating this bridging perspective
target_learners: university students using LLMs in writing tasks
target_learning_goals: text comprehension and synthesis writing
examples: In the study, learners read two texts with opposing views on predictive modelling in education and wrote a synthesis essay via a custom interface embedding LLM access

title: Learning Environment Generation (LEG): formalizing courseware artifact generation as a contract-bound task
description: LEG is the task framework the report introduces: given a course brief, produce in a single pass either a presentation slide as a renderer-valid structured JSON scene graph or a self-contained executable interactive HTML page spanning six educational sub-types (simulations, diagrams, games, code playgrounds, 3D visualizations, structured learning pages). The textual planning stage produces entities, relations, telemetry, visual features, knobs and actions; the scaffolding stage iteratively generates and critiques each level's goal; the Gen-UI stage applies generate-then-refine with visual, solution, telemetry and mechanical critiques. description: Each learning interactive decomposes a complex concept into a sequence of K=5 levelled goals the student must solve. Goals must satisfy four desiderata the article names: "Concreteness", "Clarity", "Growth" (each goal more complex than preceding ones or introducing a new concept), and "Scaffolding" (not significantly more difficult than predecessors). description: The article reads LEAGUE as a maturity progression with five levels: compliance-only review; documented governance with recorded roles and repeatable practices; ethical governance reviewing equity, agency, and utility alongside compliance; continuous monitoring with scheduled reassessment including model performance and drift; and AI-ready governance extending review to LLM, agentic, and generative student-facing systems. The article states "Institutions frequently begin at a compliance-only posture and can advance toward continuous, AI-ready governance."
requirements: Scheduled reassessment that revisits model performance rather than treating initial approval as final
constraints: The maturity levels are presented as a conceptual summary (Table 4), not a validated measurement instrument; the article calls for quantitative assessment rubrics as future work
target_learners: higher education institutions and their governance bodies
target_learning_goals: progressive institutional capability for ethical governance of student data and AI-enabled student services
examples: Table 4 lists the five levels from compliance-only review limited to FERPA and GDPR through AI-ready governance extending the same review to LLM and agentic systems

article_title: LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
citation: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429
title: LearnLM: a Gemini 1.5 Pro-based model co-trained for pedagogical instruction following
description: LearnLM is an experimental model available on Google AI Studio, built on Gemini 1.5 Pro (gemini-1.5-pro-002) by co-training: the team mixed pedagogical SFT demonstration data and human preference data (reward model and RLHF) directly into Gemini's post-training stages. The authors state they "co-train with Gemini, meaning we mix our data directly with Gemini's SFT, RM, and RL stages", which lets the model learn new instruction following without forgetting core reasoning, multimodal, factuality, safety, or multi-turn properties, and keeps LearnLM in sync as the Gemini recipe evolves.
requirements: Pedagogical data must be conditioned on specific System Instructions so it can be mixed with general conversational data without conflicts of persona or style.
constraints: A subset of LearnLM improvements is part of the recently released Gemini 2.0 models; the evaluated version is a point-in-time artifact compared against model versions as of 2024-10-01.
target_learners: students and independent learners using AI tutoring products
target_learning_goals: interactive tutor-led exercises specified by teachers or developers through system instructions
examples: The model is offered as an experimental release on Google AI Studio with documentation of example use cases and suggested prompts.

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Learning Context Framework for AI Applications: five dimensions of learner context
description: The Learning Context (LC) Framework structures what AI education systems should know about a learner across five organizing questions: Who (learner factors such as prior knowledge, misconceptions, psychosocial traits), With whom (peers and instructors), What (content, task difficulty and domain), When (stable traits versus volatile states and intraindividual change), and Where (digital environment from micro- to meso-system, based on Bronfenbrenner's ecological levels). The article proposes it because "the ﬁeld lacks a computationally tractable theory for representing LC at scale," and pairs the dimensions with AI opportunities such as contextualized instructional design strategies and edtech affordances (feedback, prompts, practice quizzes).
requirements: Representation must be grounded in learning science, computationally amenable, machine-readable, and human-interpretable
constraints: Current AI systems capture only the context visible through direct user interaction, operationalizing a narrow subset of these dimensions
target_learners: K-12 and college learners using AI-based learning tools
target_learning_goals: Deep, robust learning via context-aware personalization rather than shallow mimicry
examples: The framework's dimensions were instantiated in four LLM vignettes and translated into the LC data structure of Theme 2
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24362

title: LearnMate2: an LLM-powered personalized and adaptive learning support system integrating planning, in-session assistance, and adaptive activities
description: LearnMate2 is an LLM-based online learning support system that integrates three interconnected components into a closed-loop learning workflow. According to the authors, it integrates "(1) PlanMate, which generates personalized study plans based on four dimensions—goals, time, pace, and path; (2) StudyMate, which provides real-time contextual assistance during learning sessions through progressive disclosure, follow-up explanations, practice questions, and external resources; and (3) AdaptMate, which adjusts learning activities and study plans based on quiz performance and learning progress." The system is powered by Gemini-2.0-Pro with a React front-end, and its agents and source code are available in supplementary materials.

target_learning_goals: personalized study planning
real-time learning support
adaptive learning activities

description: AdaptMate is LearnMate2's adaptive plan modification component, introduced following insights from the preliminary study. It "analyzes learning performance data and interactions from StudyMate to identify areas requiring adjustment, then generates modifications to the personalized plan based on this analysis." Uses structured prompts to evaluate combined data and generate specific recommendations
