article_title: LecturaAgents: A Multi-Agent Framework for Adaptive Personalized AI-Assisted Learning and Embodied Teaching
citation: Jaward Sesay, Yue Yu, Siwei Dong, Börje F. Karlsson. (2026). Lect¯uraAgents: A Multi-Agent Framework for Adaptive Personalized AI-Assisted Learning and Embodied Teaching. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16428
title: LecturaAgents hierarchical multi-agent framework for end-to-end personalized lecture generation and embodied delivery
description: LecturaAgents is a hierarchical multi-agent framework in which a ProfessorAgent coordinates validator and executor agents across two sessions, Lecture Preparation and Lecture Delivery, supported by LLM, Agent, TASA, and Memory modules. The article states it "mirrors a professor–student relationship, where a ProfessorAgent coordinates specialized assistant agents (at different hierarchies) to plan, research, review, and create lecture contents tailored for the individual learner." Agents collaborate through a Swarm-of-Ranks group chat with nine message types, and personalization conditions all generated artifacts on the learner profile, preferences, and usage history.
requirements: A lecture prompt and learner profile, with optional syllabus or reference materials, plus configuration of academic level, language, voice model, handwriting mode, LLM, and research method
constraints: The framework can inherit common LLM failure modes such as factual errors, inconsistent reasoning, and tool or prompt-sensitivity; multi-agent orchestration introduces latency and compute overhead
target_learners: high school, undergraduate, and graduate learners (ages 13–35 in evaluation)
target_learning_goals: personalized lecture content generation and embodied delivery across maths, science, engineering, art, and history topics
examples: In evaluation, 280 personalized lectures were generated across seven frontier models and scored by five expert educators using rubrics for lecture content, personalization, assessment, and teaching action quality

article_title: Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System
citation: Rumble, T., Zarrin, J., Lovell, P. G., Falconer, R. (2026). Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13370
title: LEA (Learning Engagement Assistant): a tri-modal agentic AI tutoring system combining course-specific RAG, KC models, and learner-state orchestration
description: LEA is an agentic AI tutoring system delivering adaptive, personalised instruction through three integrated modes — Chat, Tutor, and Quiz — grounded in a course-specific RAG vector database and a hierarchical Knowledge Component model. Its Agent Orchestrator "continuously estimates the learner's CL, ZPD, and motivational state to dynamically adjust scaffolding type, task difficulty, and feedback timing." The system separates orchestration logic from knowledge representation, so new courses require only two interchangeable artifacts: the RAG library and the KC model.
requirements: A course-specific RAG library (ChromaDB vector store) and a KC model (hierarchical JSON of Learning Objectives and Granular Objectives) must be authored per course via the three-stage onboarding pipeline with human-in-the-loop review.
constraints: Auxiliary content-generation logic downstream of the orchestration layer can encode single-course assumptions, as shown by the hardcoded Python question generation; Faithfulness declines with curriculum distance from the original course.
target_learners: higher education students (MSc and undergraduate) in computing and social science courses
target_learning_goals: course-specific conceptual understanding, procedural skill practice, and formative self-assessment aligned with course learning objectives
examples: Deployed across CMP511, CMP202, and PSY555 at Abertay University; source code and illustrative datasets are available at https://github.com/tep00018/LEA.
key_sources: Rumble, T., Zarrin, J., Lovell, P. G., Falconer, R. (2026). Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13370

article_title: Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System
citation: Rumble, T., Zarrin, J., Lovell, P. G., Falconer, R. (2026). Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13370
title: Integrated Psychological Framework: cognitive load, ZPD, engagement, and motivation theories grounding LEA's learner-state modelling
description: LEA's adaptive mechanisms are grounded in four frameworks — Cognitive Load Theory, Zone of Proximal Development and constructivist learning theory, engagement theory (Self-Determination Theory and Situated Expectancy-Value Theory), and motivation and self-efficacy theory (Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory and Zimmerman's self-regulation model). Together these "define the Integrated Psychological Framework that informs LEA's learner-state modelling and scaffolding decisions via the Agent Orchestrator." Cognitive load is computed as a weighted combination of task difficulty, recent accuracy, fatigue, and task type; ZPD is the mean accuracy across the last four responses targeting a 50–80% performance band; motivation state is inferred from persistence, sentiment, and performance trends.
requirements: Non-invasive behavioural and performance indicators (task completion time, accuracy, persistence, sentiment) from which the orchestrator infers learner state.
constraints: The classroom pilot's qualitative reports of scaffolding rigidity and affirmation fatigue are, per the authors, the first evidence of how these models perform against learners whose states they did not generate; CL coefficient calibration remains open to refinement.
target_learners: higher education students using LEA as a voluntary study aid
target_learning_goals: adaptive scaffolding within the learner's zone of proximal development, sustained motivation and engagement, and management of cognitive load during tutoring interactions
examples: Four motivation states (cold start, motivation drop, plateau, maintained high motivation) each trigger a corresponding instructional strategy grounded in Self-Determination Theory, such as autonomy support during cold start and challenge escalation during plateau.
key_sources: Rumble, T., Zarrin, J., Lovell, P. G., Falconer, R. (2026). Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13370

article_title: Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs
citation: Smadar Szekely, Judith Gal-Ezer, and David Harel. (2018). Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs. J. ACM 37, 4, Article 111. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08543
title: Learnity graphs: representing learning as an evolving network of learning entities
description: The article proposes representing learning as a network of interconnected learning entities rather than fixed curricular sequences. A learnity is "a minimal meaningful unit, which captures a capability, concept, experience, or demonstrated competence", and learnities connected through relationships such as dependencies, integration, composition and specialization form a learnity graph. The framework integrates academic, professional, and personal learning into one developmental structure that can complement or replace conventional CVs.
requirements: Clear criteria for creating, aggregating, and validating learnities within the graph
A shared representational language and standardization for cross-institutional use, including definitions of learnities, relationships, development levels, contexts, and evidence types
constraints: Overly rigid standardization risks reproducing the limitations of traditional curricula; frameworks should guide rather than constrain
Building a full operational system remains a challenge for future interdisciplinary research
target_learners: higher education students
lifelong learners across academic, professional, and personal contexts
target_learning_goals: representing and guiding lifelong developmental learning trajectories integrating knowledge, skills, experience, and artifacts
examples: Figure 1 shows the learnity graph of a second-year computer science student combining academic and industry experience; Figure 3 shows a real estate lawyer's graph reflecting legal education and professional practice
key_sources: Smadar Szekely, Judith Gal-Ezer, and David Harel. (2018). Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs. J. ACM 37, 4, Article 111. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08543

article_title: Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs
citation: Smadar Szekely, Judith Gal-Ezer, and David Harel. (2018). Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs. J. ACM 37, 4, Article 111. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08543
title: Learnity graph design considerations: granularity, relationship types, and orthogonal structural dimensions
description: The article enumerates design considerations for constructing learnity graphs. Nodes vary in granularity, with some learnities emerging "from the integration of multiple learnities into higher-level competencies"; edges capture prerequisite dependencies, interdisciplinary interactions, specialization pathways, and compositional integration; and layers represent depth of development while subgraphs represent context such as academic, professional, or self-directed learning. These dimensions should be orthogonal and provide complementary perspectives on development.
requirements: Clear criteria for creating, aggregating, and validating learnities to avoid graph inflation and preserve interpretability
Structural dimensions designed to be orthogonal and complementary
constraints: Constructing learnity graphs may seem complex, though the authors point to the existing body of work on graph visualization as suggesting the graphs can be effectively structured and interpreted
target_learners: higher education students
lifelong learners
target_learning_goals: modeling learning processes and analyzing development and transfer across domains
examples: A programming learnity may include knowledge (syntax, control structures), skills (implementation, debugging), artifacts (code, projects), and experience (collaboration, industry work), linked by prerequisite, compositional, and interdisciplinary edges
key_sources: Smadar Szekely, Judith Gal-Ezer, and David Harel. (2018). Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs. J. ACM 37, 4, Article 111. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08543

article_title: LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University
citation: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164
title: LearnAI Framework: a two-layer model for just-in-time AI co-creation serving mixed-ability learners
description: The LearnAI Framework is a two-layer institutional model for supporting AI readiness — defined as confidence, awareness of appropriate use, and ability to apply AI tools within authentic workflows — across learners from non-coders to advanced CS majors. The article states it supports mixed-ability learners "through two complementary layers: a Wide-Exposure Layer that builds awareness at scale, and a Customized Co-Creation Layer that provides intensive, 1-on-1 scaffolding for authentic tasks." Rather than teaching programming syntax, it emphasizes problem framing, tool orchestration, critical verification of outputs, and situated ethical decision-making, operating as service-oriented infrastructure complementing traditional curricula.
requirements: Undergraduate peer tutors trained via a calibration process (observing and co-facilitating sessions before leading independently)
Faculty coordination and lightweight deployment support
A booking/intake system connecting wide-exposure outreach to opt-in co-creation sessions
constraints: The findings transfer most directly to learners with concrete needs and tentative openness to AI
Initial evidence comes from a single institution and an opt-in population
target_learners: Mixed-ability university learners: undergraduates, faculty, and administrative staff, from no coding experience to advanced CS majors
target_learning_goals: AI readiness: confidence, awareness of appropriate AI use, and applying AI tools in authentic workflows
Problem framing, tool orchestration, critical verification, and ethical decision-making
examples: At Monmouth University, Fall 2025 through Spring 2026, the Wide-Exposure Layer embedded 15-minute presentations in 18 existing courses across introductory IT, science, business, and nursing, while the Co-Creation Layer ran opt-in one-hour sessions producing 36 portfolio websites and over 20 deployed applications
key_sources: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164

article_title: Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance
citation: Gabelmann, J., Jahn, F., Baum, K., van Rossum, S., Wuenscher, E., Gros, T. P., Wolf, V. (2026). Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30187
title: Learning objective graphs for curriculum-aligned adaptive tutoring
description: The proposed architecture structures tutoring around Learning Objective (LO) graphs that represent the course curriculum as a network of nodes with edges indicating interdependencies and prerequisites between concepts. Mapping student performance on exercises onto the graph tracks progress across the course and enables adaptive learning, such as maintaining the student within their ZPD across a sequence of topics. If the system detects recurring struggle with a specific LO, it can proactively suggest lower-difficulty exercises or targeted explanations from a prerequisite node.
requirements: Exercises must be assigned to particular LOs; performance data must be mapped onto the graph
constraints: This component is proposed but not yet integrated; future work will focus on integrating learning objectives
target_learners: students in structured courses with prerequisite-based curricula
target_learning_goals: adaptive progression across course topics within the ZPD

article_title: LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization
citation: Joy Bose, Om Thomas. (2025). LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization. https://github.com/learnopt/learnopt
title: LearnOpt framework: exam preparation as constrained optimization over an LLM-built exam knowledge graph with BKT mastery updates
description: LearnOpt reframes exam preparation as a constrained optimization problem: it ingests historical question papers, LLM-tags each question with chapter, topic, difficulty and skill via a chain-of-evidence prompt, builds a knowledge graph in FalkorDB with prerequisite edges, and "produces a ranked, time-bounded study plan specifying which concept subgroups to study, in what sequence, and with what expected score gain." Mastery is initialized from self-report and updated via standard BKT; the objective is solved with Google OR-Tools CP-SAT and re-run after each study session. Its substantive extension over the Embibe PAJ precedent is a skill-weighted objective coupling the exam's empirical cognitive-operation distribution into the reward signal.
requirements: Historical question papers in PDF format, an official syllabus, and a student mastery vector as inputs; full question text including options for reliable skill tagging
constraints: Validated on MCQ exams; transfer to subjective or coding assessments requires further work
Mastery vectors initialized from self-report introduce subjective bias; optimization evaluation is simulation-based with no measured student outcomes
target_learners: NEET and JEE aspirants preparing for standardized examinations
target_learning_goals: Efficient allocation of limited preparation time across topics and cognitive skills to maximize expected exam score
examples: Applied to 1,496 NEET questions (2016-2024) and the 110-question single-correct MCQ subset of JEEBench; code, knowledge graph, and annotated dataset released publicly
key_sources: Joy Bose, Om Thomas. (2025). LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization. https://github.com/learnopt/learnopt

article_title: LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization
citation: Joy Bose, Om Thomas. (2025). LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization. https://github.com/learnopt/learnopt
title: Five-category latent skill taxonomy for science MCQs (S1-S5), chosen for surface-structural discriminability
description: The taxonomy defines five skill categories calibrated to NEET-type science MCQs: S1 Direct Recall, S2 Conceptual Application, S3 Multi-concept Integration, S4 Quantitative Reasoning, and S5 Elimination and Negation. "Categories are chosen for structural discriminability: each can be identified from the surface form of the question without requiring inference about latent cognitive depth, which maximizes inter-rater reliability." S1-S4 map approximately to revised Bloom levels, while S5 does not appear in standard taxonomies and is introduced to capture format-driven falsification operations; the design follows collapsed Bloom rubrics that achieved higher inter-rater reliability than six-level schemes.
requirements: Full question text including options, since reliable skill tagging with this pipeline requires full question-and-options text
constraints: The S2/S3/S4 boundary is where inter-model agreement is weakest (kappa 0.51 overall); the taxonomy describes exam design, not necessarily where students should focus effort
target_learners: NEET and JEE aspirants; coaching centers analyzing question banks
target_learning_goals: Characterizing the cognitive operations standardized exams demand, to weight study-time allocation by skill category
examples: S5 items include "which of the following is NOT/EXCEPT" formats, Assertion-Reason and twin-statement items; S5 rose to 30.7-35.2% of NEET questions post-2023

citation: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework
title: Assess self-directed growth through learner-driven summative self-assessment frameworks rather than task-level engagement measures
description: The article argues that sustained, purposeful engagement across multiple contexts, not task-level behavior, indicates competency development, and that task-level engagement of learner agency cannot validly assess learner agency. It therefore adopts "a specific focus on learner-driven summative self-assessment", where the evolving trajectory of learners' self-assessment frameworks serves as a key indicator of emerging SDL skills and self-directed growth. This moves beyond post-task questionnaires and self-efficacy ratings toward post-task judgments of ability based on performance and procedures.
requirements: Assessment must capture developmental process across tasks and contexts, not single-task engagement
constraints: The article states summative self-assessment alone cannot drive a sustainable SDL process unless combined with Capacity to Aspire
target_learners: learners developing self-directed learning competencies across diverse tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of sustained SDL competency development
examples: The article contrasts its approach with prior studies collecting self-efficacy assessments via backend data and summative self-assessments via researcher-administered post-task questionnaires

article_title: Rethinking Scaffolding in LLM Tutors: The Interactional Mismatch Between Benchmarks and Real-World Deployments
citation: Neagu, A., Wong, J. T. H., Messer, M., Nelson, R., & Johnson, P. B. (2026). Rethinking Scaffolding in LLM Tutors: The Interactional Mismatch Between Benchmarks and Real-World Deployments. Pluralistic Alignment Workshop @ ICML 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15766
title: Learning-context mismatch account of scaffolding uptake in student-chatbot interaction
description: The article proposes that student uptake of chatbot scaffolding is governed by a mismatch between the chatbot's pedagogical framing and the student's learning context, including immediate goals, prior knowledge, invested effort, and task stakes. It argues that "bypassing scaffolding is not necessarily detrimental; rather, it frequently highlights a mismatch between a chatbot's pedagogical framing and the student's learning goals". The account draws on help-seeking theory, distinguishing instrumental from executive help-seeking, and explains why uptake varies within single chats and across deployments.
requirements: Evaluation of scaffolding must be grounded in the student's learning context, since uptake depends on situational factors such as the student's immediate goal and task stakes.
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation of observed uptake patterns, not as a tested causal model.
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students using LLM chatbots for self-study and learning tasks
target_learning_goals: Effective use of scaffolded AI tutoring support; self-regulated help-seeking
examples: The paper cites Yang et al. (2025) documenting that mastery-oriented students asked conceptual questions while work-avoidance-oriented students asked implementation-oriented questions.

article_title: Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis
citation: Jueng, Ekkachai. (2026). Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10802
title: Learn–export–analyze loop: learners analyze a trace their own agent generated
description: The tool's central design pattern is a learn–export–analyze loop: learners run their own agent, export the complete decision trace as CSV, and analyze it themselves, producing learning curves, value heatmaps, and visitation maps. Learners 'do not analyze a canned dataset' but data 'their own agent generated minutes earlier', making the analysis an act of reflection on their own experiment rather than an exercise on foreign data.
requirements: The tool must log each transition with the full pre-action Q-row, the greedy/random provenance of each action, and the TD target and error, and export the complete trace as CSV.
constraints: The on-screen log keeps only the latest 500 steps and the fast-training mode skips logging, so long training runs are only partially traced.
target_learners: undergraduate students meeting Q-learning for the first time
target_learning_goals: interpreting learning curves and value heatmaps
connecting the Bellman update to observed learning dynamics
examples: students train an agent, export the trace, and answer analysis questions in a spreadsheet or notebook: plot return per episode; compute the exploration ratio per episode; build a visitation heatmap and compare it with the value heatmap
key_sources: Jueng, Ekkachai. (2026). Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10802

article_title: Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis
citation: Jueng, Ekkachai. (2026). Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10802
title: Learner-as-analyst: mechanistic transparency reframes the learner from spectator to analyst of a recorded process
description: The article's organizing stance holds that every quantity in the Bellman update should be inspectable at every step, with the record of those steps belonging to the learner. Existing tools 'treat the learner as a spectator of a converging process, whereas Q-Learning Lab treats the learner as an analyst of a recorded process', a stance grounded in constructionism and experiential learning theory.
requirements: Requires a tool that renders the update equation with live numeric substitution at every step and logs the full pre-decision Q-row with greedy/random provenance, so the trace is a complete record of the agent's decision process.
constraints: Instantiated here only for tabular Q-learning on a small deterministic, single-agent gridworld.
target_learners: undergraduates encountering the Bellman update for the first time
target_learning_goals: understanding the Q-learning update mechanism
developing diagnostic practices for RL agent behavior
key_sources: Jueng, Ekkachai. (2026). Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10802

article_title: Designing for Authentic Assessment: A Scoping Review
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Zilu Du. (2025). Designing for authentic assessment: a scoping review. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-025-01588-9
title: Learning-oriented and collaborative four-step design framework for authentic assessment
description: To address the design challenges of professional-authenticity dominance, passive student roles and lack of care and connection, the review proposes a learning-oriented and collaborative design framework for AA. It is 'a cyclical and recursive process which involves four steps': (1) deciding assessment goals and focus through collaborative negotiation between educators and students; (2) creating assessment context and task mirroring real-world scenarios; (3) designing assessment criteria and student engagement, including co-designed criteria and judgement activities such as peer assessment; and (4) planning feedback and students' self-reflection that is learning- and future-oriented and transformative.
requirements: Critical conversations between students and important others (institutions, educators, industry professionals, wider society) to align tasks with real-world expectations and students' needs
constraints: Designers must manage a trade-off between authenticity and feasibility, balancing real-world task complexity with practical constraints of the learning environment
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: meaningful engagement, evaluative judgement, ownership of assessment, preparation for post-graduation work and social development
examples: The framework responds to the review's findings that only three studies considered social authenticity, only eight gave students choices, and only five connected students with industry or community partners.

article_title: LearnLens: LLM-Enabled Personalised, Curriculum-Grounded Feedback with Educators in the Loop
citation: Runcong Zhao, Artem Bobrov, Jiazheng Li, Cesare Aloisi, Yulan He. (2025). LearnLens: LLM-Enabled Personalised, Curriculum-Grounded Feedback with Educators in the Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04295
title: LearnLens: a dual-interface LLM feedback system with error-aware assessment, curriculum-grounded generation, and educator oversight
description: LearnLens is a modular LLM-based system for personalised, curriculum-aligned feedback in science education. It comprises an error-aware assessment module that captures nuanced reasoning errors, a curriculum-grounded generation module using a structured topic-linked memory chain, and an educator-in-the-loop interface for customisation and oversight. Teacher tools include student grouping, quiz creation, curriculum-aligned rubric generation, performance visualisation, and interactive feedback modification; a separate student interface delivers timely, tailored feedback.
requirements: Requires local LLM deployment to address student data privacy concerns
Requires a curated bank of pre-authored questions and curriculum-aligned mark schemes
constraints: The demo focuses on GCSE science, though the authors state it can be tailored to students across all educational levels
No student evaluation has been conducted; the authors acknowledge this and plan to address it in future work
target_learners: GCSE science students
target_learning_goals: Science conceptual understanding and reasoning
Timely, actionable feedback on short-essay science answers
examples: Teachers create quizzes tied to national curriculum topics, generate mark schemes with extended reasoning time, and refine flagged feedback through a conversational interface, with edits applicable to a single question or propagated across the entire quiz

article_title: Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review
citation: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150
title: Learner agency in GenAI contexts as a multidimensional, context-sensitive construct
description: The review treats learner agency as learners' capacity to purposefully direct, monitor, evaluate, and take responsibility for their learning while interacting with GenAI, not as a synonym for autonomy or participation. It synthesizes operationalizations including L. Xia et al.'s three-dimensional scale (key abilities, active actions, essential mental characteristics) and Yang et al.'s distinction among receptive, resistive, resourceful, and reflective engagement. The review concludes "learner agency in GenAI-supported higher education should be understood as a multidimensional and context-sensitive construct."
requirements: Agency must be examined through how learners interpret, control, and act upon AI support, not inferred from tool use or attitudes alone
constraints: The construct is context-sensitive: the same technology may support agentic engagement in one context and passive dependence in another
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: directing and evaluating one's own AI-supported learning
exercising evaluative judgement over AI output
examples: L. Xia et al. (2025) developed a student learning agency scale for GenAI-supported contexts with three interrelated dimensions

article_title: The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice
citation: Carpenter, S.K., Pan, S.C. & Butler, A.C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1
title: Learner metacognition as awareness and regulation of one's own learning
description: The review organizes its third strand of findings around metacognition, defined in terms of "learners' awareness and regulation of their own learning". It argues that findings in this area show the need to improve learners' subjective mental models of effective learning, because faulty mental models lead learners away from strategies like spacing and retrieval practice. The framework connects strategy underuse to monitoring and regulation failures in self-directed study.
requirements: Learners must be in situations where they monitor and regulate their own learning for the framework's implications to apply
target_learners: lifelong learners across educational levels
target_learning_goals: effective selection and use of learning strategies such as spacing and retrieval practice
examples: The review uses this framework to interpret why learners underuse spacing and retrieval practice and to motivate improving learners' subjective mental models of how to learn effectively

citation: Scheiter, K., & Gerjets, P. (2007). Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments. Educational Psychology Review 19, 285–307. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9046-3
title: Learner control as the defining feature distinguishing hypermedia learning environments from system-controlled multimedia
description: The article frames hypermedia systems as characterized by a high level of interactivity, which "is referred to as learner control in the respective literature." Learner control is treated as a major advantage of hypermedia for learning and instruction because it might increase interest and motivation, facilitate adaptive instruction, and provide affordances for active and constructive information processing. The review uses this framing to organize its analysis of why effectiveness findings are ambiguous.
requirements: Learners must actually exercise control over navigation and information processing within the hypermedia environment for the proposed motivational and adaptive benefits to apply
constraints: The article states the advantages are potential: learner control "might" increase interest and motivation, and the review argues effectiveness is difficult to demonstrate
target_learners: Students learning with hypermedia systems
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition from hypermedia learning environments
examples: The review analyzes instructional potentials of learner-controlled hypermedia environments against the ambiguous results of effectiveness studies

citation: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283
title: LEADING/FOLLOWING prescriptive coding scheme for maternal directives

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: A working definition of learning as an experience-driven increase in capacities to respond in valued ways.
description: To anchor its framework, the article offers an explicit definition of learning in a note: "we would define learning as an increase, brought about by experience, in the capacities of an organism to react in valued ways in response to stimuli." The definition is offered defensively — the authors supply it for those who think defining formative assessment merely shifts the definitional burden onto the word learning. It makes valued response capacities, experience, and change over time the constituents of learning, which in turn delimits what counts as formative evidence of learning.
requirements: Any account of formative assessment needs a working definition of learning; this one ties learning to experience and to valued ways of responding.
constraints: The authors present it as a stipulated definition for a specific objection, not as an established empirical result.

target_learning_goals: Increasing learners' capacities to respond in valued ways
examples: The note supplies the definition in response to the objection that defining formative assessment merely moves the burden of definition onto the word learning.

citation: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html

description: The article describes learning journals as more than collections of assignments: they are tools learners use regularly to reflect on and assess their own progress over time. In the reported class, after each communicative task (e.g., preparing recommendations for a walking tour in Bogotá), learners wrote reflections and self-assessments in their journals following teacher-provided guidelines. The pattern combines authentic language-use tasks with structured written self-evaluation entries across a course cycle.

self-regulated learning and reflection on language performance

citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Levy and Murnane's expert thinking and complex communication account of 21st century work demands
description: The chapter attributes to economists Levy and Murnane (2004) the claim that declining portions of the labor force do routine cognitive or manual work that computers can be programmed to do, while growing proportions do expert thinking and complex communication that computers cannot. Expert thinking involves "effective pattern matching based on detailed knowledge" plus metacognition about when to switch strategies; complex communication involves constantly adjusted exchange of verbal and nonverbal information as communication evolves unpredictably.

article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Learning landscape: an ecological conception of the totality of interrelated learning sub-landscapes, including the instructional landscape
description: The learning landscape is the author's metaphor for the ecological whole composed of multiple sub-landscapes, such as the instructional landscape, the media landscape, and the socio-cultural organization landscape. It results both from the natural interplay of learning entities and from consciously planned action to reshape what nature tends to produce. A truly ecologically functioning learning landscape is "characterized by the smooth integration among all the various sub-landscapes" that compose it. The metaphor extends evaluation of learning environments beyond effectiveness and efficiency to their aesthetic and ethical qualities, with beauty and harmony as indicators of the quality of the ecology of cognition.
requirements: Planners and leaders whose actions impact the learning landscape must be environmentally aware of what else happens in it
constraints: The author judges that governmental planning agencies and much of the distance education effort leave considerable room for improvement in this environmental awareness
target_learners: learners across society at large, in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning responsive to global issues and concerns
examples: UNESCO's UNITWIN/UNESCO Chairs program is cited as an example of networking that supports interinstitutional collaboration in the learning landscape
