article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Redefinition of learning as the disposition to engage in continuous dialogue with the human, social, biological and physical environment
description: The chapter argues learning must be 'undefined' and recast as a disposition to dialogue, expressed at different levels of complex organization, for constructive interaction with change. The proposed redefinition sees human learning as "the disposition of human beings, and of the social entities to which they pertain, to engage in continuous dialogue with the human, social, biological and physical environment, so as to generate intelligent behavior to interact constructively with change" (J. Visser, 2001). This goes beyond learning as particular desired changes in human performance capability and draws on Gell-Mann's view of learning as complex adaptive systems making sense of regularities among randomness.
requirements: A vision of learning that is ubiquitous, unrelated to conditions such as age, time, space and circumstance, manifesting at diverse levels of complex organization
constraints: The author presents this as a possible redefinition grounded in theoretical argument rather than empirical validation
target_learners: human beings and the social entities to which they pertain
target_learning_goals: generating intelligent behavior to interact constructively with change
key_sources: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Match design components to learner locations and mobility contexts
description: The article proposes extending the formal/informal categorization of learning environments with the descriptors noisy and quiet, and presents Table 2 mapping four typical learner locations to learning preferences and information delivery styles: subway and bus (visual numerical, short articles with strong pictures), home (auditory-visual-kinesthetic combination), office (written expressive, PPT and e-books), and cafe (auditory, visual and linguistic). The typology draws on visual, auditory and tactile/kinesthetic learning-style theories and directs designers to consider both environmental factors and learner preferences.
requirements: Designers should give thought not only to environmental factors but also to learners' preferences and use different design components to meet the needs of distinctive learners in diverse situations
constraints: It will be hard to predict where learners will be using the mLearning content
target_learners: mobile learners moving across home, transit, office and cafe settings
target_learning_goals: adapting message design to learner mobility and context
examples: Table 2 pairs the subway and bus environment with visual numerical design such as short articles and strong pictures, and the home environment with music, oral content and instructional videos
key_sources: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x

article_title: The Words Children Hear
citation: Montag Jessica L., Jones Michael N., Smith Linda B. (2015). The words children hear: Picture books and the statistics for language learning. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797615594361
title: Lexical and contextual diversity of input as a driver of early language learnability
description: The article's organizing explanatory account: early language learning depends on child-directed input, and learnability is enhanced by diversity of words and contexts. The article states that "learnability is enhanced when individual words or devices are encountered in diverse contexts and when there is more variety in general in the input data," citing computational analyses of aggregated child-directed corpora and individual-differences studies linking type-token ratios to vocabulary development. Picture-book text is presented as a previously unstudied source of such diversity.
requirements: Analyses of the statistical properties of large corpora of child-directed language aggregated over many conversations.
constraints: Type-token ratios depend on sample size and cannot be easily interpreted from a single sample or measure, per the article's sampling-procedure section.
target_learners: infants and very young language learners (0 to 60 months)
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition from the statistical properties of linguistic input
examples: The study operationalized diversity as number of unique word types across multiple token sample sizes drawn randomly from the two corpora.
key_sources: Montag Jessica L., Jones Michael N., Smith Linda B. (2015). The words children hear: Picture books and the statistics for language learning. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797615594361

article_title: Beyond the phonological deficit: Semantics contributes indirectly to decoding efficiency in children with dyslexia
citation: van Rijthoven R, Kleemans T, Segers E, Verhoeven L. (2018). Beyond the phonological deficit: Semantics contributes indirectly to decoding efficiency in children with dyslexia. Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1002/dys.1597
title: Lexical restructuring account of semantics supporting decoding in dyslexia
description: The article explains its findings with the lexical restructuring hypothesis: as children's lexicons grow in size and semantic relations, pressure increases to make finer phonological distinctions, so lexical representations "start out holistic and become more specified during early and middle childhood". Strong semantic abilities thereby foster phonological awareness and lexical retrieval (rapid naming), which in turn support word and pseudoword decoding. The authors apply this to children with dyslexia, whose broad and deep semantic knowledge may compensate for weak phonological representations.
requirements: A developing lexicon with increasing numbers of words and semantic relations, providing pressure toward finer phonological distinctions
constraints: The authors state the effect of semantics was small and indirect, and that children with dyslexia showed no direct profit from semantic knowledge in learning to read
target_learners: children with dyslexia in early stages of reading development
target_learning_goals: word decoding efficiency
pseudoword decoding efficiency
examples: The study's mediation models operationalized semantics as four WISC-III NL subtests (information, similarities, productive vocabulary, comprehension) and found indirect paths via PA and RAN consistent with this account.
key_sources: van Rijthoven R, Kleemans T, Segers E, Verhoeven L. (2018). Beyond the phonological deficit: Semantics contributes indirectly to decoding efficiency in children with dyslexia. Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1002/dys.1597

article_title: Experiencing CSCL: from motivation to the embodied experience and beyond
citation: Carolyn Rosé & Sanna Järvelä & Sten Ludvigsen. (2020). Experiencing CSCL: from motivation to the embodied experience and beyond. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09319-1
title: Learning in Embodied Activity Framework: a sociocultural framework recasting Activity Theory for embodied CSCL
description: The editorial introduces the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework, described as "a Sociocultural Framework for Embodied Cognition" developed by Danish, Eynedy, Saleh and Humburg. It recasts Activity Theory for embodied CSCL experiences, motivated by the difficulty of accounting for both individual and group level phenomena within one framework. The editorial describes its empirical grounding in observations of embodied science learning in mixed reality classroom settings.
requirements: The framework is applied to characterize embodied learning in CSCL experiences, particularly mixed reality settings in naturalistic contexts
constraints: The editors note it is "challenging to account for both individual and group level phenomena within the same framework," which the framework addresses
target_learners: Students in science classrooms engaging in embodied learning activities
target_learning_goals: Embodied science learning through mixed reality collaborative experiences
examples: The article offers a rich exposition of observations from several studies where the framework was used to characterize embodied science learning in classrooms
key_sources: Carolyn Rosé & Sanna Järvelä & Sten Ludvigsen. (2020). Experiencing CSCL: from motivation to the embodied experience and beyond. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09319-1

article_title: Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment
citation: Xintian Tu, Joshua Danish, Megan Humburg, Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Noel Enyedy, Tessaly Jen. (2023). Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 18:231–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09395-z
title: LEAF: the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework connecting CHAT and embodied cognition at individual and collective levels
description: LEAF is the study's organizing framework: it synthesizes cultural-historical activity theory with cognitive theories of embodiment, so that a child running across the room as a gas particle is understood to experience the moment "at both individual and collective levels simultaneously" — feeling speed and proximity while the group negotiates producing a solid or a liquid. Like other CHAT-based theories it treats learning as occurring in activities oriented toward a shared object, with individual actions mediated by artifacts (the projected simulation), community members, rules, and division of labor. The paper uses LEAF to justify analyzing classroom embodied communication and later interview gestures as interrelated levels rather than parallel ones.
requirements: Analysis must attend to embodied cognition and learning at individual and collective levels and the interactions across them, as the framework's stated purpose requires.
constraints: Embodied meanings are activity- and culture-specific: the article notes the same gesture can imply different things in different models (e.g., a pushing gesture as force in one model versus energy transfer in another).
target_learners: elementary school students (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: science concepts such as particle behavior in states of matter
examples: The framework is applied to the STEP Particles project, where shared goals like producing a state of matter are provided by the teacher and negotiated in interaction.
key_sources: Xintian Tu, Joshua Danish, Megan Humburg, Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Noel Enyedy, Tessaly Jen. (2023). Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 18:231–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09395-z

article_title: Productive dissent in learning communities
citation: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0
title: Collins's distinction between learning communities and conserving communities
description: The article adopts Collins's (1998) distinction in which a "questioning habit of mind" demarcates two community types: learning communities, such as the science community, "aim to expand the collective knowledge of the group," while conserving communities, such as the medieval church, "aim to perpetuate and protect an established system of beliefs." The article uses this axis to argue schools should shift toward learning communities and to recharacterize seemingly dissenting groups like the alt-right as conserving communities.
requirements: A questioning habit of mind as the criterion distinguishing learning from conserving communities
constraints: The article notes, as Collins does, that conserving communities still involve a great deal of learning
target_learners: school communities
classroom learners
target_learning_goals: critical thinking as a communal habit
learning how to learn
examples: The article recasts alt-right groups as conserving communities despite their outward facade of dissent
key_sources: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0

article_title: Teachers’ learning in a learning study
citation: Mona Holmqvist. (2011). Teachers' learning in a learning study. Instr Sci 39:497–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9138-1
title: Learning Study model: a fusion of lesson study and design experiment with pre-, post- and delayed post-tests
description: The Learning Study is "a fusion between lesson study and design experiment" in which teachers and a researcher jointly plan a lesson around a chosen learning object, implement it with one pupil group, and analyze pre-test, post-test and delayed post-test results together with video-recorded lessons. The knowledge gained provides the basis for a revised lesson in a new group of pupils, forming micro-cycles of three lessons. In this study six teachers ran three Learning Study cycles over three semesters, with 54, 64 and 48 participating pupils respectively.
requirements: Two to four tape-recorded planning meetings before each lesson to identify critical aspects
Video-recording and verbatim transcription of lessons, and pre-, post- and delayed post-tests for analysis
constraints: The author notes teachers may have difficulty implementing new learning studies independently because of lack of time
target_learners: pupils aged 9-11 in school years 4-5
target_learning_goals: English as a second language learning objects such as possessive pronouns, to be and to have
examples: Learning Study A focused on dependent possessive pronouns; the work sheet and lesson design were revised across lessons A1, A2 and A3 based on test results and lesson analysis
key_sources: Mona Holmqvist. (2011). Teachers' learning in a learning study. Instr Sci 39:497–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9138-1

article_title: The relationship between student-generated learning issues and self-study in problem-based learning
citation: Dolmans, D., Schmidt, H. & Gijselaers, W. (1994). The relationship between student-generated learning issues and self-study in problem-based learning. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 22(4), 251–267. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00891779
title: Procedure measuring overlap between student-generated learning issues and pre-set faculty objectives
description: One of two procedures developed at the University of Limburg to reflect "the extent to which students are able to identify important learning issues given a particular problem". The production of learning issues was "represented as the percentage of overlap between learning issues raised by students and pre-set faculty objectives for each problem", providing a quantitative index of issue quality per problem.
requirements: Pre-set faculty objectives must exist for each problem to compute the overlap percentage
target_learners: PBL students in tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: Identifying important learning issues from a problem
examples: Overlap was computed for each problem between student-raised issues and faculty objectives
key_sources: Dolmans, D., Schmidt, H. & Gijselaers, W. (1994). The relationship between student-generated learning issues and self-study in problem-based learning. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 22(4), 251–267. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00891779

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: The learning study model: lesson study underpinned by an explicit learning theory, organised around intended, enacted and lived objects of learning
description: The learning study approach is "essentially a kind of lesson study with an explicit learning theory—the variation theory of learning". Groups of teachers teaching the same subject at the same level examine their own practice around the question of how an object of learning 'X' can be taught so students see 'X' in the intended way. Each study collects evidence on three questions: the intended object of learning (what students should learn, diagnosed via interviews and pre-tests), the enacted object of learning (what actually happens in the lesson, observed or videoed), and the lived object of learning (what students actually learned, via post-lesson interviews and pre/post-test comparison).
requirements: Teachers attend a course of no less than 12 h on the learning study approach and variation theory before participating
The object of learning is chosen by negotiation as worthwhile, central to the curriculum, and typically difficult for students
constraints: The article does not claim learning studies are generally superior to teachers' normal classroom teaching methods
target_learners: school teachers conducting collaborative professional development
target_learning_goals: pedagogical content knowledge about how best to teach a chosen object of learning
examples: Two Hong Kong cases: a primary four mathematics study run as a quasi-experiment, and a secondary four chemistry study run in action research cycles
key_sources: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4

article_title: Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation
citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Learning Buddy: structure-promoting tool supporting planning, monitoring, and control of learning
description: A structure-promoting tool developed for the direct training component that integrates goal-setting, planning, monitoring, controlling, and reflection. "With the help of this so-called 'Learning Buddy,' students have the opportunity to plan, monitor, and control their learning process when they have been assigned a learning task." Before learning, students decide what to learn and choose a cognitive learning strategy and think of possible distractions; during learning, a generated checklist helps monitor whether the cognitive strategy is used properly; after learning, students are prompted to reflect on what went well and badly. In the experiments phase of training it supported metacognitive regulation of the experiment strategy, especially in the performance phase.
requirements: Delivered by teachers who had received specialized training in facilitating learning-strategy knowledge and metacognitive regulation skills, with standardized materials
target_learners: 5th and 6th grade students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation (goal setting, planning, monitoring, controlling) of learning strategies
examples: Used in every class session of the 8-week experiments phase to systematize repeated metacognitive regulation aimed at reducing metacognitive load
key_sources: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x

article_title: Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education
citation: Marlen A. Roehe, Carmen Trost, Julia S. Grundnig, Anahit Anvari-Pirsch, Anita Holzinger. (2024). Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09952-4
title: Three learning approaches framework: deep, surface, and strategic approaches that are malleable rather than fixed traits
description: The review organises its synthesis around the learning approaches construct originating with Marton and Säljö and developed by Biggs and Entwistle, in which students' traits are "categorised into three distinct, yet complementary, learning approaches: a deep, surface, or strategic approach to learning." A deep approach involves intrinsic motivation to understand and relate ideas; a surface approach relies on rote learning driven by fear of failure; the strategic approach combines good time management with flexible shifting between understanding and memorisation. The review stresses these are not fixed: "students can shift between these approaches to adapt to educational circumstances."
requirements: Measurement via questionnaire inventories based on the established approaches constructs (e.g., SPQ, ASI, ASSIST)
constraints: Approaches are context-dependent and shift with workload, performance, motivation, and personal factors, so they are not stable learner traits
target_learners: undergraduate medical and dental students
target_learning_goals: long-term knowledge retention and application of knowledge in clinical contexts
examples: The review used this three-approach framework to code 470 co-occurrences between teaching methods, learning approaches, and academic performance across 49 studies
key_sources: Marlen A. Roehe, Carmen Trost, Julia S. Grundnig, Anahit Anvari-Pirsch, Anita Holzinger. (2024). Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09952-4

article_title: Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education
citation: Marlen A. Roehe, Carmen Trost, Julia S. Grundnig, Anahit Anvari-Pirsch, Anita Holzinger. (2024). Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09952-4
title: Taxonomy of learning-approaches measurement inventories (SPQ, R-SPQ-2F, ASI, ALSI, ASSIST)
description: The review describes the family of questionnaires used to measure learning approaches: Biggs' Study Process Questionnaire (SPQ), whose strategic approach is termed the achieving approach; its revision, the R-SPQ-2F, which "uses fewer items to narrow in on solely the deep and surface approaches"; Entwistle and Ramsden's ASI with meaning, reproducing, achieving, and non-academic orientations; the ALSI, which "splits the strategic approach into organised studying and effort management"; and the ASSIST. The review notes "the ASSIST, alongside the R-SPQ-2F, is the most commonly used inventory for studying learning approaches."
requirements: Studies must use a questionnaire based on these existing inventories for the approaches to be measured comparably
constraints: The R-SPQ-2F predominantly focuses on deep and surface approaches, so the strategic approach is examined less extensively in studies using it
target_learners: higher education students, particularly medical and dental students
target_learning_goals: measuring students' deep, surface, and strategic approaches to learning
examples: In the review's sample, ASSIST and R-SPQ-2F were each used in 38.8% of the 49 studies
key_sources: Marlen A. Roehe, Carmen Trost, Julia S. Grundnig, Anahit Anvari-Pirsch, Anita Holzinger. (2024). Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09952-4

article_title: A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward
citation: Jan D. Vermunt & Vincent Donche. (2017). A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward. Educ Psychol Rev 29:269–299. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9414-6
title: The learning patterns framework: four components of student learning forming coherent patterns
description: The learning patterns perspective conceptualizes a learning pattern as "a coherent whole of learning activities that learners usually employ, their beliefs about learning and their learning motivation". The framework discerns four components: cognitive processing strategies, metacognitive regulation strategies, conceptions of learning, and learning motivations or orientations. Processing strategies lead directly to knowledge and skill; regulation strategies plan, monitor, steer and evaluate learning; conceptions are metacognitive views about learning; orientations encompass aims, goals, motives and worries. Four qualitative patterns recur: reproduction-directed, meaning-directed, application-directed, and undirected learning. The model is dynamic, with bidirectional relations between personal and contextual factors, learning patterns, and outcomes.
requirements: Measurement via an instrument operationalizing the four components, such as the ILS inventory with its processing, regulation, conception, and orientation scales
constraints: Learning patterns are conceived not as hard-to-change traits but as the result of interplay between personal and contextual influences; patterns are prototypical dimensions and not mutually exclusive
target_learners: students in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding and describing students' characteristic ways of learning (strategies, conceptions, motivations)
examples: The ILS scales define each pattern: e.g., the meaning-directed pattern combines deep processing, self-regulation, construction of knowledge conception, and personal interest orientation
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt & Vincent Donche. (2017). A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward. Educ Psychol Rev 29:269–299. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9414-6

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Jere Brophy
citation: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note: Remembering Jere Brophy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9115-x
title: Improve education through research-based principles and strategies rather than criticism — less heat, more light
description: Carolyn Evertson's tribute presents Brophy's guiding stance for research on teaching: educational problems are not solved by heaping criticism but by finding research-based principles and strategies that enable teachers and schools to be effective. In the preface to Learning from Teaching he wrote that education needs less heat and more light, and Evertson says he dedicated his career to showing what worked.
requirements: Research must be directed at finding solutions that enable teachers and schools to be effective, as the tribute describes Brophy's commitment
target_learners: teachers and schools as improvement targets, K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: improving educational practice and teaching effectiveness
examples: Evertson cites Brophy's preface line education needs less heat and more light and his career-spanning work from effective praise to motivating students to learn and helping teachers deal with problem students
key_sources: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note: Remembering Jere Brophy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9115-x

article_title: Methods and results of a class experiment in learning.
citation: Dearborn, W. F., and Brewer, J. M. (1918). Methods and Results of a Class Experiment in Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. IX, No. 2. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/9/2/
title: Classification of individual learning curves by initial rapidity of progress: convex, concave, and rectilinear types, with plateaus common in code learning
description: From individually plotted practice curves, the article classifies learning curves "on the basis of the rapidity of the initial progress into three groups": rapid initial rise with slower later progress (convex to base line), slow initial progress with later acceleration (concave), and rectilinear even progress. The prevailing type in the code practice "approximates the rectilinear with a tendency to a small initial acceleration," and plateaus were very common and of longer duration than in digit-letter substitution practice. The article uses this taxonomy to illustrate characteristics of the learning curve in class experiments.
requirements: A practice series of sufficient trials plotted individually by each student on cross-section paper, as the class did for the twenty-two code trials.
constraints: The classification is described as rough, and the article notes initial gains were less marked in code learning than in digit-letter substitution because the associations to be formed were more difficult.
target_learners: college students in educational psychology
target_learning_goals: understanding of learning curves, individual differences, and effects of practice
examples: Plates I to IV reproduce characteristic curves selected from the students' own graphs, including curves with frequent fluctuations or ups and downs.
key_sources: Dearborn, W. F., and Brewer, J. M. (1918). Methods and Results of a Class Experiment in Learning. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. IX, No. 2. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/9/2/

article_title: Educational psychology and college administrators.
citation: J. C. H. (1915). Editorials: Educational Psychology and College Administrators; The Lecturer's Illusion. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(2), 121-122.
title: The lecturer's illusion: a teacher's warm feeling of successful presentation is mistaken for evidence of learning
description: The editorial names and describes 'the lecturer's illusion': the lecturer feels satisfaction over the ease, clearness, correctness and economy of the presentation, and this subjective well-being is reinforced by students' hearty approval and absence of friction. The fallacy is that these signs of smooth delivery are taken as evidence that learning occurred, when lecturing supplies 'predigested intellectual food' rather than eliciting the pupil's own reaction. The article uses this account to explain why the information lecture persists from graduate school to kindergarten despite long-standing condemnation by educational economy.
requirements: The illusion operates where the teacher judges success by subjective ease and student approval rather than by evidence of pupil reaction or learning.
constraints: The article offers this as a psychological interpretation, not a tested result.
target_learners: pupils and students at all levels, from kindergarten to graduate school
target_learning_goals: genuine learning through the pupil's own reaction rather than passive reception of predigested information
examples: The editorial describes the elementary teacher who 'explains' the lesson because pupils lack the habit of reacting to the lesson itself, and the secondary mathematics teacher who 'prepares' the lesson because the text lacks the right point of view.
key_sources: J. C. H. (1915). Editorials: Educational Psychology and College Administrators; The Lecturer's Illusion. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(2), 121-122. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0063797

article_title: The child's speech. I. The impulse to speech.
citation: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text
title: Do not anticipate the child's wants or interpret rudimentary expressions once speech is expected; let speaking bring reward and its absence bring consequences
description: The article recommends that, to hasten speech acquisition, the child 'should be made to feel as fully as possible the rewards of success in speaking', through profit (getting what is asked for) and praise. It adds that 'it is unwise to anticipate the child's wants and interpret his most rudimentary expressions', because this removes the motive for acquiring speech.
requirements: the child must be of an age to acquire the verbal symbol or already have attempted to use it before gratification is withheld
constraints: the article frames this as a method for children at the stage of acquiring verbal symbols, not for younger infants
target_learners: young children at the stage of acquiring first verbal symbols
target_learning_goals: acquisition and motivated use of spoken language
examples: the article's example: refusing to attend or gratify a desire indicated by gesture or inarticulate cry when the child can use verbal symbols
key_sources: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text

article_title: Nurturing a lexical legacy: reading experience is critical for the development of word reading skill
citation: Nation, K. (2017). Nurturing a lexical legacy: reading experience is critical for the development of word reading skill. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0004-7
title: The lexical legacy hypothesis: diverse, meaningful reading experiences build word-specific lexical knowledge measurable in word reading
description: The lexical legacy hypothesis holds that reading provides exposure to words in many different contexts, episodes and experiences which, over time, sum to a rich and nuanced database about each word's lexical history within an individual's experience. The article states that skilled word reading is, in part, a consequence of "experiencing words in diverse and meaningful language environments during reading experience", and that these encounters produce local variation at the word level that is measurable during word reading behaviour even in skilled adults.
requirements: Requires phonological decoding to be in place first, since reading experience can only exert its influence once children are able to read words
constraints: The article describes the hypothesis as speculative and under-specified, with mechanisms that bring about change not yet detailed
target_learners: children transitioning from novice to expert word readers
skilled adult readers
target_learning_goals: word reading skill and fluency
lexical quality and word knowledge
key_sources: Nation, K. (2017). Nurturing a lexical legacy: reading experience is critical for the development of word reading skill. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0004-7

article_title: Nurturing a lexical legacy: reading experience is critical for the development of word reading skill
citation: Nation, K. (2017). Nurturing a lexical legacy: reading experience is critical for the development of word reading skill. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0004-7
title: The lexical quality hypothesis: word representations specify spelling, sound and meaning, and quality drives processing
description: Perfetti's lexical quality hypothesis, as presented in the article, defines lexical quality as the extent to which a word's mental representation specifies its spelling, sound and meaning. High quality representations contain "tightly bound orthographic, phonological and semantic constituents" that support efficient word identification and free cognitive resources for comprehension. The article uses it as the processing framework the lexical legacy hypothesis feeds: lexical quality is both cause and consequence of reading skill differences.
requirements: A mechanism account linking knowledge to processing; the article notes lexical quality is both a cause and a consequence of differences in reading skill
constraints: The article states the mechanisms that bring about change in lexical quality are not yet detailed
target_learners: children and adult readers
target_learning_goals: word identification during reading
reading comprehension
key_sources: Nation, K. (2017). Nurturing a lexical legacy: reading experience is critical for the development of word reading skill. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0004-7

article_title: Creativity supports learning through associative thinking
citation: Luchini, S. A., Kaufman, J. C., Goecke, B., Wilhelm, O., Kenett, Y. N., Lei, D., Benedek, M., van Hell, J. G., & Beaty, R. E. (2025). Creativity supports learning through associative thinking. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00334-1
title: Learning Efficiency Test (LET) Lithuanian-English paired-associate paradigm with SemDis-scored verb generation for measuring associative learning and thinking
description: The LET assesses "how quickly and durably people acquire new verbal information" by having participants learn 45 Lithuanian-English word pairs over two days with iterative testing with immediate feedback and no-feedback final tests; Lithuanian was chosen to control for prior knowledge. Associative thinking was measured with a verb generation task scored for semantic distance via the SemDis platform using a GloVe model trained on a 6-billion-token corpus.
requirements: Participants must be English speakers with negligible prior Lithuanian exposure; the task is administered online on participants' personal computers
constraints: The authors state their studies employed a single word learning paradigm, and it remains unclear whether findings extend to non-language-based or visual learning or other task modalities
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory psychology
target_learning_goals: foreign-language vocabulary learning (paired-associate learning)
examples: Study 1 used 45 Lithuanian-English word pairs with 4 s presentation and iterative testing until all pairs were recalled; Study 2 added free and goal-directed verb generation conditions with 40 items each
key_sources: Luchini, S. A., Kaufman, J. C., Goecke, B., Wilhelm, O., Kenett, Y. N., Lei, D., Benedek, M., van Hell, J. G., & Beaty, R. E. (2025). Creativity supports learning through associative thinking. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00334-1

article_title: Language and nonlanguage factors in foreign language learning: evidence for the learning condition hypothesis
citation: Xin Kang, Stephen Matthews, Virginia Yip and Patrick C. M. Wong. (2021). Language and nonlanguage factors in foreign language learning: evidence for the learning condition hypothesis. npj Science of Learning 6:28. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00104-9
title: Learning condition hypothesis (LCH): similar learning conditions drive associations in language learning success
description: The LCH postulates that a primary factor determining proficiency levels of languages is the condition under which they are learned, rather than fundamentally different mechanisms for native and foreign languages. The article states: "We hypothesize that success in learning one language and the other may be linked, not due to a set of core functions for language learning, but because these languages are learned in similar conditions." It predicts that languages closer on a naturalistic-to-instructed continuum will show stronger associations of learning success.
requirements: Languages must be learned under describable conditions on a naturalistic-to-instructed continuum so that condition similarity between language pairs can be compared
constraints: The article acknowledges that age of learning covaries with the continuum of learning conditions and could be a confounding variable
target_learners: undergraduate foreign language learners
target_learning_goals: multilingual proficiency across first, second, and third languages
examples: 636 Hong Kong learners whose L1 (Chinese) was naturalistic, L2 (English) mostly classroom-based, and L3 instructed, spanning the continuum
key_sources: Xin Kang, Stephen Matthews, Virginia Yip and Patrick C. M. Wong. (2021). Language and nonlanguage factors in foreign language learning: evidence for the learning condition hypothesis. npj Science of Learning 6:28. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00104-9

article_title: Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex
citation: Taewon Kim, John J. Buchanan, Jessica A. Bernard and David L. Wright. (2021). Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex. npj Science of Learning 6:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00109-4
title: Left PMd plays a proprietary role in motor sequence learning and sleep-related consolidation of novel skill memories
description: The article advances and tests the account that left dorsal premotor cortex is specifically (propriately) involved in motor sequence learning and in sleep-related consolidation of novel skill memory. The authors state their data "are consistent with the proposed proprietary role of left PMd for motor sequence learning and the more recent claim that PMd is central to sleep-related consolidation of novel skill memory." The account explains why left- but not right-PMd stimulation during repetitive practice produced overnight offline gains matching interleaved practice.
requirements: Exogenous upregulation (anodal tDCS) targeted at left PMd during practice of novel motor sequences
constraints: Evidence concerns three novel six-element sequences practiced with the left index finger by right-handed young adults; the account is tested only for stimulation delivered during repetitive practice
target_learners: right-handed young adults (19–23 years) learning novel motor sequences
target_learning_goals: acquisition and sleep-related consolidation of novel motor sequence skills
examples: Anodal tDCS at left PMd during 20 min of repetitive practice produced overnight skill memory enhancement congruent with the IP-sham condition, while right-PMd stimulation did not
key_sources: Taewon Kim, John J. Buchanan, Jessica A. Bernard and David L. Wright. (2021). Improving online and offline gain from repetitive practice using anodal tDCS at dorsal premotor cortex. npj Science of Learning 6:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00109-4

article_title: Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach
citation: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8
title: Instruction should attend to how students select, link, and reorganize resources, and leverage rather than overwrite incorrect conceptions
description: Based on their neuroimaging findings, the authors recommend that physics instruction explicitly address resource selection and organization rather than focusing on accuracy alone. They state that "instruction that explicitly attends to how students select, link, and reorganize resources may be critical in developing appropriately compiled knowledge to map back onto control processes." They further argue instructors should leverage students' incorrect conceptions to facilitate conceptual change, transitioning existing resources into stable and accessible knowledge structures, because a focus on accuracy alone oversimplifies the complex processes engaged during physics reasoning.
requirements: Instructors must attend to the conceptual foundations of wrong answers, which reveal more about students' ability to succeed than simple accuracy measures
constraints: The authors caution it is a long path between brain imaging and the potential development of lesson plans
target_learners: undergraduate physics students
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in Newtonian mechanics
developing stable, coherently compiled physics knowledge structures
examples: The study used module analysis of FCI answer distributions to distinguish subgroups of similarly responding students and showed their conceptual approaches manifest as measurable brain differences during reasoning
key_sources: Bartley, J. E., Riedel, M. C., Salo, T., Boeving, E. R., Bottenhorn, K. L., Bravo, E. I., Odean, R., Nazareth, A., Laird, R. W., Sutherland, M. T., Pruden, S. M., Brewe, E. & Laird, A. R. (2019). Brain activity links performance in science reasoning with conceptual approach. npj Science of Learning 4:20. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0059-8

article_title: Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words
citation: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w
title: Two-week classroom learning sprint with counterbalanced word-to-class assignment
description: A reusable instructional-research pattern in which a fixed list of uncommon vocabulary words is semi-randomly divided among classrooms, each class teaching its assigned words for a short intensive period (~15-20 min per day, 5 days per week, two weeks) while other classes' words serve as counterbalanced controls. Activities focus on phonemic awareness, phonics, and writing, designed to help students attend to grapheme-phoneme relationships rather than rote visual memorization. Display boards and progress trackers support engagement; the word lists are matched on unigram, bigram, and trigram frequencies and orthographic neighborhood size.
requirements: Word lists matched across classes on sublexical properties; counterbalanced assignment of words to classes; daily instruction embedded in authentic classroom routines
constraints: The sprint teaches very low-frequency words (<1 per million); the article notes the design does not allow distinguishing among candidate explanations for the brain-behavior pattern
target_learners: early readers in mixed first- and second-grade classrooms
target_learning_goals: acquisition of novel written vocabulary and attention to grapheme-phoneme structure
examples: Teachers used laminated velcro display cards, vocabulary flashcards, spelling games, memory exercises, poetic exploration, Kahoot quizzes, and creative writing, all organic to the students' learning environment
key_sources: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia & Bruce D. McCandliss. (2025). Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00371-w
grain_size: unit (two weeks of daily instruction across three classrooms)

article_title: What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning
citation: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5
title: Learning analytics and the science of learning as mutually reinforcing fields bridging laboratory and classroom
description: The commentary proposes that learning analytics—"the integration and analysis of data from multiple sources to inform action", built on data science, psychology, business analytics and the science of learning—can form a fruitful collaboration with the science of learning. Psychology provides options for inferring learning from behavioural data; analytics supplies new tools to assess those options in real digital environments and helps verify laboratory patterns under controlled conditions against real-life observations. This positions analytics as bridging education, psychology and neuroscience through a common focus on behaviour.
requirements: Care about the inferences being made on the basis of data; strategies for use grounded in outcomes of education and psychology research
constraints: Learning analytics may not provide the ultimate answer to improving learning; behavioural data alone do not holistically capture student learning
target_learners: students in online and blended higher education environments
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting learning processes in real-life digital settings
examples: The article cites automated feedback provision and curriculum design as areas where learning analytics studies have been conducted, and notes potential for computational neuroscience to help refine predictive models
key_sources: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5

article_title: Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners
citation: Benjamin Gagl & Klara Gregorová. (2024). Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners. npj Science of Learning 9:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00237-7
title: Lexical Categorization Model (LCM): pre-lexical word-likeness-based filtering in the left-ventral occipitotemporal cortex
description: The LCM holds that the left-ventral occipitotemporal cortex, including the visual word form area, implements a lexical categorization process: "This process is assumed to ﬁlter non-words from further consideration for lexical or semantic processing." Categorization is easy for highly word-like words and word-unlike non-words but difficult when their word-likeness distributions overlap, producing an inverted-U relationship between categorization uncertainty and word likeness. The model has no free parameters, making simulations transparent, and word-likeness is estimated from a lexicon of all German words (SUBTLEX).
requirements: Requires a lexicon-based word-likeness estimate (OLD20 based on all German five-letter uppercase words from SUBTLEX-DE) to compute lexical categorization uncertainty.
Requires explainable machine learning methods and meaningful model-derived features for the individualized diagnostics built on it.
constraints: Prior extensive model comparisons with native German readers identified the LCM as adequate for lvOT activation; the article notes alternative approaches can simulate visual word recognition entirely, which the neuro-cognitive approaches currently cannot.
target_learners: adult non-native German language learners who are slow readers
potentially other slow-reader groups such as dyslexics and illiterates
target_learning_goals: reading speed
visual word recognition
lexical categorization ability
examples: The training procedure was motivated directly from the model: a lexical decision task with feedback trains the categorization process assumed in the left-ventral occipitotemporal cortex.
key_sources: Benjamin Gagl & Klara Gregorová. (2024). Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners. npj Science of Learning 9:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00237-7

article_title: Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners
citation: Benjamin Gagl & Klara Gregorová. (2024). Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners. npj Science of Learning 9:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00237-7
title: Three-session feedback-based lexical decision training with pre-post reading-speed diagnostics
description: The training pattern comprises three daily sessions of a lexical decision task — 1600 five-letter stimuli per week, including 800 SUBTLEX-DE words, 400 pseudowords, and 400 consonant strings — with immediate feedback (green/red squares after each response), preceded and followed by a standardized SLS reading speed assessment. Only the pre-test and first session data are used for outcome prediction. This task structure trains lexical categorization while monitoring general reading speed change at the sentence level.
requirements: Stimuli drawn randomly from a lexicon to represent natural variation in word characteristics, increasing feature generalizability.
A standardized sentence-level reading speed test (adult SLS) for pre-post diagnostics.
In control comparisons, at least 14 days between the two randomized training weeks.
constraints: The post-test placement differed across experiments (day 3 in Experiment 1, day 4 in Experiments 2 and 3), which the authors handled with a design-change variable in the predictive model.
target_learners: adult non-native German language learners
target_learning_goals: lexical categorization skill
reading speed
examples: In the font-change variant, the visual appearance of letter strings changed every 32 trials across 50 blocks, training adaptation of visual-orthographic representations alongside lexical categorization.
key_sources: Benjamin Gagl & Klara Gregorová. (2024). Investigating lexical categorization in reading based on joint diagnostic and training approaches for language learners. npj Science of Learning 9:29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00237-7

article_title: Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning
citation: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3
title: Allow learners to personalize learning paths in courses where topic dependencies are weak, using knowledge representation tools
description: The article proposes that when topic dependencies are not clearly defined, learners should be given freedom to access content without following the pre-defined sequence. It argues this is advantageous "based on their personal situations (e.g. background knowledge, time constraints)". Learning paths are to be built from finely grained, well-labelled knowledge units via backward design, and analysed with machine learning against background information and outcomes.
requirements: Learning contents must first be refined into finely grained and well labelled knowledge units
Easy-to-use software tools are needed to construct and modify learning paths
constraints: For courses with clearly defined topic dependencies (e.g. mathematics), letting all students follow the same learning path is advantageous
Learning outcomes are often hard to define and hard to measure; without a learning outcome objective function machine learning cannot compute optimized personal learning paths
target_learners: university-level MOOC learners, including working professionals with fragmented time
target_learning_goals: flexible sequencing of course content to fit learners' backgrounds and needs
examples: An Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction course was modelled in Goal Net with topics such as 'Universal Usability' and '8 Golden Rules' that can be taken in different orders
key_sources: Yu, H., Miao, C., Leung, C. and White, T. J. (2017). Towards AI-powered personalization in MOOC learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0016-3

article_title: Domain-Specific Modeling Languages in Computer-Based Learning Environments: a Systematic Approach to Support Science Learning through Computational Modeling
citation: Nicole M. Hutchins & Gautam Biswas & Ningyu Zhang & Caitlin Snyder & Ákos Lédeczi & Miklós Maróti. (2020). Domain-Specific Modeling Languages in Computer-Based Learning Environments: a Systematic Approach to Support Science Learning through Computational Modeling. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00209-z
title: Learning-by-modeling framework: knowledge acquisition through model building, simulation, analysis, evaluation and revision subprocesses
description: The framework (Fig. 1, adapted from the Common Core Mathematics Standards) characterizes computational modeling as multifaceted subprocesses of "building, evaluating, and revising of models based on the learners' underlying understanding of the domain theory and relations that govern the behavior of the model". It matches NGSS "Developing and Using Models" practices and defines the key processes an educational DSML must support; the authors investigate selected starred subprocesses in their case studies.
requirements: The modeling environment must support the subprocesses of model building, simulation, and analysis with interpretable representations
target_learners: K-12 students in STEM classrooms
target_learning_goals: STEM domain concepts and practices
computational thinking concepts and practices
examples: The authors map students' five documented difficulty categories onto the Fig. 1 subprocesses to motivate DSML design.

article_title: How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing
citation: Sovrano Francesco, Ashley Kevin, Brusilovsky Peter Leonid, Vitali Fabio. (2024). How to Improve the Explanatory Power of an Intelligent Textbook: a Case Study in Legal Writing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00399-w
title: Legal-writing case study corpus: over 16,000 documents yielding a knowledge graph of over 55 million RDF triplets
description: The case study applied YAI4Edu to 22 pages excerpted from the textbook "United States Legal Language and Culture" (Brostoff & Sinsheimer, 2013), 5,407 open access web pages from the Legal Information Institute encyclopedia and Wikipedia, and 11,198 legal cases on PTSD disability claims from the Board of Veterans' Appeals. Altogether 16,606 documents yielded 1,309,463 extracted questions and a knowledge graph whose total size was 55,046,923 RDF triplets (Table 1). The material supports teaching how to write a legal memorandum for a veteran's PTSD disability claim.
requirements: About ten manually added RDF triplets were needed to fill identified knowledge gaps such as "memo" being a synonym for "memorandum"
constraints: The whole extracted RDF graph was not thoroughly analyzed, so other knowledge gaps may yet emerge
target_learners: Students in the University of Pittsburgh course Applied Legal Analytics and AI
target_learning_goals: Writing legal memoranda, using statutes, reading and synthesizing cases, and making arguments with concrete cases
examples: The textbook is actively used in a University of Pittsburgh course co-taught by instructors from the School of Law and Carnegie Mellon's Language Technologies Institute

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: The shift from semantic learner modelling to behavioural particles interpreted by machine learning
description: Early AIED assumed a domain model, student model and tutor model gave actions semantics. New approaches capture "behavioural fragments or behavioural particles that, considered individually, do not convey very many semantics", such as gaze, posture, typing patterns and prosody, and process large data sets with machine learning. The author argues this drift from interpreting correct/wrong answers to interpreting behavioural dust is a fundamental evolution of the field.
requirements: Availability of cheap, small, non-intrusive sensors and algorithms able to process massive amounts of data
Careful selection of features, i.e. abstractions of raw data, since machine learning does not work well without them
constraints: Capturing anything that can be captured and running black box predictive algorithms may seem a caricature of science
target_learners: researchers in learning analytics and educational data mining
target_learning_goals: modelling learner states from low-semantic behavioural signals
examples: Raca et al. estimated lecture-room attention from the ratio of students' near-synchronous head co-movements
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: Jim Greer’s and Mary Mark’s Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals
citation: du Boulay, B. (2021). Jim Greer's and Mary Mark's Reviews of Evaluation Methods for Adaptive Systems: a Brief Comment about New Goals. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 622–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00198-z
title: A taxonomy of learner-focused evaluable goals extending outcome, efficiency, transfer, retention and short-term motivation measures
description: The article proposes that evaluation of adaptive systems should extend beyond Mark and Greer's goals to "a new range of evaluative goals which go beyond the quality of learning outcomes, learning efficiency, transfer, retention, and short-term motivation." Table 1 lists learner-focused evaluable goals a-n, adding metacognitive understanding and regulatory skill, meta-affective awareness and regulation of feelings, pleasure in learning for its own sake, participation in learning activities, and cooperation between learners, each with suggested measures such as think-aloud problem-solving, self-reports, open learner models and long-delayed post-questionnaires.
requirements: Evaluation designs must add measures such as think-aloud problem-solving, self-reports, open learner models, long-delayed post-questionnaires or long-term cohort studies to capture these goals
constraints: The rows a-g of Table 1 are those already covered by Mark & Greer; only h-n are new
target_learners: school and university learners using AIED and computer-based learning systems
MOOC learners
target_learning_goals: metacognitive understanding and regulatory skill
meta-affective awareness and regulation
longer-term motivation and appetite for further learning
examples: Table 1 lists goals including "Meta-cognitive understanding of the learning outcome, e.g. via think aloud problem-solving, observation of future learning" and "Increased pleasure in the act of learning for its own sake, e.g. via long-delayed post-questionnaires or interviews."

article_title: Encouraging Student Reflection and Articulation Using a Learning Companion: A Commentary
citation: Goodman, B., Linton, F., & Gaimari, R. (2016). Encouraging Student Reflection and Articulation Using a Learning Companion: A Commentary. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 474–488. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0041-4
title: Learning companion roles taxonomy: Weak Peer, Strong Peer, Expert, Motivator, Mentor, Teachable Agent, Facilitator, and Distributed Leader
description: The article organizes simulated pedagogical agents by the roles they can play: "Weak Peer, Strong Peer, Expert, Motivator, Mentor, Teachable Agent, Facilitator, and Distributed Leader." Each role carries distinct pedagogical support, from domain expertise to small-group dynamics, with pros and cons summarized in the authors' Table 3. For example, a Facilitator "requires knowledge about group dynamics to best support a group of learners." The taxonomy guides designers choosing a companion role for an ITS or CSCL environment.
requirements: The learning companion's pedagogical support depends on the pedagogical knowledge available to reason about learners' state and how to engage them
constraints: Each role carries stated cons, e.g., a weak peer's comments could confuse or frustrate the learner
target_learners: students in intelligent tutoring systems
learners in collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: domain learning through peer reflection and articulation
effective group collaboration skills

article_title: A Collaborative Case Study System for Distance Learning
citation: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307
title: LeCS: a web-based collaborative case study system for distance learning
description: LeCS (Learning from Case Studies) is a web-based system supporting collaboration between distant learners on case study activities. The article states that "LeCS is a web-based collaborative case study system that can be applied to any domain in which the learning from case studies method is used." It "provides a set of tools for geographically dispersed students working collaboratively on the case study solution," and its design was informed by an empirical qualitative study of paired distance collaboration.
requirements: Learners must be geographically dispersed and working on a case study activity suited to the learning from case studies method
target_learners: distance learning students working in pairs or small groups
target_learning_goals: solving case studies collaboratively at a distance
examples: The article describes LeCS's user interface, implementation, and agent-based architecture, and how it addresses recommendations derived from the empirical study.

article_title: Optimists’ Creed: Brave New Cyberlearning, Evolving Utopias (Circa 2041)
citation: Winslow Burleson & Armanda Lewis. (2016). Optimists' Creed: Brave New Cyberlearning, Evolving Utopias (Circa 2041). Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:796–808. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0096-x
title: Learning to Be and Learning to Live: lifelong, lifewide learning as the modus operandi of living
description: The article's organizing vision, drawing on UNESCO's 1972 'Learning to Be' treatise, frames learning as spanning the entire spectrum of life rather than age-bounded stages. It defines 'Learning to Live' as 'referring to both learning how to thrive in a new and evolving range of contexts and circumstances, as well as providing the modus operandi for living as learning.' Blended formal and informal environments, passion-based pursuits, mentoring in both directions, and the dissolution of retirement and life-stage boundaries underpin this framework, which the Holodeck is meant to serve.
requirements: Universal access to virtual and hands-on learning and innovation resources, including high-end tools and expert mentors
constraints: Articulated as a utopian projection circa 2041, not an evaluated design
target_learners: learners of all ages and stages
global population as active citizens
target_learning_goals: self-actualization
thriving across evolving contexts
passion-based learning
examples: Fig. 2 compares lifelong and lifewide learning in 2005 with 2040 conditions superimposed, expanding 2005 categories to a continuum spanning the entire spectrum of life

article_title: LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support
citation: Erwin Daniel López Zapata, Cheng Tang, Valdemar Švábenský, Fumiya Okubo, Atsushi Shimada. (2025). LECTOR: Summarizing E-book Reading Content for Personalized Student Support. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00478-6
title: LECTOR: discourse-based attention model estimating Slide-Topic relationships
description: LECTOR (Lecture slides and TOpic Relationships) is an attention-based model that estimates a Matrix of Slide-Topic relationships M from lecture slides. "LECTOR extracts a set of topic candidates from the lecture slides and assigns a unique score to each slide-topic pair"; the score is "a linear combination of two scores, one based on the words’ importance (Importance score) and the other on the similarity between the topic and the slide embeddings (Similarity score)". It uses a domain-specific pre-trained BERT model and leverages the hierarchical structure of slides, assuming the main title introduces the main discourse and each slide title introduces the slide's discourse. Multiplying M with slide-wise reading logs yields topic-based reading characteristics such as student topic preferences.
requirements: A corpus of lecture slides with textual content (extracted via BookRoll's OCR) for domain-specific BERT pre-training
Topic candidates defined as single nouns and 2-gram noun sequences extracted with a Bi-LSTM pretrained model for Japanese slides
constraints: Slides written in Japanese motivated a Bi-LSTM noun extractor because grammatical categories are harder to find; n was limited to 2 because longer noun phrases in Japanese tend to represent multi-topic ideas
target_learners: university engineering students in a programming theory course
target_learning_goals: contextualizing reading behavior with slide content to support at-risk student prediction and personalized support

citation: Gombert, S., Fink, A., Giorgashvili, T., Jivet, I., Di Mitri, D., Yau, J., Frey, A., & Drachsler, H. (2024). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00387-6
title: Learning activity: evaluating ten learning tips from a video in argumentative essays
description: A formative learning activity developed for educational psychology lectures at Goethe University Frankfurt. As the article describes it, "learners must first watch a video in which a German high school student presents ten learning tips" and then write short argumentative essays judging each tip's usefulness and connecting it to lecture contents such as learning strategies, memory concepts and motivation, with a separate paragraph per tip and APA-cited sources. examples: The ten tips include making systematic notes, not using the smartphone directly after learning, learning in rooms other than the bedroom, and staying hydrated

description: The Learning Analytics unit records, analyses and visualizes learning data related to students' activities, aiming to assist the tutor in understanding students' learning progress on search algorithms. It provides information on individual student performance, disaggregates by characteristics such as major and year of study, shows statistics and common errors, tracks hints requested, and uses data mining techniques to make predictions regarding student performance.

Automatic marking mechanism to provide grades

article_title: Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies
citation: Peters, M., & Fàbregues, S. (2024). Missed opportunities in mixed methods EdTech research? Visual joint display development as an analytical strategy for achieving integration in mixed methods studies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10234-z
title: Learning Ecology sensitizing model with learner activities, digital resources, and relationship interactions as core components
description: The article describes a Learning Ecology (LE) sensitizing model, derived from the literature on lifelong learning, online higher education, and human development and informed by Barron's (2006) ontological definition. It identifies "learner activities, material resources, and social relationships as the core components of an individual's learning ecology". Built prior to data collection following a sensitizing model technique, it served as a guiding heuristic to prepare lines of inquiry, develop research questions and interview protocols, and guide hybrid theory-driven thematic analysis.
requirements: Sensitizing models are derived from the research participants' perspective, using their language or expressions, and sensitize the researcher to possible lines of inquiry.
target_learners: Online postgraduate students
target_learning_goals: Understanding learning across formal and informal contexts
examples: The LE sensitizing model was used to develop the survey instrument through the MMR integration strategy of building at the design level.

citation: Beerwinkle, A. L. (2021). The use of learning analytics and the potential risk of harm for K-12 students participating in digital learning environments. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 327–330. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09854-6
title: Local education agencies should establish a clear oversight framework for digital learning analytics before using them
description: The article recommends that before K-12 agencies use the analytics generated by digital learning, they must first put an oversight framework in place. As printed: "local education agencies must first make sure they have a clear framework for oversight of how digital learning analytics will be used." The framework is a precondition for using analytics to improve student learning outcomes.
requirements: Local education agencies must have a clear framework for oversight of how digital learning analytics will be used before employing them.
target_learners: K-12 students in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: Ethical oversight of student data use in learning analytics
examples: The author urges this step because the 2020 pandemic move to digital learning produced a wealth of digital learning analytics available for improving student learning outcomes.

article_title: Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning
citation: de Barba, P. G., Oliveira, E. A., & English, N. (2025). Development and validation of a learning analytics rubric for self-regulated learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10521-x
title: Learning Analytics SRL Rubric for Canvas LMS
description: A learning analytics rubric developed to measure students' self-regulated learning processes within learning management systems in a scalable, consistent, and explainable manner. It maps items from validated SRL scales (MSLQ, OSLQ, MAI, A-SRL) onto Canvas LMS trace data indicators, using three key analytics features: materials and source type, study sessions, and lead-up versus normal days. The rubric employs an analytic structure with criteria based on the five-stage model of skill acquisition, and was validated with postgraduate students comparing self-assessments against system-generated scores.
requirements: Requires an LMS (Canvas) that logs page accesses with timestamps and resource type
Requires ungraded quizzes or similar identifiable extra activities in the LMS
constraints: Only 10 of 211 SRL scale items were feasible to map to LMS data (less than 5%)
Motivational and emotional/affective aspects of SRL and help-seeking behavior are under-represented
Thresholds for indicators were mostly arbitrarily defined due to lack of specific research
Indicator 8 (checking feedback on past assessments) was deemed not feasible because the software could not reliably identify when students were accessing feedback
target_learners: higher education postgraduate students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning processes including planning, monitoring, time and effort regulation, and learning strategies
examples: Indicator 1 reviews content across the semester to understand relationships between materials
Indicator 3 follows a weekly study schedule measured by average study sessions per week

article_title: Toward a Learning Technologies knowledge network
citation: Roy D. Pea, Robert Tinker, Marcia Linn, Barbara Means, John Bransford, Jeremy Roschelle, Sherry Hsi, Sean Brophy, Nancy B. Songer. (1999). Toward a Learning Technologies Knowledge Network. Educational Technology Research and Development (ETR&D), 47(2), pp.19-38. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190608
title: Learning technologies knowledge network — a distributed partnership model for TEL research
description: The article's organizing framework is a knowledge network: rather than a single laboratory, a center acts as a hub that "seeks to reach beyond these organizations to create a web of organizations, individuals, industries, schools,foundations, government agencies, and labs, that is devoted to the production, sharing and use $new knowledge about how learning technologies can dramatically improve the processes and outcomes of learning and teaching." The model works by convening theme-team workshops across disciplines and institutions, sponsoring distributed partnership projects, engaging business through an Industry Alliance Program, and training postdoctoral students, so that expertise in cognitive science, educational technologies, computer science, subject-matter learning, and engineering is combined.
requirements: Bringing together experts across cognitive science, educational technologies, computer science, subject matter learning, and engineering
Sponsoring research across disciplines and institutions
constraints: Depends on NSF funding and on the participation of partner organizations, industry, schools, foundations, government agencies, and labs

article_title: The relative effectiveness of training aids designed for use in mobile training detachments
citation: Research Abstracts. (1954). https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Choose the least complex, least expensive training aid that satisfies the training objective, since complex aids may add no effectiveness
description: Because the Air Force comparison found no appreciable effectiveness differences among six aid types, the abstract recommends economizing on aid complexity. It concludes that "some of the complex and expensive training aids may not be any more effective than less complex and less expensive devices" when objectives and lecture methods are similar. Cost and ease of production should therefore weigh in aid selection.
requirements: Training objectives and lecture methods similar to those employed in the experiment
constraints: The recommendation is limited to methods similar to those employed in the experiment

target_learning_goals: Maintenance of aircraft hydraulic, fuel, and rudder power control systems
