article_title: Exploring the impact of a CALL tool for emergent bilinguals
citation: Nicholas Feroce, Jenny Liu, Rajendra Chattergoon. (2025). Exploring the impact of a CALL tool for emergent bilinguals. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10462-5
title: Lexia English Language Development: a CALL tool for oral academic English in grades K-6
description: Lexia English is a computer-assisted language learning program for Emergent Bilinguals in grades K-6, released July 2020, intended to supplement rather than replace English language development instruction at 30-60 minutes weekly. It emphasizes oral language via speaking and listening activities, with 17 Emergent Bilingual characters guiding learners through scaffolded conversational interactions. A built-in Speech Recognition Engine measures correct usage of grammatical structures and provides instant corrective feedback by visually highlighting incorrect sentence segments, and an auto-placement tool suggests one of 19 starting levels.
requirements: Students are expected to use the online program between 30 and 60 min per week
Scripted teacher-led lesson plans are recommended for pre-teaching or reteaching skills
constraints: The program is intended to supplement, rather than replace, English language development instruction for ELs
target_learners: K-6 English learners / Emergent Bilinguals in US schools
target_learning_goals: Academic English oral language skills (speaking and listening)
English grammar and vocabulary
Discourse functions for discussing academic content
examples: A speaking activity in the lesson 'Evaluating with Esther using prepositions' focuses on the multi-word preposition 'in addition to' under the speaking purpose 'Evaluate' and the theme 'Protecting Earth's Resources'.

article_title: An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools
citation: Paul Macaruso, Shani Wilkes, Jen Elise Prescott. (2020). An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09785-2
title: Lexia Core5 Reading: a fully-blended learning program for elementary reading instruction
description: Core5 is described as "a fully-blended learning program which synchronizes the use of digital technology and offline materials employed by teachers in delivering their lessons." Its digital component targets six strands of reading—phonological awareness, phonics, structural analysis, automaticity/fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension—organized into 18 levels aligned to the Common Core State Standards. Students are placed by an embedded assessment, must complete units at 90%–100% accuracy, and struggling students receive adaptive branching to scaffolded tasks and then explicit direct instruction. Offline materials include Lexia Lessons for teacher-led small-group work and Lexia Skill Builders for independent practice.
requirements: Teachers track students' daily progress in the online component via the implementation dashboard and use these data to drive instructional plans such as administering Lexia Lessons
constraints: Students must complete each unit with 90%–100% accuracy before moving to subsequent units
target_learners: elementary school students in kindergarten through fifth grade, including at-risk and low-SES readers
target_learning_goals: reading skills across phonological awareness, phonics, structural analysis, automaticity/fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension
examples: In this study Core5 was incorporated into the ELA curriculum of three treatment charter schools alongside Wonders, with teachers offered Lexia's Implementation Support Service Package training modules
key_sources: Paul Macaruso, Shani Wilkes, Jen Elise Prescott. (2020). An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09785-2

article_title: Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review
citation: Alina Hase, Poldi Kuhl. (2024). Teachers’ use of data from digital learning platforms for instructional design: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10356-y
title: Learning analytics process model: awareness, reflection, sensemaking, impact
description: The review introduces Verbert et al.'s learning analytics process model as a framework for teachers' dashboard use. It comprises four stages: "(1) awareness, (2) reflection, (3) sensemaking, and (4) impact", in which people become aware of data, ask questions to reflect on it, answer questions to create new insights, and deduce consequences for their behavior. The review applies the stages to dashboards, noting few address the impact stage of actual behavioral consequence.
requirements: People need to be aware of the data, ask questions to reflect on the data, answer the questions and create new insights, and deduce consequences for their behavior
constraints: Few, if any, dashboards address Stage 4 of actual impact, per the review's quoted application
target_learners: K-12 teachers using learning analytics dashboards
target_learning_goals: Interpreting learning analytics data to improve teaching and enable individualized learning processes
examples: The review maps teachers' dashboard consultation during and after lessons onto the model's stages

citation: An, H., Sung, W. & Yoon, S.Y. (2022). Implementation of learning by design in a synchronized online environment to teach educational robotics to inservice teachers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10134-8
title: Learning by design (LBD) framework as the design basis for an online teacher-education robotics course
description: The learning by design (LBD) framework, associated with case-based reasoning and problem-based learning in design-based learning contexts, served as the source of the instructional design factors and teaching and facilitation strategies used to build the online robotics course. The authors state the course was designed "by applying instructional design factors as well as teaching and facilitation strategies derived from the learning by design (LBD) framework." The study examined the effects of these design factors via action research.
requirements: The framework requires instructional design factors and teaching and facilitation strategies derived from LBD to be implemented in the course design, as the article states it did.
constraints: The article examines LBD as implemented in one synchronized online robotics course for inservice teachers; effectiveness evidence comes from that single action-research study.

self-efficacy in robotics
problem-solving and collaboration strategies
confidence in teaching robotics

article_title: Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale
citation: Gandolfi, E., Soyturk, I., Kosko, K. W., Ferdig, R. E., & Clements, R. (2026). Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10619-w
title: Three-dimension framework of presence in XR (physical, social, and self-oriented presence)
description: The article adopts Lee's (2004) framework in which presence—the sensation of 'being there' in a technologically mediated environment—is examined from three angles: physical presence (interaction with physical elements, mediated by technology in XR), social presence (interaction with social actors and virtual characters), and self-presence (how users see and feel themselves, including identification with avatars). The article states these dimensions "collectively offer a holistic framework for designing, fostering, and measuring presence in XR environments" and reports the study's results support this framework.
requirements: Measurement instruments operationalizing the framework should capture emotional connectivity, co-presence, and self-awareness as distinct but related subscales
constraints: The article notes presence is one possible construct among alternatives such as immersion or engagement for evaluating mediated experiences
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and measuring presence in XR learning experiences
examples: The XRPS subscales used in this study map onto the framework's social and self-oriented dimensions

citation: Elizabeth R. Kazakoff, Paul Macaruso, Pam Hook. (2018). Efficacy of a blended learning approach to elementary school reading instruction for students who are English Learners. Education Tech Research Dev 66:429–449. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9565-7
title: Lexia Reading Core5 blended learning reading program
description: Core5 is a personalized, adaptive digital reading program for preschool through grade five, providing "a structured (i.e., explicitly teaches word identification and decoding), sequential approach" across phonological awareness, phonics, structural analysis, automaticity/fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. It contains 18 levels subdivided into 89 activities and 1,243 units of 4-8 minutes, with an adaptive auto placement tool, scaffolded guided-practice steps, immediate corrective feedback, individualized Prescriptions of Intensity (20–80 min per week), teacher reports, and offline Lexia Lessons and Skill Builders. In this study it was integrated into standard ELA instruction via station or lab rotation models.

constraints: Mastery of 90–100% accuracy within a level is required to advance to the next level

phonics
structural analysis
fluency
vocabulary
reading comprehension

article_title: Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD): Core purposes, distinctive qualities and current developments
citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Conceptions of learning (acquisition, participation, knowledge creation) change the design relation between tools and student activity
description: The article argues that writing on design for learning mostly adopts Sfard's 'acquisition' metaphor, and that the relation between what is designed and students' situated activity differs substantially across conceptions of learning. "If learning is seen as a matter of acquiring knowledge, then tools which are set in place for students are there to help them acquire that knowledge: they are solely a means to that end"; under participation, tools are there to be mastered; under knowledge creation, students design new tools as a legitimate outcome of their work.
requirements: Teachers need an expansive, nuanced conception of students' engagement in design
target_learners: university teachers
university students
target_learning_goals: designing for one's own learning as part of graduating as a lifelong learner
examples: The article states all three metaphors are valuable and cites Paavola et al. (2004) on knowledge creation

article_title: Designing AI-powered learning: adult learners’ expectations for curriculum and human-AI interaction
citation: Jinhee Kim, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick, Xi Lin, Na Li. (2025). Designing AI-powered learning: adult learners' expectations for curriculum and human-AI interaction. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10549-z
title: Three-type learner-AI interaction framework: cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interaction
description: The article organizes human-AI interaction in learning into three multifaceted types: "cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interactions" (Kim, 2024; Kim et al., 2022). Cognitive interactions are task-focused exchanges supporting content comprehension, thinking, reasoning, and knowledge construction. Socio-emotional interactions involve expression and regulation of emotions within collaboration, shaping the emotional and social dynamics of learning. Artifact-mediated interactions focus on how learners engage with AI through its interface, whose design characteristics shape the learning experience. The study uses this framework to structure its research questions and findings on supports adult learners need.
requirements: Learners need supports specific to each interaction type: metacognition and question-crafting for cognitive, ethical norms for socio-emotional, and interface design for artifact-mediated interaction
constraints: The article warns reliance on AI outputs may result in passive learning behaviors or reduce learners' critical evaluation skills, and poorly designed AI systems may frustrate users and reduce trust
target_learners: working adult learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: content mastery
lifelong learning habits
effective learner-AI interaction
examples: The study's interview guiding questions (Appendix A) were structured around cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interaction, and findings were organized into these three interaction themes
key_sources: Jinhee Kim, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick, Xi Lin, Na Li. (2025). Designing AI-powered learning: adult learners' expectations for curriculum and human-AI interaction. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10549-z

article_title: The learner centric ecology of resources: A framework for using technology to scaffold learning
citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: Learner Centric Ecology of Resources model of context
description: The model describes a learning context as "a set of inter-related resource elements, including people and objects, the interactions between which provide a particular context". The learner sits at the centre, with Knowledge/Skills filtered through Curriculum, Resources filtered through Administration, and Environment filtered through Organisation. Bi-directional arrows link Knowledge, Resources and Environment and link Curriculum, Administration and Organisation, while learner-to-Knowledge and learner-to-Environment arrows are uni-directional. It is offered as a design tool, an evaluation framework, and a lens for reconceptualising the learning-teaching process.
requirements: Requires mapping the elements present in an existing context, the links between them and potential barriers
constraints: Uni-directional learner arrows reflect the article's observation that learners' activity has little impact upon the nature of knowledge, curricula and environment organisation
target_learners: learners across formal school, home and informal community contexts
target_learning_goals: matching available resources to individual learners' needs across contexts
examples: The HOMEWORK system was analysed to show that for a limited curriculum and resources it addresses all links between the model's elements
The VeSEL Kambu water-melon scenario was mapped onto the framework to identify tensions and design interventions
key_sources: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2007.09.018

article_title: The learner centric ecology of resources: A framework for using technology to scaffold learning
citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: Learner Generated Contexts as a future direction for technology-supported learning
description: The article proposes that growing tools for capturing and publishing materials extend the capacity to create learning contexts beyond teachers, academics, designers and policy makers. "a Learner Generated Context is one in which a learner or group of learners marshall the resources available to them to create an ecology that meets their needs"; its key aspect is creation "through the enterprise of those who would previously have been consumers in a context created for them". The author identifies scaffolding learners to generate their own contexts as the key future challenge.
requirements: Increased understanding of how to scaffold learners to effectively generate their own learning contexts
constraints: Proposed as a future research agenda; the article offers a hypothetical community environmental centre example rather than an implemented system
target_learners: learners and communities acting as creators rather than consumers of learning contexts, e.g. community environmental centre volunteers
target_learning_goals: self-directed, collaborative learning around common, self-defined goals
examples: A sketched scenario in which community centre members collect and publish pollution data, maintain an environmental wiki, discuss local issues, attract politicians' attention and ground a volunteer course

article_title: The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction
citation: Hazzam, J., & Wilkins, S. (2023). The influences of lecturer charismatic leadership and technology use on student online engagement, learning performance, and satisfaction. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104809
title: Lecturer technology use as three-dimensional practice: delivery, enrichment, and transformation
description: Drawing on Lai and Jin (2021) and Ertmer et al. (2012), the article defines lecturer technology use as "the ability of the lecturer to use technology to deliver, enrich, and transform teaching and learning," measured via three sub-scales: technology use for delivery (presenting content effectively), for enrichment (engaging students in collaborative and interactive learning that fosters excitement), and for transformation (implementing new methods that enhance students' strategies and skills). This framework underpins the study's measurement of lecturer technology use and its hypothesized effects on engagement.
requirements: Lecturer knowledge about technology is described as "a crucial factor influencing the design of learning activities that engage students" — availability of technology alone is not sufficient

higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: online engagement
effective use of educational technology in teaching

article_title: Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation
citation: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010

description: The article recommends that mobile learning in museums allow learners' own devices rather than unfamiliar loaned hardware. constraints: Based on a project using loaned Jasjar PDAs with brief visits; the authors note distraction would likely lessen with more use.
target_learners: university-level design students
target_learning_goals: object-based learning in museums
independent research skills
examples: The project distributed 23 iMate Jasjar PDAs that students had not used before; 88.9 percent of surveyed students had never used a PDA.
key_sources: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010

article_title: Learning by explaining through digital devices: The role of the modality of oral explaining and extraversion
citation: Waldeyer, J., Hoogerheide, V., & Roelle, J. (2025). Learning by explaining through digital devices: The role of the modality of oral explaining and extraversion. Computers and Education, 237, 105394. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105394
title: Learning by explaining through digital devices as a generative learning strategy with theoretically plausible moderators
description: Learning by explaining through digital devices (e.g., computers or tablets) is a generative learning strategy in which learners explain lecture content to fictitious peers via digital media. The article frames it within meta-analytical evidence showing effectiveness "but also reveals substantial heterogeneity in effect sizes", motivating the study of moderators such as the modality of oral explaining and learners' extraversion.
requirements: Learners must explain lecture content to fictitious peer students using a digital device
constraints: Effects may be moderated by learner personality traits such as extraversion
target_learners: University students
target_learning_goals: Deep-level knowledge of lecture content
Surface-level knowledge of lecture content
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., Hoogerheide, V., & Roelle, J. (2025). Learning by explaining through digital devices: The role of the modality of oral explaining and extraversion. Computers and Education, 237, 105394. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105394

article_title: Exploring adaptive learning, learner-content interaction and student performance in undergraduate economics classes
citation: Ipinnaiye, Olubunmi; Risquez, Angelica. (2024). Exploring adaptive learning, learner-content interaction and student performance in undergraduate economics classes. Computers & Education, 215, 105047. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105047
title: LearnSmart adaptive learning tool on McGraw-Hill Connect platform
description: LearnSmart is an adaptive learning tool on McGraw-Hill Connect, a web-based assignment and assessment platform. It "allows content to be actively tailored to students' needs", assessing answers to practice questions, identifying struggling topics and adapting accordingly. A reading assignment is not marked complete until the student demonstrates adequate understanding, with immediate feedback and confidence rating options.
requirements: McGraw-Hill Connect platform access
Instructor content design dashboard for topic selection and assignment configuration
constraints: Licensed and hosted on McGraw-Hill Connect; assignments were only implemented during the first half of the course over one academic semester
target_learners: first-year undergraduate Business students
target_learning_goals: mastery of threshold concepts in Macroeconomics
metacognition and identification of knowledge gaps
examples: Used to create five weekly adaptive reading assignments with one-week deadlines in an introductory Macroeconomics course
key_sources: Ipinnaiye, Olubunmi; Risquez, Angelica. (2024). Exploring adaptive learning, learner-content interaction and student performance in undergraduate economics classes. Computers & Education, 215, 105047. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105047

article_title: Exploring adaptive learning, learner-content interaction and student performance in undergraduate economics classes
citation: Ipinnaiye, Olubunmi; Risquez, Angelica. (2024). Exploring adaptive learning, learner-content interaction and student performance in undergraduate economics classes. Computers & Education, 215, 105047. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105047
title: Learner-content interaction as a theoretical lens for adaptive learning effects on performance
description: The article uses learner-content interaction — "time spent with course content such as textbooks and class notes" — as a theoretical lens to explain how adaptive learning affects performance. It distinguishes learner-content interaction from learner-instructor, learner-learner and student-LMS interaction types, and measures it through two indicators: time spent and number of completed adaptive assignments. The lens frames assignment completion as capturing both adaptive learning use and cognitive engagement.
requirements: Multiple indicators of learner-content interaction, as a single measure may inadequately capture online participation
constraints: Generalisability is recognised as a challenge of using online traces to measure self-regulated learning
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: student engagement
academic performance in large undergraduate cohorts
examples: Applied to interpret patterns of engagement with LearnSmart adaptive assignments in first-year Macroeconomics
key_sources: Ipinnaiye, Olubunmi; Risquez, Angelica. (2024). Exploring adaptive learning, learner-content interaction and student performance in undergraduate economics classes. Computers & Education, 215, 105047. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105047

article_title: Tracking e-learning through published papers: A systematic review
citation: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007
title: Align e-learning usability with pedagogical quality and learner needs
description: The review's literature synthesis argues that usability in e-learning must be learner-centered: "The focus must be on the pedagogical aspects and not the technology in order to develop useful and functional tools." Usability is described as vital because it mitigates high dropout rates, low satisfaction, and staff workload. The review recommends aligning ease of use with pedagogical quality when developing e-learning tools.
requirements: Usability evaluation must place the user/learner at the center of the design process
constraints: The review notes there is still no consolidated evaluation methodology for e-learning applications
target_learners: higher education students
university staff and instructors
target_learning_goals: effective use of e-learning systems
reduced dropout and improved satisfaction
examples: The review cites usability features such as navigating and organizing educational contents according to individual cognitive styles
key_sources: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007

article_title: Tracking e-learning through published papers: A systematic review
citation: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007
title: Leximancer text-analysis software for systematic review coding
description: Leximancer is the qualitative data-analysis software the review used to extract meaning from the 99 retrieved articles. The article describes it as "a tool that adopts a quantitative approach, to conduct a qualitative analysis", using "Bayesian measurements that record the event of a word and associates it to the event of a progression of different words", coding fragments of content from one sentence to groups of sentences. It produced the concept map underlying the review's four-dimension framework.
requirements: Requires a corpus of text documents to analyze and produces concept maps from word co-occurrence
constraints: The article notes limitations due to the qualitative nature of the analysis
target_learners: researchers conducting systematic reviews
target_learning_goals: coding and synthesizing large bodies of educational literature
examples: The software produced the concept map in Fig. 1 grouping concepts into the four dominant topics
key_sources: Rodrigues, H., Almeida, F., Figueiredo, V. & Lopes, S. L. (2019). Tracking e-learning through published papers: a systematic review. Computers and Education. 136, 87-98. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.03.007

article_title: The Effects of Learning Stations Technique on Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Study
citation: Mevlut AYDOGMUS & Cihad SENTURK. (2019). THE EFFECTS OF LEARNING STATIONS TECHNIQUE ON ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYTIC STUDY. Research in Pedagogy, Vol.9, No.1. https://doi.org/10.17810/2015.87
title: Learning stations technique
description: The learning stations technique is a form of course processing in which students, divided into heterogeneous groups, rotate through pre-prepared learning and activity areas, working individually or in groups under teacher guidance. The article defines it as "a series of learning activities in specific areas created in the learning-teaching process" undertaken to learn or review a topic. It is presented as a student-centered, cooperative technique rooted in Montessori, Dewey, Piaget and Vygotsky, supported by multiple intelligences theory, and used in Turkish curricula since the 2005 constructivist reforms.
requirements: Stations are pre-prepared according to the feature of the subject
Students are divided into heterogeneous groups considering interest, dominant intelligence, learning profile, and classroom
target_learners: primary education students
secondary school students
university students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement across disciplines such as science, mathematics, social studies and Turkish
examples: In the included studies the technique was applied for 2 weeks in 30.8% of studies, 3-4 weeks in 38.5%, and 5 weeks or more in 30.8%, mostly in science and technology classes at primary level.
key_sources: Mevlut AYDOGMUS & Cihad SENTURK. (2019). THE EFFECTS OF LEARNING STATIONS TECHNIQUE ON ACADEMIC ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYTIC STUDY. Research in Pedagogy, Vol.9, No.1. https://doi.org/10.17810/2015.87

article_title: Improving Team Performance and Patient Safety on the Job Through Team Training and Performance Support Tools: A Systematic Review.
citation: Costar, D. M., & Hall, K. K. (2020). Improving Team Performance and Patient Safety on the Job Through Team Training and Performance Support Tools: A Systematic Review. Journal of Patient Safety. https://doi.org/10.1097/PTS.0000000000000746
title: Secure leadership involvement and project champions, and budget time to educate staff on a new teamwork tool's purpose and workflow fit, when implementing team training or performance support tools
description: Across the reviewed studies, the authors stress that leadership involvement and project champions are needed regardless of the specific teamwork practice used. Leadership support helps launch the practice, signals that tools are "critical to quality and safety of care rather than merely an additional administrative task", and reinforces sustained, correct use over time. Implementers should also educate staff on why a tool is being implemented, how it should be used, and how it fits established workflows.
requirements: Leadership endorsement and participation, plus time and due diligence to educate staff on the tool's purpose, use, and fit with established workflows, are needed for implementation and sustained compliance.
constraints: New protocols sometimes require greater time and team participation (e.g., longer handoffs, more team members completing checklist items), which the review notes may lead to some resistance and dissatisfaction.
target_learners: Frontline hospital staff in units such as operating rooms, intensive care units, emergency departments, and perinatal units
target_learning_goals: Sustained transfer of teamwork knowledge, skills, and attitudes to on-the-job performance; improved clinical processes and patient safety
examples: The review reports that leaders may endorse and promote training programs and participate in team training workshops, and that leadership can provide reinforcement when staff use support tools as intended.
key_sources: Costar, D. M., & Hall, K. K. (2020). Improving Team Performance and Patient Safety on the Job Through Team Training and Performance Support Tools: A Systematic Review. Journal of Patient Safety. https://doi.org/10.1097/PTS.0000000000000746

article_title: Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges
citation: Majid Memari, Krista Ruggles. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00105
title: Learning-by-teaching paradigm with AI tutees grounded in cooperative learning mechanisms
description: The review articulates a theoretical framework in which elementary students learn by teaching artificial tutees rather than receiving instruction from AI tutors. This pedagogical inversion—positioning the child as expert and the AI as learner—is justified by analogy to cooperative learning: meta-analytic evidence shows peer explanation and collaborative problem-solving link social interaction to cognitive growth in elementary mathematics. Educational robots and teachable agents can be designed to systematically elicit these processes through programmed responses "signaling confusion, requesting clarification, or demonstrating partial understanding", creating structured opportunities for explanatory and metacognitive verbalization within STEM contexts.
requirements: Robot or agent responses must be programmed to elicit explanation, clarification requests, and monitoring of the tutee's understanding
Measurement should capture concept explanations, strategy statements, metacognitive verbalizations, and scaffolding behaviors in student-robot dialogue
constraints: Direct experimental evaluations of educational robots or teachable agents deployed in elementary STEM classrooms remain limited; the framework rests on theoretical parallels with cooperative peer learning rather than direct tests
target_learners: Elementary students ages 5-12 acting as tutors to AI tutees
target_learning_goals: Content knowledge, metacognitive skills, and explanatory elaboration in STEM domains
examples: The review describes children explaining mathematical concepts to a robot "student", which requires articulating understanding clearly and revealing their own misconceptions
key_sources: Majid Memari, Krista Ruggles. (2025). Artificial Intelligence in Elementary STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Challenges. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00105

article_title: Educational technologies in problem-based learning in health sciences education: a systematic review.
citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Learning software and digital learning objects as PBL interventions
description: Learning software and digital learning objects were the most frequently examined technology type in the review, with 20 of 28 studies. Software included interactive distance learning programs, concept mapping, 3D visualization, CD-ROMs, Web-based learning portfolios, online virtual/simulated patients, video cases, online cases, and surgical decision-making simulations. The review reports these were used as an aid/supplement or a replacement for traditional formats such as lectures, dissection, and clinical practice, and for bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and clinical practice.
requirements: Integration of a computer-based learning tool into the curriculum is as important as the optimization of the software itself
constraints: One study found the PBL video scenario to be cumbersome and not imitating real life, therefore of little educational value
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate health sciences students
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction
clinical decision-making
collaboration outside the classroom
examples: The review reports that 91% of respondents rated the ErgoROM CD-ROM as either excellent or very good
key_sources: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240

article_title: Educational technologies in problem-based learning in health sciences education: a systematic review.
citation: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240
title: Learning management systems as PBL interventions
description: Learning management systems (LMSs) were examined in 3 of the 28 reviewed studies, including WebCT, VMS Portal, and iSUS. LMSs combine course or subject management and pedagogical tools to offer a means of designing, building, and delivering online learning environments. The review reports positive effects including practical guidance about what to learn and how to learn, feedback on accumulated real patient learning, peer comparison, and self-management support, with students perceiving LMSs as the most useful means of communication and resource delivery for PBL.
requirements: Monitoring, support, and development are important for efficient and positive implementation of an LMS in PBL curricula
constraints: Insufficient support, resources, and training might result in less successful implementation of educational technologies
target_learners: medical students in PBL curricula including placement students
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
communication and resource delivery
managing the learning environment
examples: The review reports that a Web-based LMS included 66 placement students in a PBL medical curriculum with questionnaire responses from 100% of students
key_sources: Jun J, Bridges SM. (2014). Educational Technologies in Problem-Based Learning in Health Sciences Education: A Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3240

article_title: Animation Model to Conceptualize ATP Generation: A Mitochondrial Oxidative Phosphorylation
citation: Jena, A. K. (2015). Animation model to conceptualize ATP generation: A study of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 61-76. https://scholar.google.com
title: Learner-controlled web animation of the electron transport system and ATP synthesis with student-authored animation models
description: The experimental treatment centered on a web-based animation of the electron transport system and ATP synthesis that learners could "forward, backward, and to run in slow modes or to stop the animated model at any time and at any step". Students used worksheets to prepare flow diagrams of ATP synthesis and were advised to install CorelDraw 7.0 to prepare animation models of different concepts themselves. Instruction covered respiration, glycolysis, Kreb's cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, ATP generation in mitochondria, and the electron transport system in 45-minute periods.
requirements: Viewing of the animation and graphic was under the supervision of the author; students needed system access to install CorelDraw 7.0
constraints: The application of technology and pedagogy in a single time is difficult for the teachers, as the article states
target_learners: undergraduate B.Sc. biology students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of chemiosmosis, the electron transport chain, and ATP generation
examples: The animated picture on chemiosmosis pumped protons through special channels in the mitochondrial membranes from the inner to the outer compartment
key_sources: Jena, A. K. (2015). Animation model to conceptualize ATP generation: A study of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 61-76. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1107841

article_title: The Effectiveness of CPS-ALM Model in Enhancing Statistical Literacy Ability and Self Concept of Elementary School Student Teacher
citation: Takaria. J, Rumahlatu. D. (2016). The Effectiveness of CPS-ALM Model in Enhancing Statistical Literacy Ability and Self Concept of Elementary School Student Teacher. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.25. https://www.iiste.org
title: Lecturers should foster positive academic self-concept through motivation, reinforcement, praise, developing strengths, responsibility, and objective judgment
description: The article holds that student academic self-concept is formed through learning interaction, and that lecturers can trigger positive self-concept by six actions, including "giving motiv ation and encouragement to students in lecturing", always giving reinforcement, praising academic achievement without jeering, developing students' interests and abilities, giving responsibility, and giving objective judgment of performance.
requirements: A lecturer acting as facilitator who gives attention, appreciation, praise and motivation while students solve statistical items
constraints: Stated in the context of statistics lecturing for elementary school student teachers
target_learners: elementary school student teachers
target_learning_goals: positive academic self-concept
motivation in statistics learning
examples: In the CPS-ALM condition the lecturer gave confidence for students to express themselves without differentiating ability, with attention and appreciation as enforcement when solving statistical items

article_title: The Impact of a Cooperative Learning Program on the Academic Achievement in Mathematics and Language in Fourth Grade Students and Its Relation to Cognitive Style
citation: Mery Luz Vega; Christian Hederich M. (2015). The Impact of a Cooperative Learning Program on the Academic Achievement in Mathematics and Language in Fourth Grade Students and its Relation to Cognitive Style. New Approaches in Educational Research 4(2), 84-90. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.2015.7.124
title: Learning Together cooperative program structure: small mixed teams with positive interdependence, individual responsibility, group processing and cooperative skills training across subject areas
description: The article implemented the Learning Together program following Arias et al. (2003): students were placed in small teams (groups of 2-4 students) that chose an identifying name, slogan and song, and classes were prepared "to promote Positive Interdependence and Individual Responsibility between students". Across 35 sessions (July-November 2009) covering math, language, natural sciences and social sciences, sessions included evaluations, group processing and cooperative skills training, with constant monitoring, support and a structured group-based evaluation of idea contribution, work quality, partners' support and group orientation.
requirements: Small teams with positive interdependence and individual responsibility, prepared materials, and monitoring with intervention in the groups from the fourth session onward
constraints: In this study the program's measured academic benefit appeared in mathematics but not in language, where reading activities were largely individual
target_learners: fourth-grade primary school students (ages 8-12)
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
language achievement
social and cooperative work skills
examples: Two groups of 4 students, eight groups of 3 and one group of 2 were formed; the first three sessions introduced cooperative learning and later sessions were divided by subject area, some including evaluations, group processing and cooperative skills training
key_sources: Mery Luz Vega; Christian Hederich M. (2015). The Impact of a Cooperative Learning Program on the Academic Achievement in Mathematics and Language in Fourth Grade Students and its Relation to Cognitive Style. New Approaches in Educational Research 4(2), 84-90. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.2015.7.124

article_title: Difference among Levels of Inquiry: Process Skills Improvement at Senior High School in Indonesia
citation: Hardianti, T. & Kuswanto, H. (2017). Difference among Levels of Inquiry: Process Skills Improvement at Senior High School in Indonesia. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 119-130. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_8.pdf
title: Levels-of-inquiry framework: teacher involvement decreases and student activity increases across inquiry levels
description: The article adopts Sutman, Schmuckler & Joyce's (2008) six-level inquiry framework, in which levels differ "in the roles of the teacher and the student." The Levels of Inquiry Instructional Matrix (Table 1) distributes pre-laboratory, laboratory, and post-laboratory responsibilities (proposing the problem, planning procedure, carrying out procedures and analyzing data, supplying answers, considering applications) between teacher and students. "The higher the level of inquiry, the more active the students in the learning; conversely, the lower the level of inquiry, the greater the role of the teacher." The study applied Levels 2, 3, and 4 of this matrix.
requirements: Teachers should understand the levels and choose one appropriate to students' competence and experience
constraints: Most students require lengthy training to develop their inquiring ability, motivating the division of inquiry into levels
target_learners: senior high school (SMA) science students
target_learning_goals: development of science process skills through staged inquiry independence
examples: Table 1 assigns at Level 3: teacher proposes problem and plans procedure; students carry out procedures, supply answers, and consider applications
key_sources: Hardianti, T. & Kuswanto, H. (2017). Difference among Levels of Inquiry: Process Skills Improvement at Senior High School in Indonesia. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 119-130. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_8.pdf

article_title: Gender-Related Effects of Group Learning on Mathematics Achievement among the Rural Secondary Students
citation: Hossain, M.A., & Tarmizi, R.A. (2012). Gender-related effects of group learning on mathematics achievement among the rural secondary students. Egitim Arastirmalari-Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 47, 1-22.
title: Learning Together model of group learning with five basic elements
description: The Learning Together Model is a group learning strategy developed by Johnson and Johnson (1994) that the authors implemented in rural Bangladeshi mathematics classrooms. It "consists of five basic elements such as positive interdependence, individual accountability, face to face promotive interaction, interpersonal and small-group skills, and group processing." Heterogeneous groups of two high-ability and two low-ability students, assigned by pre-test median, worked cooperatively on shared mathematical problems.
requirements: Groups must combine high-ability and low-ability students (two of each, assigned by pre-test median scores)
Teachers must be trained in the model and in selecting and assigning group members
constraints: The article reports implementation in grade-nine secondary mathematics classrooms in rural Bangladesh over 15 weeks
target_learners: grade-nine secondary school students in rural Bangladesh
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
examples: Students were assigned to four-member groups of two high-ability and two low-ability students and encouraged to share knowledge and solve assigned mathematical problems together
key_sources: Hossain, M.A., & Tarmizi, R.A. (2012). Gender-related effects of group learning on mathematics achievement among the rural secondary students. Egitim Arastirmalari-Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 47, 1-22. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057355

article_title: Effect of Teaching of Algebra through Social Constructivist Approach on 7th Graders' Learning Outcomes in Sindh (Pakistan)
citation: Bhutto Muhammad Ilyas, Khalid Jamil Rawat, Muhammad Tariq Bhatti, & Najeeb Malik. (2013). Effect of Teaching of Algebra through Social Constructivist Approach on 7th Graders' Learning Outcomes in Sindh (Pakistan). International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). http://www.e-iji.net
title: Reform teacher training, management, and curriculum toward learner-friendly, interactive pedagogy in developing countries
description: From the finding that social constructivist teaching outperformed traditional one-way teaching, the authors recommend systemic change: bringing professional degrees and courses in line with learner-friendly skills, creating a dedicated cadre of teacher trainers, changing head-teacher appointment criteria so teachers ensure learner-friendly pedagogy, revising curricula and examinations away from regurgitation toward standardized formative and summative assessment, and extensive refresher courses. They note low- or no-cost activities — "individual and group work, asking two-way questioning, allowing discussions" — "cost nothing but can change everything".
requirements: Stakeholder action on teacher training institutions, management and monitoring systems, and curriculum/examination bodies
constraints: The authors state a lot of work remains for a paradigm shift throughout developing countries; the supporting evidence is a single quasi-experiment
target_learners: public sector students and teachers in Pakistan and developing countries
target_learning_goals: learner-centered algebra and mathematics teaching
social interaction and collaborative learning skills
examples: The article recommends short-term country-wide refresher courses training public sector teachers in learner-friendly activities including two-way questioning, discussions, and low or no cost audio-visual aids
key_sources: Bhutto Muhammad Ilyas, Khalid Jamil Rawat, Muhammad Tariq Bhatti, & Najeeb Malik. (2013). Effect of Teaching of Algebra through Social Constructivist Approach on 7th Graders' Learning Outcomes in Sindh (Pakistan). International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085370

article_title: An Empirical Study on the Application of Cooperative Learning to English Listening Classes
citation: Min Han. (2015). An Empirical Study on the Application of Cooperative Learning to English Listening Classes. English Language Teaching, 8(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n3p177
title: Learning Together listening lesson pattern: heterogeneous four-member groups through pre-, while- and post-listening phases
description: The article implements Johnson and Johnson's (1987) Learning Together (Circles of Learning) model, which "lays stress on four aspects: face-to-face interaction; interpersonal and small-group skills; positive interdependence and individual accountability". Lessons divide the class into small heterogeneous groups (one advanced, two average, one weak student per group, chosen by pretest scores), then run pre-listening group discussion and prediction, while-listening discussion across three readings of the passage, and post-listening theme discussion with self, peer and teacher assessment and a reflection report.
requirements: Groups must be heterogeneous in cognitive ability, academic level, gender and language proficiency
A group of four students is recommended as the optimal number
Students need instruction in basic CL definitions and procedures before starting
constraints: The article notes listening materials may be too simple for some students and too difficult for others, and that tasks such as presentation and evaluation need much time
target_learners: college sophomores, non-English majors, B-class proficiency
target_learning_goals: English listening comprehension
oral expression and story-telling
cooperation and communication skills
examples: Unit 5 of Listening and Speaking (Course 3): students discussed youth-related questions, predicted the passage main idea, filled blanks across three readings with group discussion between readings, then discussed and presented on the Ashley story
key_sources: Min Han. (2015). An Empirical Study on the Application of Cooperative Learning to English Listening Classes. English Language Teaching, 8(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n3p177

article_title: The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students' Performance in Fractions
citation: Charalambos Lemonidis & Ioanna Kaiafa. (2019). The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students’ Performance in Fractions. Journal of Education and Learning, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v8n2p165
title: Lemonidis curriculum for rational number teaching (fractions before decimals, understanding-first, learning trajectories)
description: An integrated proposal for teaching fractions and decimals in elementary school from the 1st to the 5th grade, used as the common curriculum for both study groups. Its main innovations are that fraction teaching precedes decimal teaching (fractions in 3rd grade, decimals in 4th), emphasis on "understanding of the concept of fraction and the procedures" before rules and written algorithms, support for developmental progressions based on a Learning Trajectories Approach, use of everyday contexts, problem solving, storytelling and educational technologies, many fraction models for visualization, and emphasis on mental calculation and estimation.
requirements: teaching materials (student book, workbook, teacher's book) developed in accordance with the curriculum's principles and objectives
constraints: in this study only the trajectory part addressed to 3rd grade students was used
target_learners: elementary school students, grades 1-5
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of fractions and decimals
number sense
problem-solving skills
examples: Key points of the 3rd-grade learning trajectory: recognizing and formatting unit fractions and simple fractions, placing fractions on a number line, comparing fractions with common numerator or denominator, recognizing and creating equivalent fractions using models
key_sources: Charalambos Lemonidis & Ioanna Kaiafa. (2019). The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students’ Performance in Fractions. Journal of Education and Learning, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v8n2p165

article_title: Constructive Feedback: An Effective Constituent for Eradicating Impediments in Writing Skills
citation: Malik Ajmal Gulzar, Sartaj Fakhar Jilani & Choudhary Zahid Javid. (2013). Constructive Feedback: An Effective Constituent for Eradicating Impediments in Writing Skills. English Language Teaching, 6(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n8p21
title: Match writing tasks to learner proficiency: controlled, guided and free writing by level
description: The article recommends differentiating writing tasks by student proficiency: "controlled writing tasks for very poor students guided writing tasks for moderate students and free writing tasks for relatively good students". Combined with error rectification and positive feedback, the authors claim this can raise students' written English standard. It responds to the mixed-ability, overcrowded classrooms described in the Pakistani context.
requirements: The teacher must assess student levels and assign controlled, guided, or free writing tasks accordingly while rectifying errors and giving positive feedback.
target_learners: mixed-ability secondary EFL students
target_learning_goals: written English composition skills
examples: The recommendation is offered as a method teachers can apply while rectifying errors and giving positive feedback about mistakes.

The article reports that "Most of the activities, such as a KWL (Know, Want, Learned) Table, mind maps, and videos, addressed different learning styles at the same time", with separate activity lists for visual (pictures, highlighting, scanning, videos), auditory (group discussion, listening to the text, oral summaries), and kinesthetic/tactile learners (role-play, paragraph puzzles, drawing). article_title: Applying Computer-Assisted Musical Instruction to Music Appreciation Course: An Example with Chinese Musical Instruments
citation: Lou, S.-J., Guo, Y.-C., Zhu, Y.-Z., Shih, R.-C., & Dzan, W.-Y. (2011). Applying computer-assisted musical instruction to music appreciation course: An example with Chinese musical instruments. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Learning-theory bases for computer-assisted teaching styles
description: The article organizes computer-assisted teaching system styles by their underlying learning theories: behavioral, cognitive, constructivist and situated learning. It states that "Style models for computer-assisted teaching systems can be characterized as tutoring, practicing, simulating, game playing or testing," and maps the behavioral approach to practice-style multimedia CAI emphasizing existing knowledge, the cognitive approach to tutor-style CAI emphasizing new information, and situation learning theory to simulation-style multimedia CAI. Constructivism implies giving students appropriate freedom to control the learning process, with the teacher as guide and assistant.

citation: Serin, O. (2011). The effects of the computer-based instruction on the achievements and problem solving skills of the science and technology students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Three-category taxonomy of computer use in science education: learning about, with, and through computers
description: The article adopts a categorization, attributed to Bybee, Poewll, & Trowbridge (2008), in which "the overlapping terms related to the uses of computer and associated technologies in science education are categorized into three": learning about computers (knowledge of computers and their parts), learning with computers (computers as tools for data acquisition, analysis, communication and information retrieval), and learning through computers (computer as an aid for presentations, practice and drill, with immediate feedback and self-paced work). The study itself involves mainly learning through computers as well as learning about computers.
requirements: The categories distinguish the learner's relationship to the computer: object of study, tool, or medium of instruction.
constraints: The taxonomy is attributed to Bybee, Poewll, & Trowbridge (2008) as reported via Owusu et al. (2010); the article applies it to science education terminology.

article_title: Mixed Results from Six Large Randomized Controlled Trials of Learning Communities in Community Colleges
citation: Mayer, A. K., Weiss, M. J., Visher, M. G., Sommo, C., Weissman, E., & Wathington, H. D., with Durkin, K., Fresques, H., & Teres, J. (2013). Mixed Results from Six Large Randomized Controlled Trials of Learning Communities in Community Colleges. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Theory of change for learning communities: linked classes increase engagement and connection, leading to higher-order thinking, course mastery, and persistence
description: The article describes the theory of change underlying learning communities as a causal chain: grouping students into cohorts enrolled together in linked classes fosters engagement and social connection, which in turn supports skill development and continued enrollment. As printed, "The theory of change for learning communities predicts that students in them will become more engaged in what they are learning and more connected with each other and with their instructors." The theory then predicts students "will then be more likely to develop higher-order thinking skills, master the course material, pass their classes, and persist from semester to semester." The six trials test this chain, and the mixed results qualify its later links.
requirements: Programs consist of groups of students who enroll together in two or more linked classes, often with shared assignments and curricula and collaboration between faculty teaching pairs
constraints: The trials tested typical programs as enacted, not the ideal or advanced learning communities described in the literature
target_learners: community college students, nearly all of whom required some developmental education classes
target_learning_goals: course passing and persistence
higher-order thinking skills
degree completion
examples: The six trials measured the chain's outcomes: engagement-related supports, credits in the targeted subject, persistence, and six-year degree completion at Kingsborough
key_sources: Mayer, A. K., Weiss, M. J., Visher, M. G., Sommo, C., Weissman, E., & Wathington, H. D., with Durkin, K., Fresques, H., & Teres, J. (2013). article_title: Mixed Results from Six Large Randomized Controlled Trials of Learning Communities in Community Colleges
citation: Mayer, A. K., Weiss, M. J., Visher, M. G., Sommo, C., Weissman, E., & Wathington, H. D., with Durkin, K., Fresques, H., & Teres, J. (2013). Mixed Results from Six Large Randomized Controlled Trials of Learning Communities in Community Colleges. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: One-semester learning community programs with four components: linked courses and cohorts, faculty collaboration, integrated instructional practices, and student supports
description: The intervention evaluated across the six trials was a one-semester learning community built from four components, with variation in emphasis and implementation across sites. The components are linked courses and student cohorts (groups of students enrolling together in two or more courses, often scheduled back-to-back), faculty collaboration (instructors of linked courses planning and running classes together), instructional practices emphasizing integrated instruction and active and collaborative learning such as group work and hands-on assignments, and student supports such as tutors, designated counselors, or supplemental instruction. At Kingsborough some learning communities did not include developmental education classes, while at the other colleges all did.
requirements: Instructors of the linked courses collaborated to plan and run their classes
Teaching methods focused on integrated instruction, emphasizing the interconnections between the linked courses
constraints: There was variation in the emphasis and implementation of the four components across programs

target_learning_goals: credits earned in the targeted subject
persistence
degree completion
examples: At Houston Community College, the largest college in the study, the learning communities operated within a six-college system serving over 40,000 students each fall

article_title: Writing-Reading Relationships: Effectiveness of Writing Activities as Pre-Reading Tasks to Enhance L2 Inferential Reading Comprehension
citation: Wickramaarachchi, T.I. (2014). Writing-Reading Relationships: Effectiveness of Writing Activities as Pre-Reading Tasks to Enhance L2 Inferential Reading Comprehension. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(5). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.5p.213
title: Levels-of-comprehension theory: literal, inferential and evaluative reading comprehension
description: The article adopts the levels of comprehension theory, which "hypothesizes three levels of reading comprehension as, literal, inferential and evaluative". Inferential comprehension is positioned as the level after literal comprehension, requiring readers to go beyond recognizing what an author wrote by "reading between the lines" to infer intended meaning. The study targets this level specifically, measuring it through sub-skills drawn from Keene and Zimmerman (1997) and Barret (1974), such as drawing conclusions, making predictions, and inferring main idea and sequence.
requirements: Measurement must target inferential sub-skills such as drawing conclusions, predictions, main idea, sequence, and critical judgment, as the study's MCQs did
constraints: The study examines only inferential comprehension, not literal or evaluative levels
target_learners: first-year ESL undergraduates with lower intermediate English proficiency
target_learning_goals: inferential reading comprehension in English as a second language
examples: The study's instrument used 10 MCQs per passage mapped to seven inferential sub-skills including drawing conclusions and identifying sequence

article_title: The Effect of Lexical Bundles on Iranian EFL Learners Linguistic Production Fluency
citation: Ranjbar, N., Pazhakh, A., & Gorjian, B. (2012). The Effect of Lexical Bundles on Iranian EFL Learners Linguistic Production Fluency. International Education Studies, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n4p243
title: Lexical bundles: recurrent formulaic multiword expressions with a four-category functional taxonomy
description: Lexical bundles, coined by Biber, Johansson, Leech, Conrad, and Finegan (1999), are defined as "recurrent expressions, regardless of their idiomaticity, and their structural status", with frequency the most salient defining characteristic. The article applies a functional taxonomy whose "four core categories in this taxonomy, used in the current study are: referential bundles, text organizers, stance bundles, and interactional bundles", tied to Halliday's ideational, interpersonal, and textual metafunctions. The study uses this framework to justify teaching bundles as prefabricated units that learners can memorize and automatically retrieve during writing.
requirements: A word combination counts as a bundle only if it meets the frequency and range criterion: at least ten occurrences per million words across at least five different texts
constraints: The taxonomy was designed using the most frequent bundles in conversation and academic prose, not classroom teaching registers
target_learners: Iranian EFL university students majoring in TEFL
target_learning_goals: Paragraph writing production fluency
examples: The study instructed the experimental group on lexical bundles extracted from the True to Life textbook across conversation, role play, paragraph writing, and discussion contexts

article_title: A Study of Geometry Content Knowledge of Elementary Preservice Teachers
citation: Fatma Aslan-Tutak and Thomasenia Lott Adams. (2015). A Study of Geometry Content Knowledge of Elementary Preservice Teachers. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(3), 301-318. https://www.iejee.com
title: Learning for geometry teaching activities: geometry activities plus student work analysis
description: The intervention consisted of two activity types: geometry activities (sorting shapes, attributes of shapes, classification of polygons) and a pedagogical activity analyzing elementary students' geometry work. Participants completed a worksheet of open-ended definition questions and 10 quadrilateral figures, then analyzed six selected student worksheets in pairs and small groups using a protocol, discussing what the student knew, misconceptions, and how to teach the concepts. The combination of activities "provided coherence" across individual, pair, and whole-class formats.
requirements: Student work used for professional development should be challenging in terms of students' errors, per Kazemi and Franke
constraints: Preservice teachers only experienced the materials as students without teaching them, which the authors flag as possibly limiting effectiveness
target_learners: elementary school preservice teachers
target_learning_goals: specialized content knowledge of geometry and analysis of student mathematical thinking
examples: Six students' worksheets providing the most challenging geometry ideas were selected from classrooms with mathematically struggling students

article_title: Closing the Loop: Automated Data-Driven Cognitive Model Discoveries Lead to Improved Instruction and Learning Gains
citation: Ran Liu, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2017). Closing the loop: Automated data-driven cognitive model discoveries lead to improved instruction and learning gains. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 9, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/
title: Learning Factors Analysis: automated combinatorial search for improved knowledge component models
description: Learning Factors Analysis (LFA) is a data-driven method for improving cognitive (KC) models. It "performs a combinatorial search process across hypothesized knowledge components (KCs) drawn from existing cognitive models," using split, merge, or add operators on expert-labeled variables, and outputs the best-predicting model as a symbolic model that eases interpretation. Applied across 11 DataShop datasets, it improved fit beyond the best human-generated KC models in all of them. In this article, LFA's circle-area split was interpreted, validated on novel data, and used to redesign a geometry tutor.
requirements: Requires an initial expert-labeled KC model and hypothesized difficulty factors that can be used to attempt splits and merges.
constraints: It cannot produce large structural changes to KC models, per the article's stated limitations.
target_learners: K-12 and high school students using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Improved cognitive models for adaptive practice and accurate assessment of student knowledge
key_sources: Ran Liu, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2017). Closing the loop: Automated data-driven cognitive model discoveries lead to improved instruction and learning gains. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 9, No 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1155896

article_title: The Visual Memory-Based Memorization Techniques in Piano Education
citation: Yucetoker, I. (2016). The visual memory-based memorization techniques in piano education. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 65, 111-128. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.65.07
title: Learning-style-matched memorization instruction in piano education
description: The article proposes that piano students have different learning styles (visual, audio, kinesthetic) and that memorization instruction should be matched to the student's dominant style. Visual students perceive notes as figures and are good note readers but struggle with memorization; supporting them with visual elements addresses this specific difficulty. The framework draws on the distinction between primary learning areas (playing, reciting, interpretation) and secondary learning areas in piano pedagogy.
requirements: Assessment of each student's learning style before selecting memorization techniques
constraints: Only the visual student type was empirically tested in this study

citation: Aljraiwi, S. (2019). Effectiveness of Gamification of Web-Based Learning in Improving Academic Achievement and Creative Thinking Among Primary School Students. International Journal of Education and Practice, 7(3), 242-257. https://doi.org/10.18488/journal.61.2019.73.242.257
title: Level-based lesson structure with points-gated progression
description: In the designed environment, "Each lesson represents a level. At the end of the level, the teacher runs a formative assessment and educational activities in which the learner receives points." Learners scoring below the established percentage repeat the lesson, while those exceeding it move to the next level until reaching the top. Content was sequenced easiest-first to build understanding and motivation.

article_title: The Effect of Using Learning Journals on Developing Self-Regulated Learning and Reflective Thinking among Pre-Service Teachers in Jordan

description: A learning journal is defined in the study as "a hand written in a notebook or on a pad of paper as a means for recording thoughts, reflections, feelings, personal opinions, and even hopes or fears during an educational experience (Hiemstra, 2001)". In this study, students filled journals at the beginning or end of lessons, in class or at home, about their understanding, the learning process, difficulties, attitudes and feelings. The instructor checked entries and used notes as feedback to modify teaching decisions. Journals were initially evaluated pass/fail with extensive feedback rather than numerically graded.

Instructor checking of entries and feedback

university students

The first hour introduced systems and troubleshooting and taught subjects to use the Visual Understanding Environment (VUE) open-source software to develop conceptual and process maps on a simple practice problem. The second phase presented two technical problems developed with industrial partners — an electrical grid distribution system and a malfunctioning heat exchanger — for which subjects analyzed system descriptions and operational tables and produced process maps.

article_title: Lesson Study with Mathematical Resources: A Sustainable Model for Locally-Led Teacher Professional Learning
citation: Catherine Lewis & Rebecca Perry. (2014). Lesson Study with Mathematical Resources: A Sustainable Model for Locally-led Teacher Professional Learning. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development. https://www.merga.net.au
title: Lesson study as collaborative study-plan-do-reflect inquiry cycles that build knowledge, beliefs, norms, routines, and materials for continuing instructional improvement
description: The article models lesson study as collaborative inquiry cycles in which "teachers conduct collaborative 'study–plan–do–reflect' inquiry cycles designed to improve classroom instruction". Teams study curriculum content and long-term goals, plan a research lesson taught by one member while others collect data on student learning, then discuss the data in post-lesson reflection. A theoretical model (Figure 1) links Desimone's five features of effective professional learning — active learning, collective participation, content focus, duration, coherence — to intervening changes in teacher knowledge, beliefs, professional community, and instructional materials.

constraints: Honing a single lesson is not typically the primary goal of lesson study as practised in Japan

educator teams conducting professional learning
target_learning_goals: improvement of classroom instruction and student learning
teacher content and pedagogical knowledge
examples: Experimental groups in this study independently completed the four-phase cycle over an average period of 91 days, video-recording meetings and mailing artefacts to researchers

article_title: Effects of Cooperative Learning on Learning Achievement and Group Working Behavior of Junior Students in Modern French Literature Course
citation: Orprayoon, S. (2014). Effects of Cooperative Learning on Learning Achievement and Group Working Behavior of Junior Students in Modern French Literature Course. The Journal of Effective Teaching, Vol. 14, No.1, 80-98. https://uncw.edu/jet
title: Learning Together technique of cooperative learning (Johnson & Johnson)
description: Learning Together is one model of cooperative learning presented by Johnson & Johnson (1994), whose principles the article lists as "heterogeneous grouping, positive interdependence, individual accountability, social skills, and group processing". Positive interdependence is formed through common goals, identity, resources and rewards; individual accountability is regulated through individual preparation and testing, responses to teacher questions, and presentation of group work; group processing gives evidence of group achievement and plans further cooperative activity. The article selected it as the most appropriate method because it requires equal contribution and accountability of each member.

Positive interdependence formed through a common goal, common identity, same resources and same reward
Individual accountability through individual preparation and testing and presentation of group work

group process and problem solving skills
presentation skills
learning achievement in Modern French Literature

article_title: Enhancing Information Systems Auditing Knowledge with Role-Playing Game: An Experimental Investigation
citation: Nitaya Wongpinunwatana. (2013). Enhancing Information Systems Auditing Knowledge with Role-Playing Game: An Experimental Investigation. International Education Studies, 6(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n9p72
title: Involve the lecturer as an in-game actor who instructs and guides students throughout a role-playing game
description: The article finds that learning from a role-playing game occurred only when the lecturer participated as an actor. The lecturer "instructed and provided guidelines to students to perform information systems audit throughout the game", answered questions in role, coached interviewing, and defended audit findings during discussion. The author attributes the observed learning gains to this mediation, contrasting them with prior findings that games interfered with learning.
requirements: A lecturer willing to take on company-staff roles and provide step-by-step guidance and support during the game sessions
constraints: The study tested this only in an IS audit course with graduate accounting students using a one-group pretest-posttest design, so the mediation account is the author's interpretation rather than a tested contrast
target_learners: graduate accounting students training as IS auditors
target_learning_goals: information systems audit knowledge and practical auditing skills
examples: In the experiment the lecturer played company staff, provided answers to students' questions, helped students explore the art of interviewing, and discussed and defended audit findings with each group

article_title: Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China
citation: Xiaoye Lu, Xin Cheng, Ke Li, Kenneth Ka Ho Lee & Xuesong Yang. (2016). Integration of Histology Lectures and Practical Teaching in China. International Journal of Higher Education, 5(4). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n4p157
title: Interleaved lecture-practice-lecture-practice sessions alternating with practice-lecture-practice according to content
description: The integrated histology course replaces separated lecture blocks with sessions in the morphology laboratory where short lecture segments alternate with immediate microscope practice. Teaching patterns "lecture-practice-lecture-practice" and "practice-lecture-practice" were "alternatively employed according to the content", with theory and practice in a 2:1 proportion. For example, muscular tissues began with slide observation to build perceptual knowledge before the lecture, then a second observation round.
requirements: Sessions held in a laboratory equipped with light microscopes, virtual microscopy, computers with digital panorama imaging system and multimedia teaching system
constraints: Theory-to-practice time proportion of 2:1 in the integrated course; capacity limited by laboratory size
target_learners: second-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: histology: microscopic structure of human tissues and organs
examples: The Epithelial Tissues session (Table 1) used three 120-minute class sessions alternating teacher explanations with guided slide viewing, an on-class practical quiz, and homework via a digital panoramic system and Blackboard course website.
