article_title: Raising Awareness of Lexical Semantic Relations in Undergraduate EFL Context
citation: Mehmet ALTAY. (2017). Raising Awareness of Lexical Semantic Relations in Undergraduate EFL Context. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(1), 42-52. https://novitasroyal.org
title: Taxonomy of lexical semantic relations as constituents of learners' schemata
description: The article organizes lexical semantic relations into 'has-a' relations and 'is-a' relations, noting "there is not only one specific taxonomy in the literature". Has-a relations cover meronymy (part to whole, with necessary or optional parts) and its converse holonymy. Is-a relations include hyperonymy and hyponymy (super-subordinate inclusion), troponymy for verb synsets expressing manner, plus polysemy, homonymy, metonymy, synonymy and antonymy. The article treats these relations as basic lexical constituents necessary for large-scale and long-term vocabulary growth within learners' schemata.
requirements: Awareness of these relations is assumed to support relating new vocabulary items to existing schemata rather than treating words as isolated
constraints: The article states the taxonomy is conflicting in many occasions and offers only vague descriptions due to the flexible nature of context
target_learners: Undergraduate EFL learners
lexicographers and language teachers
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary growth through structured mental lexicon development
key_sources: Mehmet ALTAY. (2017). Raising Awareness of Lexical Semantic Relations in Undergraduate EFL Context. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(1), 42-52. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1167230

article_title: Glossing Frequency and L2 Reading Comprehension: The Influence of CALL Glossing
citation: Taylor, A. M. (2014). Glossing Frequency and L2 Reading Comprehension: The Influence of CALL Glossing. CALICO Journal, 31(3). https://doi.org/10.11139/cj.31.3.374-389
title: Lexical threshold and noticing-the-gap account of how L1 glossing supports L2 reading comprehension
description: The article frames L1 glossing through lexical threshold theory, in which "95% lexical coverage is a threshold for basic understanding of most texts" and optimal comprehension is about 98% coverage, with glosses making up the small percentage of unknown text. It links gloss consultation to noticing the gap (Schmidt; Swain): the learner notices a comprehension mismatch, compares L2 to L1, and forms a form-meaning connection if developmentally ready. Glossing is treated as input manipulation whose benefit depends on learner attention and need.
requirements: Glossed items must be essential to understanding the text and the learner must attend to the glossed item
constraints: Learners may not be developmentally ready for a glossed item, in which case it may be partially learned but not fully integrated into the interlanguage system
target_learners: L2 readers of glossed texts
target_learning_goals: L2 reading comprehension
lexical acquisition
examples: The article re-analyzes Prichard and Matsumoto (2011), arguing that combining pretest and posttest effect sizes (-.73 and .27, yielding 1.01, p = .0001) suggests approaching the 95% threshold can still produce a significant result.
key_sources: Taylor, A. M. (2014). Glossing Frequency and L2 Reading Comprehension: The Influence of CALL Glossing. CALICO Journal, 31(3). https://doi.org/10.11139/cj.31.3.374-389

article_title: The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course
citation: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Learning mode as a combination of learning style and multimedia preference
description: The article defines learning mode as "a combination of learning style and multimedia preference that is used in the adaptive e-learning system". It is measured by online questionnaires yielding an ls dimension (sequential versus global) and an mm dimension (multimedia versus non-multimedia), each scored from -11 to +11 with six preference-interpretation levels. Depending on questionnaire scores, the system presents material in one of four learning modes: Global-Multimedia, Global-nonMultimedia, Sequential-Multimedia, or Sequential-nonMultimedia.
requirements: Students must complete questionnaires on learning-style tendency and multimedia preference when first accessing the adaptive course
constraints: The adaptivity mechanism deciding a student's learning mode is described as very simple
target_learners: first-year second-semester undergraduate electronics students
target_learning_goals: analogue electronics course content
examples: A student with a positive ls result (1 to 11) is given global presentation; a negative result (-1 to -11) gives sequential presentation; negative mm results trigger additional multimedia resources such as music, video clips and flash animation.
key_sources: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057334

article_title: The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course
citation: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Learning style constructs classified into wholist-analytical and verbaliser-imager categories
description: Drawing on Riding and Cheema (1991), the article classifies learning style constructs into two broad categories: wholist-analytical, describing how individuals process information (wholists learn globally, analysts in details), and verbaliser-imager, describing how individuals represent information (verbalisers in words, imagers pictorially). It maps these to Felder et al.'s terms global/sequential and verbal/visual, and reviews three measurement instruments: Honey and Mumford's Learning Styles Questionnaire, the Grasha-Riechmann Student Learning Style Scales, and Felder's Index of Learning Styles with its four dimensions.
requirements: Measurement of learning styles requires one of the available instruments, such as Felder's Index of Learning Styles
target_learners: learners whose styles are assessed for individualized instruction
target_learning_goals: matching instruction to learners' preferred way of perceiving, processing and representing information
examples: Felder's Index of Learning Styles focuses on aspects significant in engineering education and has four dimensions: visual-verbal, sequential-global, active-reflective, and sensing-intuitive.
key_sources: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057334

article_title: Research into Learning Process in a Vocational Secondary School in the Context of Sustainable Development
citation: NataÔja van Gejeka. (2013). Research into Learning Process in a Vocational Secondary School in the Context of Sustainable Development. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 15, no. 2. https://doi.org/10.2478/jtes-2013-0012
title: Learners' Integrative Collaboration Model
description: A model developed by the author in which learners act as a united unit in a team context, constructively reconciling their actions while each participant is responsible for his/her own part of the work. It defines seven functions of integrative collaboration (learning, socio-cultural, communicative, self-realisation, diagnostic, correction, motivating) and didactic principles including learners' cognitive activation, learning process intensification, learning material flexibility and the reflection principle. The article developed and experimentally verified the model for teaching Building Constructions at Riga Construction College.
requirements: A common objective and fulfilling tasks assigned by the teacher in which each individual expresses creativity and individuality as part of a fully integrated team
Pedagogical conditions including content enrichment, compromise and cooperation as conflict-resolution strategies, non-verbal communication tools and a changed approach to evaluation
constraints: Tested and can be used for teaching the study subject Building Constructions at Riga Construction College
target_learners: vocational secondary school learners studying basic level building management
target_learning_goals: working in a team
mutual learning
business communication
creative action
professional self-education and creative potential
examples: Learners in two experimental sections joined teams of three to four members after a short introductory lecture and worked on team projects simulating constructors' office work
key_sources: NataÔja van Gejeka. (2013). Research into Learning Process in a Vocational Secondary School in the Context of Sustainable Development. Journal of Teacher Education for Sustainability, vol. 15, no. 2. https://doi.org/10.2478/jtes-2013-0012

article_title: Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps
citation: Nadezhda M. Andreeva, Ivan P. Artyukhov, Elena G. Myagkova, Nikolay I. Pak, Zhamilya K. Akkasynova. (2018). Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 9(2), 47-64. http://www.jsser.org
title: Learning roadmap with action, check and risk points for student-designed mastery paths
description: A learning roadmap is a planning tool the article defines as "a diagram mapped along the temporal axis and reflecting the current or target condition of an object, and possible target achievement scenarios". Students fill their own roadmaps guided by educational needs and personal preferences, choosing a desirable IC-competency formation level, and may adjust content, duration and performance of each stage as they progress. The roadmap's nodal points are action points where students perform assignments of various complexity levels, check points such as the initial test, test works and summative assessment, and risk points where students decide their further route, including cyclical repetitions of understudied topics. The communicative format was implemented in MS Excel with correction assignments highlighted in colour.
requirements: An expert teacher's roadmap is provided as a sample and correction-behaviour scenario for students preferring to study in line with the teacher's requirements
A subject information environment that draws up individual roadmaps and controls their fulfilment
constraints: Roadmaps operate within the general requirements for mastering the discipline; deviations trigger additional correction assignments rather than free choice of content
target_learners: university students studying computer science
target_learning_goals: independent planning of individual learning paths
self-assessment and task selection
mastery of discipline content at a chosen competency level
examples: The roadmap for Biology-direction students in MS Excel listed assignments, classroom and distance test works, training sessions, marks for completed assignments and the current score, with recommended correction assignments highlighted in colour
key_sources: Nadezhda M. Andreeva, Ivan P. Artyukhov, Elena G. Myagkova, Nikolay I. Pak, Zhamilya K. Akkasynova. (2018). Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 9(2), 47-64. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1181973

article_title: Effect of Learning Cycle Approach-Based Science Teaching on Academic Achievement, Attitude, Motivation and Retention
citation: Gökhan Uyanık. (2016). Effect of Learning Cycle Approach-based Science Teaching on Academic Achievement, Attitude, Motivation and Retention. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(5): 1223-1230. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040536
title: Learning cycle approach: a three-phase student-centered science teaching model
description: The learning cycle approach is a student-centered teaching approach based on Piaget's mental development theory and first developed by Karplus, composed of three main sections: exploration, term introduction and concept implementation. In exploration, students collect and record data from observations, measurements and experiments while the teacher takes a passive role; in term introduction students define science concepts in their own words under teacher guidance; in concept implementation students apply the concepts to new situations. The article implements this model in 4th-grade science teaching over 7 weeks and 14 lessons.
requirements: Implementation in three steps: exploration, term introduction and concept implementation
A teacher role of constituting a social and logical education environment cooperatively rather than giving knowledge directly
constraints: The article states the approach was studied at primary school 4th grade level in science lessons
target_learners: primary school 4th grade students
target_learning_goals: science concept learning
meaningful and retentive learning
motivation towards science learning
examples: In the study, each activity started with a demonstration experiment based on prediction-observation-explanation strategy, students worked in small groups of 4-6 students, and students adapted configured concepts to new situations encountered in daily life.
key_sources: Gökhan Uyanık. (2016). Effect of Learning Cycle Approach-based Science Teaching on Academic Achievement, Attitude, Motivation and Retention. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(5): 1223-1230. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040536

article_title: The Effect of Meaning-Focused Listening Input on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Productive Vocabulary Size
citation: Mostafa Azari Noughabi. (2017). The Effect of Meaning-focused Listening Input on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Productive Vocabulary Size. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(15). https://www.iiste.org
title: Lex30 productive vocabulary size test
description: Lex30, introduced by Meara and Fitzpatrick (2000), is a test "designated for measuring learners' productive vocabulary size". It presents thirty stimulated words from the first 1000-word band, to which learners write at most four recalled words each; responses are scored via the online version at lognostics.co.uk. The article used its pencil-and-paper format, untimed, in both pretest and posttest sessions, citing evidence of its reliability and validity.
requirements: Stimulated words are of first 1000 words band so lower-proficiency learners can participate and content words are elicited
constraints: The article notes a concern that Lex30 could also measure vocabulary recall, which is considered one part of productive vocabulary knowledge
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners at university
target_learning_goals: productive vocabulary size measurement
examples: In this study, 63 learners took Lex30 in a 30-minute-maximum untimed session before and after 12 treatment sessions, with responses typed into the online version for scoring
key_sources: Mostafa Azari Noughabi. (2017). The Effect of Meaning-focused Listening Input on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Productive Vocabulary Size. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(15). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143810

article_title: Becoming Chemists through Game-Based Inquiry Learning: The Case of "Legends of Alkhimia"
citation: Yam San Chee and Kim Chwee Daniel Tan. (2010). Becoming Chemists through Game-Based Inquiry Learning: The Case of Legends of Alkhimia. Electronic Journal of e-Learning, Volume 8, Issue 1. https://www.ejel.org
title: Legends of Alkhimia multiplayer game and associated curriculum
description: Legends of Alkhimia is an educational multiplayer game for 13- to 15-year-olds, an eight-session chemistry curriculum for lower secondary school science designed to foster learning of chemistry through inquiry. "7KH PXOWLSOD\HU JDPH VXSSRUWV IRXU FRQFXUUHQW SOD\HUV" on personal computers connected via a local area network, typically in a school computer laboratory. It embeds students in problem-solving challenges related to the use of chemistry in realistic contexts and requires individual laboratory work using an in-game virtual chemistry lab. As used in the study, "/HJHQGV RI $ONKLPLD FRPSULVHV VL[ OHYHOV RI JDPH SOD\", with levels building incrementally and a narrative arc providing coherence to the whole gameplay experience.
requirements: PCs connected over a local area network, typically in a school computer laboratory
In-game virtual chemistry laboratory for individual experimental work
Associated curricular materials, including activity sheets structuring inquiry-phase learning activities before class-level dialog
constraints: The school could not support one student per PC, so the study ran with a dyad model of two students sharing one computer
The first and last curriculum sessions were devoted to research surveys and student tests rather than game play
target_learners: lower secondary school students (average age 14) in a high-ability Express academic stream
target_learning_goals: separation of mixtures, solutes, and immiscible liquids
properties of substances in the context of separation of mixtures
inquiry practices of questioning, hypothesizing, investigating, analyzing, synthesizing, and evaluating
examples: Level 5 trapped students in an underground chemistry lab where they had to test liquid mixtures, separate pure forms of substances in the virtual lab, and impregnate a metal door with an effective substance to escape

article_title: The Effectiveness of Immersive Multimedia Learning with Peer Support on English Speaking and Reading Aloud
citation: Muslem, A., & Abbas, M. (2017). The Effectiveness of Immersive Multimedia Learning with Peer Support on English Speaking and Reading Aloud. International Journal of Instruction, 10(1). http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_1_13.pdf
title: Levelt's lexicon model of language acquisition as the basis for immersive multimedia learning with peer support
description: The study grounds its intervention in Levelt's (1989) lexicon model of language acquisition and production, "as simplified by de Bot (1997)". The model "explains the acquisition of a language through the development of internal structures in the form of speech motor patterns, conceptual systems, articulatory motor systems and phonemization", treating language as reconstruction from learned phonological codes. The article uses this account to justify an immersive multimedia program in which English is the main medium of instruction and students repeatedly replay video clips and recordings until they can reproduce the language as native speakers do.
requirements: A linguistically rich immersive environment with recorded native-speaker video and audio inputs in place of the teacher
Peer support activities so students can negotiate meaning and form, with teacher scaffolding and feedback when peers cannot push learners' ZPD
constraints: The teacher's role is limited to facilitator or organizer rather than model
Social interaction extends the ZPD only with meticulous scaffolding strategies and appropriate feedback
target_learners: First-year university EFL students
target_learning_goals: Oral production skills in reading aloud and speaking in English as a foreign language
examples: Students immersed themselves by listening to and watching teacher-provided video clips and recordings, repeating playback several times to master each learning material
key_sources: Muslem, A., & Abbas, M. (2017). The Effectiveness of Immersive Multimedia Learning with Peer Support on English Speaking and Reading Aloud. International Journal of Instruction, 10(1). http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_1_13.pdf

article_title: Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner's Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary
citation: Chainikova, G.R., Zatonskiy, A.V., Mitiukov, N.W., Busygina, H.L. (2018). Development of Foreign Language Lexical Competence on the Basis of a Learner’s Terminological Thesaurus and Dictionary. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.1.51
title: Learner's English-Russian and Russian-English Electronic Thesaurus and Dictionary of Software Terms
description: A learner's electronic bilingual dictionary and thesaurus of software terms aimed at Software Engineering students, containing about 1000 terms and related words. It has four components: a classification part of charts demonstrating the inner logic of the subject area, a glossary with definitions of key terms (67 terms with definitions), an ideographic thesaurus part showing paradigmatic, syntagmatic and associative relations of entry terms, and a bilingual alphabetical dictionary. Its context part is expanded with an encyclopedic part on main topics, plus supplements on English prefixes, suffixes and reading characters; the electronic model was built with Microsoft FrontPage 2003.
requirements: Selection of lexical means in accordance with curricula and students' future occupational context; different entry points allowing switching from word to concept and concept to word; openness, i.e. the possibility to make changes and supplement
constraints: Full implementation of the functions of the learner's thesaurus and dictionary is possible only in electronic format, per the authors
target_learners: second-year university students majoring in Software Engineering studying English for professional purposes
target_learning_goals: foreign language occupational lexical competence
knowledge of software terminology and its semantic relations
examples: Topics covered include general software topics studied in the first and second years plus Software licensing and Software piracy sections; each topic was presented as a classification scheme, e.g. on Operating systems

article_title: Efficacy of Multimedia Learning Modules as Preparation for Lecture-Based Tutorials in Electromagnetism
citation: James Christopher Moore. (2018). Efficacy of Multimedia Learning Modules as Preparation for Lecture-Based Tutorials in Electromagnetism. Educ. Sci. 2018, 8, 23. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci8010023
title: Lecture-based adaptation of Tutorials in Introductory Physics with whole-class checkouts and micro-lectures
description: An adaptation of Tutorials in Introductory Physics for large-enrollment settings where "students proceeded through TIP materials in groups, but with whole-class 'checkouts' rather than instructor-intensive, individual group checkouts". Short micro-lectures and Peer Instruction activities are interspersed between TIP activities. This adaptation strays in some significant ways from the intentions of the curriculum developers but was necessary for logistical reasons at institutions without graduate teaching assistants.
requirements: A SCALE-UP-style classroom with round tables seating six students each, a primary instructor, backup instructors, and at least one undergraduate Learning Assistant
constraints: This adaptation strays in some significant ways from the intentions of the curriculum developers
target_learners: natural science majors in large-enrollment introductory physics
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of electricity and magnetism through guided group tutorials

article_title: Can Videogames Be Used to Develop the Infant Stage Educational Curriculum?
citation: Marín Díaz, V.; Martín-Párraga, J. (2014). Can videogames be used to develop the infant stage educational curriculum? New Approaches in Educational Research, 3(1), 20-25. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.3.1.20-25
title: Videogame-based lesson plan pattern for early-years mathematics
description: The article proposes a lesson plan pattern using the videogame Lemmings to develop early mathematics. Its general goals include learning "the possibilities offered by the body" and taking first steps toward logic-mathematics skills. Specific goals cover ordering, quantifying and classifying, problem solving, playful computer use, experimenting, and knowing quantity and space concepts, developed through conceptual, procedural and attitudinal contents.
requirements: Curricular anchoring in the areas permitted by the regional decree (Self-knowledge and personal autonomy; Knowledge of the environment and languages; Communication and representation)
constraints: The Math and Value Formation areas used are not contained per se in the 2006 Spanish Education Act or Decree 428/2008, but are understood to fall within the decree's three macro areas
target_learners: Children in the third year of early education, aged 4 to 5
target_learning_goals: Mathematical skills such as ordering, quantifying and classifying
Logic-related skills through problem solving
examples: The proposal identifies qualities and features of object collections, establishing groups, classifications, orders and quantification

article_title: A Study of the Relationship between Type of Dictionary Used and Lexical Proficiency in Writings of Iranian EFL Students
citation: Vahdany, F., Abdollahzadeh, M., Gholami, S., & Ghanipoor, M. (2014). A Study of the Relationship between Type of Dictionary Used and Lexical Proficiency in Writings of Iranian EFL Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.6p.31
title: Lexical proficiency as a two-dimensional construct: vocabulary breadth and depth
description: The article adopts a framework in which lexical proficiency comprises two dimensions. Citing Meara (2005), it describes "breadth of knowledge features (i.e. how many words a learner knows, also called vocabulary size) and depth of knowledge features (i.e. how well a learner knows a word and also how this knowledge of words is structured in his mind)". The study operationalizes lexical proficiency in writing with a six-feature rating scale: syntax, semantics, pragmatics, collocation, morphology, and variety.
requirements: Measurement requires a rating scale covering word use correctness and appropriateness across syntactic, semantic, pragmatic, collocational, morphological, and variety features
constraints: In this study the construct is applied specifically to skill in using words correctly and appropriately in writing
target_learners: upper-intermediate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: lexical proficiency in L2 writing
examples: The study rated 20 compositions on the six-feature scale with two raters whose inter-rater reliability was checked via Pearson correlation

article_title: Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students' Vocabulary Repertoire
citation: Ira Rasikawati (2019). Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students’ Vocabulary Repertoire. International Dialogues on Education, 6(2), 83-98.
title: Integrate lexico-grammatical instruction — teaching multi-word sequences and complex syntax together — in corpus-based EAP reading classrooms
description: The article argues for a lexico-grammatical approach that treats lexis and grammar as integral (Sinclair, 1991) and teaches multi-word sequences or language chunks. Because "learning vocabulary and grammar often takes place simultaneously, instruction of the two domains should be done at the same time" (Liu & Jiang, 2009). Acquisition of common lexico-grammatical patterns is expected to improve reading by enabling students to process receptive vocabulary faster (Conklin & Schmitt, 2008), and EAP reading classrooms should include teaching of complex syntax with extensive practice chunking ideas at the sentence level.
requirements: Instruction of vocabulary and grammar domains at the same time
Extensive practice for students to chunk ideas at the sentence level
constraints: Prior findings indicate students' word-by-word processing and unfamiliarity with complex sentence structures result in unsuccessful chunking of ideas into meaningful units
target_learners: Undergraduate EAP reading students
EFL learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of academic texts
Processing receptive vocabulary faster
Chunking ideas at the sentence level
examples: Rasikawati (2012) found medical students' word-by-word processing and unfamiliarity with complex sentence structures led to unsuccessful chunking, recommending complex-syntax teaching in reading EAP classrooms
key_sources: Ira Rasikawati (2019). Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students’ Vocabulary Repertoire. International Dialogues on Education, 6(2), 83-98. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1245249

article_title: Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher
citation: Mirzagitova, A. L. & Akhmetov, L. G. (2016). Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(14), 6675-6689. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1118411
title: Didactic objectives and performance indicators of the structural elements of the lesson
description: As part of Stage 2, the authors formulated didactic objectives and performance indicators for seven structural elements of the lesson: actualization of previous work, presentation of new information, guided practice, independent practice, self-control and self-assessment, summing up, and homework. Each stage pairs a didactic objective with a performance criterion, such as obtaining objective information on pupils' achievement of the expected results.
requirements: The matrix was formulated for the formation of a substantial and methodical component of professional and didactic culture of the future history teacher.

teacher training students
target_learning_goals: assurance of perception, comprehension and absorption of knowledge
timely elimination or prevention of mistakes
examples: For independent practice of pupils, the didactic objective is assurance of the assimilation of new information and its application in the changed situation.

article_title: Application of Education Management and Lesson Study in Teaching Mathematics to Students of Second Grade of Public School in District 3 of Tehran
citation: Farhoush, M., Majedi, P., & Behrangi, M. (2017). Application of Education Management and Lesson Study in Teaching Mathematics to Students of Second Grade of Public School in District 3 of Tehran. International Education Studies, 10(2), 104. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n2p104
title: Lesson study follows a ten-stage cycle of collaborative planning, teaching, observation, revision, and sharing.
description: The article describes lesson study as "the participative research of teachers in school and classroom" executed through ten stages: establishing the group, defining the subject, studying and discussing it, lesson planning, teaching and observing, evaluation and reflection, revision, re-teaching the revised lesson, re-evaluation, and sharing results through reports or exhibitions. It is grounded in social constructivism theory emphasizing the social nature of knowledge.

Schools need "conditions, elements and facilities" to facilitate the lesson study process
A group member volunteers to teach the final plan while others record classroom events
constraints: Changing old methods of professional development and organizing schools as places for teacher learning "is not an easy task"

Students in mathematics and science classes
target_learning_goals: Professional development of teachers
Improving quality of teaching
Improving students' learning
examples: Implemented in five pilot schools in District 3 of Tehran with second-grade mathematics classes

article_title: Effects of Peer Tutoring on Reading Self-Concept
citation: Flores, M., & Duran, D. (2013). Effects of Peer Tutoring on Reading Self-Concept. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 2(3), 297-324. https://doi.org/10.4471/ijep.2013.29
title: The Leemos en pareja peer tutoring reading programme as a framework for developing Reading Self-Concept
description: The Leemos en pareja programme is a peer tutoring reading intervention grounded on three conceptual bases: peer tutoring, reading competence and family involvement, with a teacher training process implementing peer tutoring. It runs for 12 weeks, with two 30-minute sessions each week, revolving around an Activity Sheet designed by teachers to guide the pairs' interaction through pre-reading, while-reading and post-reading activities. The article uses this framework to examine changes in Reading Self-Concept and to identify the processes responsible for the observed changes.
requirements: All students received basic training on the programme's theoretical framework and functioning before starting, with interactive guidelines aimed at creating appropriate scaffolding and tailored support.
constraints: The programme's design allows for a sufficiently long intervention so as to consider its possible effect on the Reading Self-Concept of the students taking part in it.
target_learners: Primary education students in years 3 to 6
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Reading Self-Concept
examples: The programme involved 577 students in years 3 to 6 across 10 schools during academic years 08-09, 09-10 and 10-11, with 441 students in the intervention team and 136 in the comparison group.
key_sources: Flores, M., & Duran, D. (2013). Effects of Peer Tutoring on Reading Self-Concept. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 2(3), 297-324. https://doi.org/10.4471/ijep.2013.29

article_title: The Impact of Web-Assisted Instruction on Student Writing Outcomes in Business Communication
citation: Austin, T. L., Sigmar, L. S., Mehta, G. B., & Shirk, J. L. (2017). The impact of web-assisted instruction on student writing outcomes in business communication. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies, 20. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1148293
title: McGraw-Hill Connect LearnSmart Achieve (LSA) adaptive learning modules
description: McGraw-Hill's Connect LearnSmart Achieve is an interactive study tool that adaptively assesses students' skill and knowledge levels, adjusting content based on student responses and expressed confidence. Each module has three phases: Tune In (diagnostic with confidence ratings), Focus (reading and videos), and Practice (new questions with confidence ratings). Students work at their own pace outside class. In this study, ten modules targeting grammar, sentence problems, punctuation, and mechanics were assigned for 5-10 course points each, totaling over 10% of the final course grade.
requirements: Students need a subscription or purchase of the combined ebook and Connect package
constraints: Modules were completed outside classroom time within a six-week period early in the semester
target_learners: Junior-level business communication students at a regional AACSB-accredited university
target_learning_goals: Grammar and common sentence problems
Punctuation and mechanics
examples: Ten LSA modules were assigned: Fused (Run-on) Sentences and Comma Splices; Phrases, Clauses, and Fragments; End Punctuation; Verbs and Verbals; Semi-Colons; Commas; Wordiness; Parallelism; Apostrophes; Capitalization

article_title: Resilience and academic performance in mathematics and science among middle school students: The mediating role of computational thinking.

title: Learning environments aimed at supporting mathematics and science achievement may consider the potential relevance of psychological resilience and computational thinking
description: The article suggests that learning environments aimed at supporting mathematics and science achievement may consider the potential relevance of psychological resilience and CT. This recommendation is grounded in the finding that CT statistically mediated the association between resilience and achievement. The authors emphasize that "whether educational practices targeting these constructs can improve academic achievement remains an empirical question that should be examined in future intervention-based research."

constraints: The cross-sectional correlational design does not permit causal inferences about whether targeting these constructs would improve achievement.

title: LEARNBOT structured training program for robotic pancreatoduodenectomy
description: LEARNBOT is a pan-European, multicenter training program for robotic pancreatoduodenectomy implemented by E-MIPS in 20 high-volume centers without prior RPD experience, training at least 2 surgeons per center as a consistent operative team. Per the article, "The program included a video library, biotissue simulation (pancreaticojejunostomy and hepaticojejunostomy), off-site RPD case observations, and on-site proctoring." article_title: Effectiveness of the "Level-Points" online training model and influencing factors in enhancing scoring accuracy among surgical examiners.
citation: Zhang Lina, Yan Mengling, Qiu Yiwen, Cai Haolei, Yu Yunxian. (2026). Effectiveness of the “Level-Points” online training model and influencing factors in enhancing scoring accuracy among surgical examiners. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10033-z
title: “Level-Points” online examiner training platform with level-based progression and point-reward system
description: A custom-built online platform delivering examiner calibration training in three sequential phases: pre-assessment, level-based and point-reward training, and post-assessment. "The "Level-Points" training model integrates two complementary mechanisms": five competency-dimension modules are unlocked sequentially like game levels, and examiners earn points for scoring accuracy (e.g., 2 points for a deviation within 15 points of the reference score), with a minimum of 2 cumulative points required to unlock the next dimension. The platform provides real-time numerical and visual feedback on scoring deviations and tracks progress through a personalized dashboard.
requirements: Examiners must meet the clearance requirements of the current dimension, earning a minimum of 2 cumulative points, to unlock the subsequent dimension.
Reference scores are established by a five-member expert panel rating every rubric item with scoring rubrics and a deduction reference sheet.
constraints: The point-reward system may inadvertently encourage conformity to reference scores rather than independent judgment; this was not empirically examined.
target_learners: surgical examiners (attending physicians and above) in residency training programs
target_learning_goals: accurate application of national scoring rubrics across five surgical competency dimensions
examples: 45 videos across five dimensions (8 pre-assessment, 8 parallel post-assessment, 29 training videos) were scored on a 100-point scale against expert reference scores.
key_sources: Zhang Lina, Yan Mengling, Qiu Yiwen, Cai Haolei, Yu Yunxian. (2026). Effectiveness of the “Level-Points” online training model and influencing factors in enhancing scoring accuracy among surgical examiners. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10033-z

At the time of writing it hosts 239.6 TB of data comprising 591,091 individual WSIs and received 4.7 million page views in the last year. title: VR simulation offer at Levanger Hospital: Oxford Medical Simulation platform on Meta Quest 2 headsets with 20 emergency medical cases
description: The intervention evaluated was a VR simulation offer at Levanger Hospital from October 2022 to August 2023, delivered using head-mounted Meta Quest 2 headsets providing a fully immersive first-person experience. The software platform from Oxford Medical Simulation included 20 emergency medical cases from various disciplines, with interaction via head movement and hand/controller input. Residents could borrow headsets freely within the hospital during working hours or free time.
requirements: Information about the offer and training in the use of the headsets and controllers was provided to all first-year residents at the beginning of their residency period
constraints: Residents were permitted to use the headsets freely only within the hospital area; the borrowing system was described as inadequate

article_title: How differentiated can a new tablet-based reading screening measure the reading proficiency of students with intellectual disabilities? Comparing the impact of disability, disability type and grade level on reading skills.
citation: Ebenbeck Nikola, Zentel Peter, Gebhardt Markus. (2024). How differentiated can a new tablet-based reading screening measure the reading proficiency of students with intellectual disabilities? Comparing the impact of disability, disability type and grade level on reading skills. Journal of Intellectual Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/17446295241282750
title: LES-IN-DIG: a tablet-based digital reading screening with four Rasch-conform subtests on the Levumi.de platform
description: LES-IN-DIG is a digital reading screening on the online test platform Levumi.de comprising four subtests: phonological awareness (35 items), vocabulary (52 real/pseudoword items), flash reading (30 items with word display times of 0.5–2 seconds), and sentence comprehension (35 gap-filling items). "All tests of the screening conform to the unidimensional Rasch model", allowing separate administration and individual scores without an overall screening score. The entire screening takes approximately 20 minutes and is designed for inclusive classrooms focusing on students with lower reading abilities.
requirements: Students need prerequisites such as letter acquisition for subtest 1 and synthetic reading for the other three subtests; subtests require no special motor skills and use single-choice format
constraints: Participating students had only learning or cognitive disabilities; no student used alternative communication or had motor or visual problems
Test 4's five-minute time limit means students with intellectual disabilities tend to respond to only a few items

students with intellectual disabilities in special schools
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness
vocabulary
reading speed and fluency
sentence comprehension

article_title: A digital recipe for enhancing clinical reasoning: the role of e-learning by concordance (E-LbC): a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Aboueisha Hadeel, Abouzeid Enjy, Sallam Moataz A., Talaat Wagdy. (2025). A digital recipe for enhancing clinical reasoning: the role of e-learning by concordance (E-LbC): a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08005-w
title: Learning by Concordance as a script-theory-based approach to clinical reasoning under uncertainty
description: Learning by Concordance (LbC) is an instructional approach grounded in illness script theory and Croskerry's dual-process theory, supporting both intuitive (Type 1) and analytical (Type 2) reasoning. The article describes it as follows: "LbC simulates real-life decision-making by presenting learners with contextualized clinical scenarios, asking them to make judgments, and comparing their responses with those of expert panels." It follows a cognitive apprenticeship model in which learners observe expert thinking and progressively gain independence, and integrates knowledge acquisition and application in a single interactive experience. In this study it was delivered online (e-LbC) to teach painless vision loss during an ophthalmology clerkship.
requirements: Requires a panel of experts whose aggregate responses serve as the reference key against which learner judgments are scored
constraints: The article notes effectiveness may be influenced by factors such as prior knowledge, cognitive load, and case complexity
LbC is particularly suited for cases where multiple responses may be appropriate, emphasizing the reasoning process over identifying a single correct answer
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning under diagnostic uncertainty
illness script formation
examples: In this study, e-LbC sessions on painless vision loss used breakout rooms of 5–7 students on Microsoft Teams, with students formulating diagnostic hypotheses, judging the effect of new what-if information, and receiving expert feedback

title: Interactive e-learning modules with videos, quizzes, and case-based exercises on the Lernbar platform
description: All theoretical input of the emergency medicine training week was converted into e-learning modules, "which included specific learning activators such as videos, quizzes, and case-based exercises with accompanying images". The modules were delivered asynchronously on the Lernbar platform developed by the University of Frankfurt, allowing students to complete them at their own pace from self-selected environments. Module time was held equal to the classic classroom training, and content was aligned with the detailed training blueprint of the regular curriculum.

Time for each e-learning module held equal to the classic classroom training

article_title: The role of leadership in enhancing non-technical skills in healthcare: a qualitative study in a Balkan context.
citation: Hodza-Beganovic R, Berggren P, Edelbring S. (2025). The role of leadership in enhancing non-technical skills in healthcare: a qualitative study in a Balkan context. Human Resources for Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12960-025-01022-2
title: Leadership as enacted behaviors and a developmental process shaping team non-technical skills
description: The study frames leadership in two complementary ways: as "a set of behaviors enacted by healthcare leaders" and as "a developmental process in which competencies are built over time through continuous learning." It draws on team-centric, transformational, and task- versus person-focused leadership theory, and applies this framing to explain how leadership fosters non-technical skills such as communication, teamwork, and role clarity in hierarchical, resource-constrained LMIC healthcare settings.
requirements: Leadership must be understood and enacted at both formal and informal levels within healthcare teams
constraints: The framework was developed and interpreted within Balkan LMIC healthcare contexts characterized by hierarchical structures and limited resources

examples: The study explored leadership practice across three sequential workshops, examining how understandings and enactment of leadership evolved over time

title: The left middle frontal gyrus as a domain-general hub integrating reading and cognitive flexibility via salience network regulation
description: The article proposes that the left MFG serves as a "central neural hub supporting the development of both abilities", integrating language information processing and higher-order cognitive control. Its gray matter growth and its functional connectivity to the salience network (ACC and insula) mediate the reciprocal longitudinal associations between reading achievement and cognitive flexibility. The authors suggest this reflects a "domain‐general capacity for executive control of complex information streams rather than language‐specific processing".
requirements: Longitudinal behavioral and neuroimaging data with structural (VBM) and resting-state functional connectivity measures
constraints: Based on two time points only; task-based fMRI might reveal additional common regions; not compared across different language systems
target_learners: school-aged children aged 6-12

cognitive flexibility

article_title: "Learning, Thinking & Conveying" training with experiential learning in the emergency department for undergraduate nursing students: A quasi-experimental study.
citation: Li Y, Cheng S, Liu D, Jiang W. (2025). “Learning, Thinking & Conveying” training with experiential learning in the emergency department for undergraduate nursing students: A quasi-experimental study. Medicine 2025;104:28(e43231). https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043231
title: "Learning, Thinking & Conveying" pedagogy: a five-step recursive instructional framework
description: "Learning, Thinking & Conveying" pedagogy was proposed by Zhang Huicheng, Taiwan, China in 2013 and emphasizes "self-studying," "thinking" and "conveying." Problem-solving is undertaken by student groups to shift the classroom dynamic toward cooperation and competition, aiming to motivate students toward independent learning and analytical thinking. As the article states, "The pedagogy follows a five-step recursive process: self-studying, thinking, discussing, conveying and integrating, promoting continuous engagement and enhancing learning."
requirements: Student group collaboration and problem-solving so that the classroom dynamic shifts to cooperation and competition
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students on clinical internship
target_learning_goals: independent learning
analytical thinking
critical thinking disposition
examples: The study applied the pedagogy weekly: Monday self-studying from the textbook, Tuesday thinking through three case issues, Wednesday group discussion, Thursday nursing-round reporting with teacher summary, Friday to Sunday bedside clinical practice.

citation: Wang Erqian, Yu Qianyi, Xu Haiyan, Geng Shuang, Shao Enhua, Yang Zhikun, Zhang Meifen, Li Hui. (2025). Incorporating a dynamic extraocular muscle simulation model into the undergraduate ophthalmic curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07039-4
title: Lecture-then-hands-on-simulation sequence for complex three-dimensional anatomy
description: The instructional pattern tested in this study: both groups receive the same one-hour didactic lecture and Q2, then diverge into a half-hour hands-on simulator session or video review before Q3. The quiz design targeted "the specific learning difficulties reported by medical undergraduates", and equal difficulty was ensured across the three quizzes. The pattern links a preparatory lecture with an interactive practice phase.
requirements: Students unfamiliar with the topic receive the lecture on basic terminology, definition, and innervation before the simulation session
Equal-difficulty quizzes to measure gains across phases

citation: Bolgova O, Shypilova I, Mavrych V. (2025). Large Language Models in Biochemistry Education: Comparative Evaluation of Performance. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/67244
title: Leverage the differing topic-specific strengths of individual LLMs for targeted support in biochemistry courses
description: The article proposes that because different AI models exhibit different accuracy profiles across biochemistry topics, educators can match specific models or topics to targeted educational support rather than treating LLMs as interchangeable. The study found that "eicosanoids, bioenergetics and electron transport chain, hexose monophosphate pathway, and ketone bodies" were the best-answered topics while globular proteins and hemoglobin, lipoproteins, and fructose and galactose metabolism were weakest, and that Claude alone scored 100% in 12 of 23 categories. This supports using per-topic AI performance data when selecting AI tools for study support.
requirements: Educators need topic-level item analysis of a candidate chatbot's accuracy before assigning it as a study aid for a specific course content area.
constraints: The article states its findings on chatbot proficiencies are limited to MCQs from the biochemistry course and may not represent other medical questions or contexts.
The article notes GPT-4, which performed well, is not freely available, potentially limiting widespread educational use.
target_learners: medical students in a medical biochemistry course
target_learning_goals: biochemistry factual recall and concept application
examples: The study evaluated Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4-1106, Gemini 1.5 Flash, and Copilot on 200 exam-database MCQs across 23 topics over 5 attempts each, item-analyzed per topic.

article_title: The effect of promoting factors on learning by four different delivery modes.
citation: Tolonen M, Arvonen M, Renko M, Paakkonen H, Piippo-Savolainen E. (2024). The effect of promoting factors on learning by four different delivery modes. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05864-7
title: Learning-promoting factors framework: Concentration, Anticipation, Liking and Desire to reuse as measurable promoters of learning outcomes
description: The article organizes its inquiry around four self-reported "learning-promoting factors" — Concentration, Anticipation, Liking and Desire to reuse — measured with single statements on a 1–10 scale immediately after a lesson. The framework holds that "learning arises from the interplay of various factors that mutually influence one another," with concentration supporting working-memory transfer to long-term memory and anticipation promoting concentration. The factors are treated as working in synergy, with the realization of any factor affecting the others.
requirements: Experience survey administered immediately after teaching, with participants split into high (≥ median) and low (< median) groups per factor
constraints: Factors were measured by self-report single statements in one lesson context; the framework was tested in a single 45-minute pediatric lesson with medical and nursing students
target_learners: higher-education health science students
target_learning_goals: improving learning outcomes across live and digital teaching modalities
examples: Statements used: "I was able to concentrate on the teaching" (Concentration), "I believe the learning method produced learning" (Anticipation), "I liked the teaching method" (Liking), "I would like to use this learning method in the future" (Desire to reuse)

article_title: Optimal Duration of High-Fidelity Simulator Training for Bronchoscope-Guided Intubation: A Noninferiority Randomized Trial.
citation: Jiang Luyang, Yang Qingyue, Li Qingyue, Jiang Bailin, Laba Ciren, Feng Yi. (2023). Optimal Duration of High-Fidelity Simulator Training for Bronchoscope-Guided Intubation: A Noninferiority Randomized Trial. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000739
title: Learning curve-based individualized training modality for simulator skill acquisition
description: The article introduces a competency-based training modality in which each trainee's individualized learning curve is generated from their first 16 simulator procedures using a previously validated exponential equation, and training continues until the individualized end point is achieved. The trainees stop when "the following procedure time fell into the 95% CI of the asymptote 3 consecutive times," meaning performance has reached the curve's plateau. This replaces time-based training with skill-acquisition-based training, addressing variable learning pace among trainees.
requirements: A simulator that automatically records procedure time and performance scores so individual learning curves can be fitted
At least 16 initial training procedures to generate the individualized learning curve before end-point assessment
constraints: Some simulation training may not be construed by a learning curve, per the authors
Whether the method detects trainees who require more time was not investigated in this study
target_learners: Anesthesiology residents and interns who are novices at FOB intubation
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of basic flexible optical bronchoscopic intubation skill
examples: Participants in group New were trained 16 times, individualized learning curves were fitted, and training continued until three consecutive procedure times fell within the 95% CI of the fitted asymptote

citation: Zhang Jun, Luo Zai, Zhang Renchao, Ding Zehao, Fang Yuan, Han Chao, Wu Weidong, Cen Gang, Qiu Zhengjun, Huang Chen. (2024). The transition of surgical simulation training and its learning curve: a bibliometric analysis from 2000 to 2023. International Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000001579
title: Learning curve as a measure of surgical training method effectiveness
description: The article uses the learning curve as its central organizing measure for judging surgical training approaches: it "applies the learning curves as a measure to demonstrate their teaching ability" and compares simulation types by analyzing their learning curves. Learning curves track how operative performance (e.g., operating time, conversions, complications) changes with accumulated operative experience, allowing identification of case thresholds at which performance stabilizes. The review surmises the applicability of different surgical simulation types by comparing and analyzing learning curves across procedures such as laparoscopic hemihepatectomy, pancreatoduodenectomy, and robotic pancreatoduodenectomy.
requirements: Objective and standardized evaluation methods appropriate to the application scenario, as the review states appropriate and standardized evaluation methods should be selected for different scenarios
constraints: The review states this analysis does not encompass a retrospective comparative examination of included studies because of the absence of standardized, objective, universally applicable competence-measurement tools
target_learners: surgical residents
surgeons acquiring minimally invasive and robotic techniques
target_learning_goals: acquisition of surgical technical skills
reaching stable operative performance within a defined number of cases
examples: The review reports a multicenter robotic pancreatoduodenectomy training program whose learning curve showed an inflection point at 22 cases for operating time, with median operative time 52 min shorter in the second stage

article_title: Comparison between two asynchronous teaching methods in an undergraduate dental course: a pilot study.
citation: Alharbi F, Alwadei SH, Alwadei A, Asiri S, Alwadei F, Alqerban A, Almuzian M. (2022). Comparison between two asynchronous teaching methods in an undergraduate dental course: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03557-7
title: Knowledge-acquisition and application stages across five learning models (passive, active, online, flipped, virtual flipped)
description: Table 1 organizes five learning models by where knowledge acquisition and application occur: conventional passive learning uses a face-to-face lecture with self-directed homework; conventional flipped learning uses self-directed prework with face-to-face discussion; and virtual flipped learning uses "Self-directed (prework/pre-recorded lecture)" acquisition with "Virtual (Discussions, interactive exercises, case studies)" application. health professions students

article_title: Defining the learning curve for endotracheal intubation in the emergency department.
citation: Lee Gun Tak, Park Jong Eun, Woo Sook-young, Shin Tae Gun, Jeong Daun, Kim Taerim, Lee Se Uk, Yoon Hee, Hwang Sung Yeon. (2022). Defining the learning curve for endotracheal intubation in the emergency department. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-19337-8
title: Set minimum procedural experience requirements for complex psychomotor skills from learning-curve evidence rather than convention, since existing minimums may fall below the proficiency threshold
description: The principle is that mandated minimum experience counts for procedural skills should be calibrated against measured learning curves for the relevant setting and proficiency definition. The article found 119 cases were needed for ≥ 85% FAS while the ACGME mandates 35, concluding "the 35 ETI cases may not be sufficient for establishing the proficiency of EM trainees" and that "additional training for EM trainees might be necessary".

constraints: Learning-curve thresholds vary by statistical method, study population, devices, setting, and proficiency definition, per the article
target_learners: emergency medicine residents and other novice trainees learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: reaching procedural proficiency in endotracheal intubation
examples: The article compared the ACGME's 35-ETI minimum with its own finding that at least 119 cases were needed for an 85% FAS probability in the ED

article_title: On video lectures during remote teaching and beyond.
citation: Schwarz G, Bleiner D, Günther D. (2022). On video lectures during remote teaching and beyond. Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00216-022-03983-y
title: Lecture delivery modalities: synchronous versus asynchronous online formats with distinct pedagogical trade-offs
description: The article organizes lecture delivery into modalities contrasting online with offline and synchronous with asynchronous delivery. Synchronous teaching "allows for easier two-way live communication," while asynchronous teaching "offers more flexibility due to on-demand availability"; the modalities "can be combined to mitigate disadvantages, e.g. by recording synchronous lectures." The authors used this framing to plan and switch formats across semesters of a large analytical chemistry course.
requirements: Lectures needed to be recorded in any case for subsequent viewing by students unable to attend synchronous meetings, per institutional regulation
constraints: With insufficient technical equipment, support, or unreliable internet connectivity, asynchronous lectures are preferred, per the literature the article cites
target_learners: undergraduate chemistry and related majors in large-enrolment university courses
target_learning_goals: maintaining a lecture hall-like learning experience for quantitative analytical chemistry content
examples: Spring 2020: pre-recorded lectures in a lecture hall released at scheduled times; spring 2021: synchronous videoconference lectures recorded and posted; the final spring 2020 lecture ran live as a videoconference because it required interaction

article_title: Social contagion of academic behavior: Comparing social networks of close friends and admired peers.
citation: Huiyoung Shin. (2022). Social contagion of academic behavior: Comparing social networks of close friends and admired peers. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0265385
title: Attend to admire networks and integrate admired peers in classroom peer dynamics to support academic engagement
description: The article recommends that researchers and educators attend to the admire networks to support classroom peer social dynamics. It argues that admired peers could be most helpful in peer-led interventions, since "high-status peers can be employed as role models who set the group norms and spread perceptions of appropriate academic behavior". The recommendation follows from findings that admired peers' engagement influenced adolescents' own engagement as strongly as close friends' engagement did.
requirements: Knowledge of classroom admire networks via peer nominations of peers students admire, respect, and want to be like
constraints: The article's models used classroom-only nomination measures; relations outside the classroom were not captured
Social tie strength or quality was not taken into account in the network measure
target_learners: early adolescents in elementary school classrooms
target_learning_goals: academic behavioral engagement
examples: The study estimated separate SAOMs for friend and admire networks and found significant influence of admired peers on engagement; the authors recommend motivating less-engaged adolescents to connect with highly engaged peers and using peer-led programs.

As printed, "Offline teaching consisted of lectures on specific topics, which lasted 20 min. Each lecture was followed by in-class activities such as concept mapping, quizzes, role playing, puzzle, and crosswords which lasted for 20 to 40 min." The identical pattern was replicated in the Zoom sessions to keep the two platforms comparable, with all three modules completed in 36 hours for both groups.
requirements: Lectures of about 20 minutes on specific topics
Follow-up activities such as concept mapping, quizzes, role playing, puzzles and crosswords lasting 20 to 40 minutes
constraints: The pattern was applied to Periodontics modules for final-year BDS undergraduates over one week

(2021). Prioritising topics for developing e-learning resources in healthcare curricula: A comparison between students and educators using a modified Delphi survey. title: Conduct students' learning needs assessment as the starting point when designing eLearning resources
description: The article argues that needs assessment among students must precede e-learning resource development so that educators can identify the topics, skills and knowledge learners actually need. It states that "Learning needs assessment should be the starting point when designing eLearning resources for healthcare curricula", and argues teaching approaches should prioritise students' needs and preferences over those of educators, since students know which topics they struggle with and where multimedia interaction would help.

article_title: Leveraging E-Learning Infrastructure in Times of Rapid Change: Use of the National Sexually Transmitted Diseases Curriculum in the Era of COVID-19.
citation: Bauer KM, Corcorran MA, Budak JZ, Johnston C, Spach DH. (2021). Leveraging E-Learning Infrastructure in Times of Rapid Change: Use of the National Sexually Transmitted Diseases Curriculum in the Era of COVID-19. Sex Transm Dis. https://doi.org/10.1097/OLQ.0000000000001462
title: Leverage well-developed e-learning platforms to meet rapidly changing health professions training needs
description: The article's central design recommendation is that institutions maintain well-developed e-learning infrastructure that can be scaled up when in-person training is disrupted. The authors state that the surge in NSTDC use "points toward the importance and scalability of well-developed e-learning platforms to address rapidly changing educational needs across a variety of health care settings." Flexible designs offering both self-directed modules and quick access, plus group functionality with leader assignment, let existing platforms absorb displaced laboratory, rotation, and clinic training.
requirements: A well-developed e-learning platform already in place before the disruption
Flexible design allowing both self-directed modular learning and quick access to content
Group functionality allowing leaders to assign and monitor modules
constraints: Only 31% of new groups explicitly cited COVID-19 as their reason, and the authors note this is likely an underestimate because the question was optional and not systematically collected
The authors had not systematically evaluated how the NSTDC was used throughout the pandemic
target_learners: health care professionals
undergraduate and graduate health professions students
clinic staff
target_learning_goals: maintaining training continuity and competency development when in-person education is disrupted
examples: Undergraduate laboratory coursework groups, an adolescent medicine rotation, a pediatric residency rotation, and a clinic staff training group were run on the NSTDC during clinic and classroom closures

article_title: The implementation of a flipped classroom approach at a UK dental school.
citation: Binnie Rebecca S. L., Bonsor Stephen J. (2021). The implementation of a flipped classroom approach at a UK dental school. British Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41415-021-3125-6
title: Lecturette podcasts with slide attachments on the university VLE as pre-class flipped material
description: The redesigned ADM&B course replaced didactic lectures with short recorded 'lecturettes': "Mini lectures called 'lecturettes' were adapted from the previously available didactic lecture material, recorded and saved as a PowerPoint" presentation per theme. Each was recorded as a podcast by video capture using Panopto and made available on the university's virtual learning environment, with the session shown in the student calendar and the slide deck attached. Short length was chosen to make it "easier for the student to concentrate and be less likely to lose interest", and the modular format let shared topics such as impression materials serve several courses.
requirements: Students were expected to view the podcasts and slides before mandatory tutorials and practicals, as communicated verbally and in the course handbook
constraints: Significant preparation time was required to record the podcasts, plus a learning curve with the software and editing skills
target_learners: undergraduate dental students (BDS)
target_learning_goals: applied dental materials and biomaterials knowledge
examples: Common dental impression material lecturettes were reused across removable dentures and fixed prosthodontics courses

article_title: How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program.
citation: Bollipo Steven, Bilal Mohammad, Siau Keith, Charabaty Aline. (2020). How to Introduce Scopemanship Into Your Training Program. Gastroenterology. https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2020.08.013
title: Trainers should lead by example because trainees learn mainly through observation
description: The article holds that trainers and mentors should be role models for scopemanship through their actions, words, attitudes, and work philosophy, because "trainees learn mainly through observation." Trainers should empower trainees to keep the patient at the center of what they do and to focus on the quality and purpose of their work beyond acquiring technical skills and procedure counts, inspiring them to go the extra mile for patients, colleagues, and team members.
requirements: Trainers who themselves demonstrate scopemanship qualities in daily practice
target_learners: Endoscopy fellows and trainees observing their mentors
target_learning_goals: Professional attitudes, work ethic, and patient-centered practice
examples: The article frames inspirational trainers as remembered not only for knowledge but for an X-factor attribute it identifies with scopemanship

article_title: Case presentation methods: a randomized controlled trial of the one-minute preceptor versus SNAPPS in a controlled setting.
citation: Fagundes E. D. T., Ibiapina C. C., Alvim C. G., Fernandes R. A. F., Carvalho-Filho M. A., Brand P. L. P. (2020). Case presentation methods: a randomized controlled trial of the one-minute preceptor versus SNAPPS in a controlled setting. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-020-00588-y
title: Use learner-guided case presentation (SNAPPS) to foster an active learner role, reserving teacher-guided methods for less experienced learners
description: The article concludes that giving case-presentation instructions to learners rather than teachers helps students take on an active role: SNAPPS students initiated discussion about diagnosis and management significantly more often and spoke almost one minute longer, without extending the session. The authors note that when closer guidance is needed, OMP might be the preferable method to help less experienced students express their clinical reasoning, and that with progressive improvement of clinical competences, SNAPPS can help shape a more active role.
requirements: Learners must receive information about what is expected during case presentation: a summary of the case, presentation of the most likely diagnosis, a differential diagnosis and a management plan
constraints: Beginner students may have more difficulties managing different demands at the same time, such as gathering patient data, summarizing the case, elaborating the diagnosis and planning care
Evidence derives from written cases in a controlled setting
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical clerkships
less experienced students needing closer guidance
target_learning_goals: learner autonomy during case presentation
expression of clinical reasoning
engagement in the patient's care
examples: OMP students were more likely to wait for teachers to prompt them on their clinical reasoning, while SNAPPS students led the discussion

article_title: Testing a new active learning approach to advance motor learning knowledge and self-efficacy in physical therapy undergraduate education.
citation: Vaz DV, Ferreira EMR, Palma GB, Atun-Einy O, Kafri M, Ferreira FR. (2021). Testing a new active learning approach to advance motor learning knowledge and self-efficacy in physical therapy undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education 21:62. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02486-1
title: Learning by Doing: a personally meaningful direct-experience project for acquiring motor skills
description: An active learning methodology in which each student "chose a motor skill of their preference (e.g. dance styles, musical instruments, sports, circus skills, etc.) to acquire and practice for 10 weeks so that students experimented with ML strategies within their own experience." Students defined a performance goal, chose performance measures, practiced 3–8 h per week, kept a log, joined biweekly discussions, wrote a paper with recommendations for learning the skill, and demonstrated their skill level. The article reports this gave students firsthand experience putting ML theory into context and let them experience what patients experience.
requirements: A 10-week window with regular practice time (3–8 h per week) and biweekly structured reflection forms
A teacher role of offering timely feedback and opportunities for students to create personal, new knowledge rather than transmitting knowledge
constraints: The article states the differential effects of the experiential approach compared to an exclusively lecture-based version of the course must be tested
target_learners: undergraduate physical therapy students in early semesters without clinical placements
target_learning_goals: applying motor learning theory to personally meaningful skill acquisition
developing affective skills by experiencing learning as a patient would
examples: Students chose skills such as belly dance, guitar, slackline, juggling, calligraphy and typing; 132 biweekly forms were submitted and completion rates ranged from 100% to 89%

article_title: Usability of Learning Moment: Features of an E-learning Tool That Maximize Adoption by Students.

title: Learning Moment: a web-based experiential learning platform for documenting and sharing clinical learning moments
description: Learning Moment is a web-based application, built on Kolb's experiential learning cycle, asynchronous learning, and learning portfolios, in which students record self-identified "learning moments" and their take-away "learning pearls." Entries form a searchable, shareable repository for vicarious learning through a Community Feed; a three-member faculty panel reviews entries, and faculty lead monthly in-person reflection small groups.

Monthly in-person Learning Moment Reflection small groups led by experienced clinical faculty
constraints: Participation by students was entirely voluntary and did not affect their grade or evaluations
target_learners: third and fourth year medical students on emergency medicine clerkships
physician assistant students on rotation
target_learning_goals: reflection and abstract conceptualization during clinical rotations
sharing and vicarious learning of practical clinical pearls
examples: Students introduced to LM during rotation orientation logged learning moments voluntarily at an urban tertiary care emergency department
Experienced clinical faculty led monthly in-person Learning Moment Reflection small groups discussing moments logged during rotations

article_title: Effect of project-based experiential learning on the health service delivery indicators: a quasi-experiment study.
citation: Chelagat T., Kokwaro G., Onyango J., Rice J. (2020). Effect of project-based experiential learning on the health service delivery indicators: a quasi-experiment study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-020-4949-5

target_learning_goals: Applying leadership and management practices to resolve persistent health service delivery challenges
examples: The LeHHO program implemented in 6 cycles between 2010 and 2016 trained 165 leaders who undertook 69 institutional improvement projects across 39 health facilities in 19 counties.

The article describes it as "a learner-centered dialogue that stimulates reflection by allowing the learner to identify and explore issues of particular interest." article_title: An educational study to investigate the efficacy of three training methods for infiltration techniques on self-efficacy and skills of trainees in general practice.
citation: Michels Nele R., Vanhomwegen Els. (2019). An educational study to investigate the efficacy of three training methods for infiltration techniques on self-efficacy and skills of trainees in general practice. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-019-1023-7
title: Combine a theoretical lecture with practical training on cadavers (or anatomical models) to teach infiltration techniques, and add refresher courses for long-term effect
description: The article's evidence-based advice to teaching organizations is that all three studied strategies work, but combining theoretical knowledge with practical training—especially on cadavers—yields better skill performance. Based on their results the authors "suggest the combination of a theoretical lecture with a training on cadavers to teach infiltration techniques", and note that "To achieve an optimal long-term effect, additional refresher trainings may be necessary". The preferred method also depends on costs and practical feasibility.
requirements: Both anatomical-model and cadaver training require surveillance and assistance of an experienced physician.
A theoretical lecture must be available as a PowerPoint presentation trainees can peruse at their own pace.
constraints: For the carpal tunnel and knee joint infiltrations, anatomical models seemed to work better than cadavers for proficient, systematic and complete performance.
Costs and feasibility of the three strategies were not considered in the study; cadaver supply may be limited by body donation shortage.
Sample size was too small for some conclusions and participants and observers were not blinded.
target_learners: General practice trainees in postgraduate training
target_learning_goals: Performing intra- and periarticular infiltration techniques of the glenohumeral joint, subacromial region, lateral epicondyle, carpal tunnel and knee joint
examples: 48 trainees were randomized into a theoretical lecture group, a lecture plus anatomical-models group and a lecture plus cadavers group; the cadaver group practiced on a fixated corpse in prone position and a fresh-frozen leg.
key_sources: Michels Nele R., Vanhomwegen Els. (2019). An educational study to investigate the efficacy of three training methods for infiltration techniques on self-efficacy and skills of trainees in general practice. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-019-1023-7

title: Learning How to Ask one-day training on trauma inquiry and response
