Basic rules are "discussed and practiced in role-plays", and participants reflect on their current routine practice and barriers. A 1.5-hour refresher was conducted 3 months later, delivered by an experienced psychiatrist and/or graduated psychologist in groups of 5 to 16 professionals.

constraints: The article states the training cannot remove structural barriers to trauma-specific treatment, which need changes in the health care system

adequate response to reports of traumatic events
documentation of traumatic events
knowledge of trauma-related resources
examples: In the trial, trainings were conducted at the university medical center or on-site at SUD centers, with a short 1.5-h refresher 3 months later

article_title: Paracentesis Simulation: A Comprehensive Approach to Procedural Education.
citation: Sall D, Wigger GW, Kinnear B, Kelleher M, Warm E, O'Toole JK. (2018). Paracentesis Simulation: A Comprehensive Approach to Procedural Education. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10747
title: The 'learn, see, practice, prove, do, maintain' model as a pedagogical framework for procedural skill training
description: The curriculum is structured around the 'learn, see, practice, prove, do, maintain' model (attributed to Sawyer and colleagues), which sequences procedural education through six phases: learners "completed online comprehensive preprocedural education modules and assessments on paracentesis and ultrasound (learn), viewed a video of the procedure properly performed (see), practiced the procedure in a simulation laboratory with faculty guidance and deliberate practice (practice), and were assessed completing the simulated procedure (prove)". Once a competence standard is demonstrated, learners perform live procedures under supervision (do), then return to simulation and case reviews at intervals (maintain). The authors state this model "creates a more systematic and reliable way to teach procedural skills in order to ensure competency" and organize the article's curriculum phases end to end.
requirements: Phase progression gated by demonstrated minimum competence before live supervised performance
constraints: Applied here to a single bedside procedure with resident learners; the article presents it as a framework the authors followed rather than a tested comparison
target_learners: Internal medicine and medicine-pediatric residents of all training years
target_learning_goals: Systematic acquisition and maintenance of invasive bedside procedural skills
examples: Each model phase maps onto a curriculum component: online modules and quizzes (learn), video (see), assisted simulation practice (practice), PCAT-evaluated unassisted attempt (prove), supervised live paracentesis (do), and 3–6-month return sessions plus case conferences (maintain)
key_sources: Sall D, Wigger GW, Kinnear B, Kelleher M, Warm E, O'Toole JK. (2018). Paracentesis Simulation: A Comprehensive Approach to Procedural Education. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10747

article_title: Teacher Knowledge for Active-Learning Instruction: Expert-Novice Comparison Reveals Differences.
citation: Auerbach A. J., Higgins M., Brickman P., Andrews T. C. (2018). Teacher Knowledge for Active-Learning Instruction: Expert–Novice Comparison Reveals Differences. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-07-0149
title: Lesson-analysis survey instrument for eliciting teacher noticing of active-learning instruction
description: A survey instrument modeled after K–12 teacher-noticing instruments, using videos of authentic active-learning lessons in large (50+ student) undergraduate biology courses as stimuli followed by writing prompts asking participants to evaluate the lesson and suggest improvements. It was iteratively refined with instructor responses and expert feedback, and paired with Section 3 of the Teaching Practices Inventory and professional-experience questions.
requirements: Videos of authentic lessons no more than 5 minutes long
Written prompts asking what was effective and what needs improvement, with reasons
constraints: The TPI section relies on instructors to accurately self-report their teaching
target_learners: Undergraduate biology instructors using active learning in large courses
target_learning_goals: Eliciting and assessing teacher knowledge for active-learning instruction
examples: The final version included three videos; after the first two, instructors answered two written prompts, and after the third, one prompt
key_sources: Auerbach A. J., Higgins M., Brickman P., Andrews T. C. (2018). Teacher Knowledge for Active-Learning Instruction: Expert–Novice Comparison Reveals Differences. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-07-0149

article_title: Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences.
citation: Van der Wath, A.E. & Du Toit, P.H., 2015, 'Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences', Curationis 38(2), Art. #1537. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v38i2.1537
title: LEARN-guided written reflection after each learning opportunity
description: The LEARN layout is a structured written-reflection framework the module used to facilitate deep self-reflection: "students were requested to write a reflection during each learning opportunity, using a layout based on the acronym, LEARN". Its steps move from looking back on the situation, through examining detail and analysing influences and values, to revising future actions and adopting a new perspective. The resulting reflections served as the study's qualitative data.
requirements: A written reflection completed after each learning opportunity, following the Look back, Examine, Analyse, Revise, New perspective steps
target_learners: second-year undergraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: self-reflection on experiences of learning end-of-life care
examples: Sixty-two of the sixty-four students voluntarily handed in written reflections guided by the LEARN layout, which were analysed by open coding until data saturation
key_sources: Van der Wath, A.E. & Du Toit, P.H., 2015, 'Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences', Curationis 38(2), Art. #1537. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v38i2.1537

article_title: Fighting adult illiteracy with the help of the environmental print material.
citation: Iqbal Tassawar, Iqbal Saqib, Hussain Syed Sajid, Khan Iftikhar Ahmed, Khan Hikmat Ullah, Rehman Attiqa. (2018). Fighting adult illiteracy with the help of the environmental print material. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0201902
title: Learner-driven, situated design guidelines for adult basic education content
description: The article organizes prior literature into guidelines for designing and delivering learning content for adult non-literates. Content-design features are multimodality, building on previous knowledge and past experiences, and contextualized learning, where "learning is embedded within an activity, context, and culture" (situated learning theory). Delivery features are facilitated learning, repetition of content, and frequent feedback with positive reinforcement, drawing on Keller's motivational design model (attention, relevance, confidence, satisfaction). The article maps the selected EPM content onto these features.
requirements: Learning content must be relevant to the learners' background, culture, interests, and preferences
constraints: The article notes there are no standards to design learning content for adult learners, only proposed guidelines
target_learners: adult non-literate learners in adult basic education programs
target_learning_goals: basic literacy skills: alphabet-letter recognition, pronunciation, reading, writing, and counting
examples: The authors selected EPM content via two ethnographic studies and mapped its characteristics onto the Table 1 design features before building the CAL applications
key_sources: Iqbal Tassawar, Iqbal Saqib, Hussain Syed Sajid, Khan Iftikhar Ahmed, Khan Hikmat Ullah, Rehman Attiqa. (2018). Fighting adult illiteracy with the help of the environmental print material. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0201902

article_title: Advancing clinical reasoning in virtual patients - development and application of a conceptual framework.
citation: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Berman Norman B., Lenzer Benedikt, Kiesewetter Jan. (2018). Advancing clinical reasoning in virtual patients – development and application of a conceptual framework. GMS Journal for Medical Education 35(1):Doc12. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2018-35/zma001159.shtml
title: Framework of learning clinical reasoning organized around five main categories with related concepts and interrelations
description: The framework integrates the learning of clinical reasoning under a core category, the "multifactorial nature of learning clinical reasoning", with five main categories tied to main actors: Learner-centeredness (learner), Patient-centeredness (patient), Psychological Theories (researcher), Teaching/Assessment (teacher), and Context (healthcare professional). Each category contains four to six concepts, such as dual processing, knowledge encapsulation, illness scripts, metacognition, adaptability, learning analytics, errors and biases, management decisions, time, and the balance between authenticity and cognitive load. The authors apply the framework to virtual patients to derive improvement recommendations and state it is "also applicable when developing or advancing clinical reasoning curricula or faculty development courses".
requirements: Derived via grounded theory from coded data sources and reviewed with an interdisciplinary expert panel of two healthcare educators, two healthcare professionals, two healthcare education researchers, an undergraduate medical student, and a computer scientist
constraints: The authors acknowledge it "is fairly complex" and that the study sample was relatively small and excluded the patient perspective
target_learners: Healthcare students, especially medical students
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning skill acquisition, including diagnosis and management planning
examples: Applied to VP analysis: most VPs implicitly include illness-script components such as a problem list, differential diagnoses or a final diagnosis; VPs provide a safe environment for learning from errors.
key_sources: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Berman Norman B., Lenzer Benedikt, Kiesewetter Jan. (2018). Advancing clinical reasoning in virtual patients – development and application of a conceptual framework. GMS Journal for Medical Education 35(1):Doc12. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2018-35/zma001159.shtml

article_title: E-learning or educational leaflet: does it make a difference in oral health promotion? A clustered randomized trial.
citation: Al Bardaweel Susan, Dashash Mayssoon. (2018). E-learning or educational leaflet: does it make a difference in oral health promotion? A clustered randomized trial. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-018-0540-4
title: Use printed educational leaflets as the delivery tool for school-based oral health education where digital access is unreliable
description: The article concludes that traditional educational leaflets are an effective and economical tool for improving oral health knowledge and clinical oral hygiene indices among children, and that "Leaflets can be used in school-based oral health education for a positive outcome". Leaflets reached children regardless of dental visit frequency, socioeconomic status, home computer ownership and internet access, making them suited to settings where electronic delivery faces technical barriers.
requirements: Leaflet content should be engaging and age-appropriate, as the trial's story-format leaflet was designed "with particular emphasis on creating interest amongst the children"
constraints: Evidence is short-term (12 weeks) and from one small geographic area; the authors call for longitudinal and multicenter validation
target_learners: primary schoolchildren
target_learning_goals: oral health knowledge
oral hygiene and gingival health behaviors
examples: In the cluster-randomized trial, leaflet recipients outperformed the E-learning cluster on knowledge, plaque index and gingival index at both follow-ups
key_sources: Al Bardaweel Susan, Dashash Mayssoon. (2018). E-learning or educational leaflet: does it make a difference in oral health promotion? A clustered randomized trial. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-018-0540-4

article_title: An integrative review of e-learning in the delivery of self-management support training for health professionals.
citation: Lawn Sharon, Zhi Xiaojuan, Morello Andrea. (2017). An integrative review of e-learning in the delivery of self-management support training for health professionals. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1022-0
title: LeRoy et al. multimedia library of action-oriented SMS resources with three companion videos
description: An element reported in the review: LeRoy et al. developed "a multimedia library of action-oriented SMS resources and 3 companion videos illuminating SMS skills and concepts", illustrating what SMS is, why it is important and how to provide it clinically. Development began with an environmental scan involving a technical expert panel of 10 clinicians; the scan found 17% of SMS resources were interactive and 13% were videos, with most being print materials. When clinicians tested the videos, they suggested adding more images of patient interactions and improving interactivity.
requirements: Clinician expert panel review and clinician feedback during development, as in the environmental scan process
constraints: The review notes a need for translating tools into languages other than English and Spanish, customising tools for specific ethnic groups, and creating materials for non-physician providers and staff
target_learners: Clinicians serving populations with chronic disease across healthcare
target_learning_goals: Understanding and delivering patient self-management support, including agenda setting, goal setting, action plans, problem-solving and follow-up
examples: Videos were tested by being shown at the Annual AHRQ Conference, USA, and by 12 clinicians who voluntarily viewed them and completed short self-administered feedback forms
key_sources: Lawn Sharon, Zhi Xiaojuan, Morello Andrea. (2017). An integrative review of e-learning in the delivery of self-management support training for health professionals. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1022-0

article_title: Ethnic and social disparities in different types of examinations in undergraduate pre-clinical training.
citation: Stegers-Jager K. M., Brommet F. N., Themmen A. P. N. (2016). Ethnic and social disparities in different types of examinations in undergraduate pre-clinical training. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-016-9676-7
title: Design assessment strategies that create a level playing field for diverse student populations
description: The article concludes that medical schools facing increasingly diverse student populations should design assessment strategies that avoid disadvantaging non-traditional students. It states medical schools "should ensure their assessment strategies create a level playing field for all students" and that diversity should be considered "both in test construction and implementation". This includes balancing competency assessment with retaining a diverse student population, in analogy to the validity-diversity dilemma.
requirements: Assessment strategies must fulfil the goal of assessing required standards of competency while retaining a diverse student population
constraints: The article notes data on disparities do not reveal whether they result from bias or actual skill differences, and recommends differential predictive validity and differential item functioning analyses to examine bias
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students, including ethnic minority and first-generation university students
target_learning_goals: Valid assessment of required competencies for all student groups
examples: The study examined pass/fail disparities across six cohorts on CPSTs, block tests, a language test, writing tests and OSCEs, showing which examination types disadvantage which groups
key_sources: Stegers-Jager K. M., Brommet F. N., Themmen A. P. N. (2016). Ethnic and social disparities in different types of examinations in undergraduate pre-clinical training. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-016-9676-7

article_title: Capturing judgement strategies in risk assessments with improved quality of clinical information: How nurses' strategies differ from the ecological model.
citation: Yang Huiqin, Thompson Carl. (2016). Capturing judgement strategies in risk assessments with improved quality of clinical information: How nurses’ strategies differ from the ecological model. BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-016-0243-1
title: Lens Model of judgement analysis for capturing clinical judgement policies
description: The article applies the Lens Model of cognition, based on Brunswik's probabilistic functionalism, to characterise nurses' risk judgements as a relationship between judgement and environmental information (the ecology). It distinguishes "ecological validity" (cue–criterion correlations), "cue utilisation validity" (cue–judgement correlations) and "achievement" (judgement–criterion accuracy), and compares nurses' cue weights with the ecological model's optimal weights to diagnose suboptimal judgement strategies.
requirements: Requires a set of judgement tasks with cues whose ecological validities can be estimated from real outcome criteria, and enough tasks to handle cue intercorrelations
constraints: The article notes high cue intercorrelations from vicarious functioning challenge analysis of relative cue importance and require a large number of judgement tasks, which is practically limiting
target_learners: student nurses
experienced registered nurses
target_learning_goals: risk assessment of acute patient deterioration
calibration of clinical cue weighting
examples: Five NICE-recommended cues were used to build 25 scenarios sampled from 673 real patient cases, with ecological criteria defined as ICU admission, CPR or death
key_sources: Yang Huiqin, Thompson Carl. (2016). Capturing judgement strategies in risk assessments with improved quality of clinical information: How nurses’ strategies differ from the ecological model. BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-016-0243-1

article_title: 'I wouldn't get that feedback from anywhere else': learning partnerships and the use of high school students as simulated patients to enhance medical students' communication skills.
citation: Cahill Helen, Coffey Julia, Sanci Lena. (2015). ‘I wouldn’t get that feedback from anywhere else’: learning partnerships and the use of high school students as simulated patients to enhance medical students’ communication skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0315-4
title: Learning Partnerships workshop: high school students as simulated patients and communication coaches for medical student HEEADSSS screening practice
description: Learning Partnerships is a two-hour communication-training workshop in which fifth-year medical students in groups of 20–25 work with around 25 adolescent students aged 15–16. Medical students play the family physician and "use the HEEADSSS psychosocial screening tool to practice asking questions about the simulated patient’s home, education, eating, activities, drug and alcohol use, sexual activity and safety". School students play a fictional character, Jo, acting as simulated patients and as coaches giving formative feedback; simulations are interrupted at each screening phase for coaching, with additional fishbowl demonstrations of key skills such as making the confidentiality statement and using non-judgemental smorgasbord questions.
requirements: Sessions are co-facilitated by a classroom teacher and a medical educator using a detailed agenda; classroom teachers prepare school students in about 3–5 lessons in authentic portrayal and feedback techniques
constraints: The program has run in the University of Melbourne undergraduate medical curriculum since 2003, with workshops placed in the school during scheduled class time within a subject home such as Drama or English
target_learners: Fifth-year medical students
High school students aged 15–16
target_learning_goals: Communication and screening skills with adolescents about sensitive health issues
Adolescent preparedness and confidence to seek help from doctors
examples: Medical students played the family physician using the HEEADSSS tool with the fictional character Jo; simulations were interrupted at each phase so school students could coach and give feedback, with fishbowl demonstrations of confidentiality statements and normalising questions
key_sources: Cahill Helen, Coffey Julia, Sanci Lena. (2015). ‘I wouldn’t get that feedback from anywhere else’: learning partnerships and the use of high school students as simulated patients to enhance medical students’ communication skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0315-4
